The Sauternes appellation covers five communes: Sauternes, Bommes, Fargues, Preignac and Barsac. Barsac also has its own appellation, and its wines may be labelled either Barsac or Sauternes. Good examples taste of honey, apricot and marmalade, with acidity that keeps them fresh for decades.

The 1855 Classification also ranked the sweet white wines of Sauternes and Barsac. Château d'Yquem, in Sauternes, stands alone as Premier Cru Supérieur. Below it come the Premiers Crus and then the Deuxièmes Crus.

sections.h: Other sweet wines of the Garonne
p: Cérons, inside the Graves just north of Barsac, makes sweet white wine in a similar way. Across the Garonne, on its right bank, Cadillac, Loupiac and Sainte-Croix-du-Mont also make sweet whites from Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc and Muscadelle. They face Sauternes across the river and are usually lighter and less concentrated.

key: The Graves is named after its gravel and makes both red and dry white wines.
Pessac-Léognan, the northern Graves, became an appellation in 1987.
The Graves Classification (1953, revised 1959) has one rank, Cru Classé de Graves, for red, white or both.
Haut-Brion is in both the 1855 and the Graves classifications.
In Sauternes, mist from the cool Ciron meeting the Garonne encourages noble rot; grapes are picked in several tries.
In the 1855 sweet wine ranking, Château d'Yquem is the only Premier Cru Supérieur.

questions.q: When was the Pessac-Léognan appellation created?
questions.explain: Pessac-Léognan was carved out of the northern Graves in 1987. 1953 and 1959 are the dates of the Graves Classification.

questions.q: How many ranks does the Graves Classification have?
options: Two: Premier Cru and Deuxième Cru
questions.explain: The Graves Classification has a single rank. Each château is listed for its red, its white or both.

questions.q: Which estate appears in both the 1855 Classification and the Graves Classification?
questions.explain: Haut-Brion, in Pessac, was ranked a first growth in 1855 and is also a Cru Classé de Graves.

questions.q: What local feature encourages noble rot in Sauternes?
options: Morning mists where the cool Ciron meets the warmer Garonne
Heavy summer rain from the Atlantic
questions.explain: The cool Ciron meeting the warmer Garonne creates autumn morning mist; dry afternoons then let botrytis develop in its noble form.

questions.q: Why is Sémillon the main grape of Sauternes?
options: It ripens latest of all Bordeaux grapes
It is the only white grape allowed
Its thin skin makes it prone to noble rot
It has the highest natural acidity
questions.explain: Sémillon's thin skin lets botrytis take hold. Sauvignon Blanc is added for acidity and freshness.

questions.q: In Sauternes, what are 'tries'?
options: Successive passes through the vineyard to pick only botrytised grapes
Tasting panels that approve each vintage
questions.explain: Because noble rot spreads unevenly, pickers make several passes, called tries, to harvest only affected grapes.

questions.q: How may a sweet wine from Barsac be labelled?
questions.explain: Barsac is one of the five communes of Sauternes and also has its own appellation, so producers may use either name.

questions.q: Which sweet wine appellations face Sauternes from the right bank of the Garonne?
questions.explain: Cadillac, Loupiac and Sainte-Croix-du-Mont lie across the Garonne from Sauternes. Cérons is on the same side as Sauternes.

lessons.title: The Right Bank: Saint-Émilion, Pomerol and Fronsac
lessons.intro: This lesson crosses the Dordogne to the Libournais, where Merlot and Cabernet Franc grow on clay and limestone. It covers Saint-Émilion and its classification, Pomerol, Fronsac, the satellites and the other Right Bank areas.

sections.h: Merlot and Cabernet Franc on clay and limestone
p: The Libournais is named after Libourne, the river port where the Isle joins the Dordogne. Its soils hold more clay and limestone than the Médoc gravels. Clay stays cool and holds water, which suits early-ripening Merlot. Cabernet Franc, known locally as Bouchet, does well on limestone and gives freshness and fragrance.

Cabernet Sauvignon plays a small role here, because it ripens late and struggles on cool soils. Right Bank reds are therefore Merlot-led blends, often softer and rounder in their youth than Left Bank reds.

sections.h: Saint-Émilion: town, soils and two appellations
p: Saint-Émilion is a medieval hill town whose surrounding jurisdiction is a UNESCO World Heritage site. Around the town lies a limestone plateau, edged by steep clay-limestone slopes called the côtes. Below are sandier soils towards the Dordogne, and in the north-west, by the Pomerol border, a zone of gravel.

Two appellations share the same area. Saint-Émilion AOC is the basic one. Saint-Émilion Grand Cru AOC has stricter rules, such as lower maximum yields. 'Grand Cru' on its own is therefore an appellation, not a rank. Across the Barbanne stream to the north lie four satellites: Montagne, Lussac, Puisseguin and Saint-Georges.

Saint-Émilion has its own classification, first published in 1955 and intended to be revised about every ten years. Only wines of the Saint-Émilion Grand Cru appellation can be classified. There are three ranks: Premier Grand Cru Classé A, Premier Grand Cru Classé B and Grand Cru Classé. Châteaux apply and are judged on tastings of several vintages and on other criteria.

Because the list is revised, estates can be promoted or demoted, and some have chosen to leave the classification. Results have been challenged in court more than once. The list of châteaux in each rank changes, so always check the current edition instead of learning a fixed list.

Pomerol is a small, gently sloping plateau north-east of Libourne, bordering Saint-Émilion. Its soils mix gravel, sand and clay, and at the highest point a dense clay subsoil underlies the most famous estate, Petrus. Merlot dominates, giving rich, plush wines. Estates are small and often lack the grand château buildings of the Médoc.

Pomerol has no official classification. Prestige rests on reputation and price alone. The appellation is for red wine only. Lalande-de-Pomerol lies just north, across the Barbanne stream, and makes similar Merlot-based reds.

sections.h: Fronsac and the wider Right Bank
p: Fronsac lies west of Libourne, on hills of clay and limestone above the Dordogne and the Isle. Canon Fronsac is a smaller appellation within it, on the slopes. Both make Merlot-led reds, often firmer than those of Pomerol.

Further downstream, Bourg and Blaye face the Médoc across the Gironde and make mainly Merlot-based reds. East of Saint-Émilion, Castillon and Francs are part of the Côtes de Bordeaux, on similar clay and limestone.

key: Right Bank reds are led by Merlot, with Cabernet Franc (Bouchet); cool clay suits Merlot.
Saint-Émilion and Saint-Émilion Grand Cru are two appellations over the same area; Grand Cru has stricter rules.
The Saint-Émilion classification (first 1955) applies only to Grand Cru wines and is revised periodically.
Its three ranks are Premier Grand Cru Classé A, Premier Grand Cru Classé B and Grand Cru Classé.
Pomerol has no official classification; its wines are Merlot-dominated and red only.
Montagne, Lussac, Puisseguin and Saint-Georges are the Saint-Émilion satellites north of the Barbanne.

questions.q: Why does Merlot dominate on the Right Bank?
options: It is the only red grape allowed there
It ripens early and suits the cool, water-retentive clay soils
It needs hot gravel to ripen
It resists noble rot better than other grapes
questions.explain: Merlot ripens early and thrives on cool clay, where late-ripening Cabernet Sauvignon struggles.

questions.q: What is the local name for Cabernet Franc in Saint-Émilion?
questions.explain: Cabernet Franc is called Bouchet on the Right Bank. Côt and Auxerrois are names for Malbec, Mansois for Fer Servadou.

questions.q: A label reads 'Saint-Émilion Grand Cru'. What does this tell you?
options: The wine comes from the Saint-Émilion Grand Cru appellation, which has stricter rules
The château is a Premier Grand Cru Classé A
The wine is from the Pomerol border gravels
The château is in the 1855 Classification
questions.explain: Saint-Émilion Grand Cru is an appellation. Only a 'Grand Cru Classé' or 'Premier Grand Cru Classé' is ranked in the classification.

questions.q: Which wines are eligible for the Saint-Émilion classification?
options: Wines from the four satellite appellations
Wines of the Saint-Émilion AOC only
Wines of the Saint-Émilion Grand Cru appellation only
questions.explain: Only châteaux producing Saint-Émilion Grand Cru can be classified.

questions.q: What is the top rank of the Saint-Émilion classification?
questions.explain: The ranks are Premier Grand Cru Classé A, then B, then Grand Cru Classé. Premier Cru Supérieur is Château d'Yquem's rank in 1855.

questions.q: How are the leading estates of Pomerol officially classified?
options: They are not: Pomerol has no official classification
questions.explain: Pomerol has never had an official classification. Its reputation rests on the wines and their prices.

questions.q: Which stream separates Saint-Émilion and Pomerol from their northern neighbours such as Montagne and Lalande-de-Pomerol?
questions.explain: The Barbanne stream runs to the north, with the Saint-Émilion satellites and Lalande-de-Pomerol beyond it.

questions.q: Where is Fronsac?
options: On the Left Bank, south of Margaux
Inside the Graves, next to Pessac
Across the Gironde from the Médoc, next to Blaye
West of Libourne, on clay-limestone hills above the Dordogne and the Isle
questions.explain: Fronsac and Canon Fronsac sit on hills west of Libourne, where the Isle meets the Dordogne.

lessons.title: The South-West
lessons.intro: This lesson covers the South-West (Sud-Ouest), the scattered vineyards between Bordeaux and the Pyrenees. Some use Bordeaux grapes, others local ones such as Malbec, Tannat and the Mansengs. Key areas are Bergerac and Monbazillac, Cahors, Madiran and Jurançon.

p: The South-West is not one block but a set of separate vineyard areas along the rivers that flow towards Bordeaux, and in the foothills of the Pyrenees. For centuries these upriver wines had to wait until Bordeaux had sold its own before they could be shipped from its port, which held back their trade.

Close to Bordeaux, in Bergerac, Côtes de Duras, Côtes du Marmandais and Buzet, the grapes are mainly the Bordeaux varieties. Further inland and south, local grapes take over: Malbec in Cahors, Tannat in Madiran, Négrette in Fronton, Fer Servadou in Marcillac and Gaillac, and Gros and Petit Manseng in Jurançon.

Bergerac lies on the Dordogne, upstream of Saint-Émilion. It makes red, rosé and white wines from Bordeaux varieties. Côtes de Bergerac has stricter rules. Pécharmant, on slopes north-east of the town, makes reds, and Rosette makes lightly sweet whites. In Montravel, to the west, Montravel is known for dry whites, while Côtes de Montravel and Haut-Montravel make sweet ones.

Monbazillac lies on the south bank of the Dordogne opposite Bergerac. It makes sweet white wine from Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc and Muscadelle, concentrated by noble rot as in Sauternes. Saussignac, to the west, also makes sweet whites.

Cahors lies in the valley of the Lot. Its red wines must contain at least 70% Malbec, known locally as Côt or Auxerrois, with Merlot and Tannat making up the rest. Vines grow on terraces along the river and on the limestone plateau (causse) above. Cahors was long called the 'black wine' for its deep colour. The appellation is for red wine only.

Further east, Gaillac on the Tarn uses local grapes such as Mauzac, Len de l'El, Braucol (Fer Servadou) and Duras, in many styles including sparkling wine made by the méthode ancestrale. Fronton, north of Toulouse, is based on Négrette. Marcillac makes reds mostly from Fer Servadou, called Mansois there.

Madiran, in Gascony, makes red wine based on Tannat, a grape with very high tannin and deep colour. It is often blended with Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon or Fer. Young Madiran can be hard, and the technique of micro-oxygenation was developed here in the 1990s to soften its tannins.

Pacherenc du Vic-Bilh covers the same area for white wines, dry or sweet, from Gros Manseng, Petit Manseng, Petit Courbu and Arrufiac. Saint-Mont, next door, also uses Tannat. In the French Basque Country, Irouléguy makes mostly Tannat-based reds on steep mountain slopes.

Jurançon lies in the Pyrenean foothills near Pau. Its grapes are Petit Manseng and Gros Manseng. Sweet Jurançon is mostly made by passerillage: grapes are left on the vine late into autumn, where dry, sunny weather shrivels them and concentrates sugar. Noble rot is not the main method. Petit Manseng, with small, thick-skinned berries, suits this well.
The Mansengs keep high acidity, so sweet Jurançon tastes fresh and lively, with flavours of tropical fruit and spice. Jurançon sec is the dry version, usually led by Gros Manseng.

key: Bergerac, Côtes de Duras, Côtes du Marmandais and Buzet mainly use the Bordeaux grape varieties.
Monbazillac, opposite Bergerac on the Dordogne, makes sweet white wine from noble-rotted grapes.
Cahors reds must contain at least 70% Malbec (Côt, Auxerrois), with Merlot and Tannat.
Madiran is based on Tannat; micro-oxygenation was developed there to soften its tannins.
Sweet Jurançon is made mainly by passerillage of Petit and Gros Manseng, not by noble rot.
Pacherenc du Vic-Bilh is the white wine (dry or sweet) of the Madiran area.

questions.q: What is the minimum share of Malbec in a Cahors red?
questions.explain: Cahors must contain at least 70% Malbec, with Merlot and Tannat allowed for the rest.

questions.q: Which grape is the basis of Madiran?
questions.explain: Madiran is built on Tannat, a deeply coloured and very tannic variety.

questions.q: How is sweet Jurançon mainly made?
options: By passerillage: grapes shrivel on the vine in dry autumn weather
By noble rot encouraged by river mists
By adding grape spirit during fermentation
By freezing the grapes on the vine
questions.explain: Jurançon relies mostly on passerillage, the drying of late-harvested Manseng grapes on the vine, rather than on botrytis.

questions.q: Which appellation lies opposite Bergerac and makes sweet whites from noble-rotted grapes?
questions.explain: Monbazillac, on the south bank of the Dordogne, makes botrytised sweet whites from Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc and Muscadelle.

questions.q: Which appellation makes the white wines, dry or sweet, of the Madiran area?
questions.explain: Pacherenc du Vic-Bilh covers the same zone as Madiran but for whites from the Mansengs, Petit Courbu and Arrufiac.

questions.q: What technique was developed in Madiran in the 1990s to soften Tannat?
questions.explain: Micro-oxygenation, the controlled addition of small amounts of oxygen, was developed in Madiran to tame Tannat's tannins.

questions.q: Which grapes are used in Bergerac?
questions.explain: Bergerac, on the Dordogne upstream of Saint-Émilion, uses Merlot, the Cabernets, Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc and the other Bordeaux grapes.

questions.q: Fronton, north of Toulouse, is known for which local red grape?
questions.explain: Fronton is based on Négrette. Mansois is Fer Servadou in Marcillac, and Len de l'El is a white grape of Gaillac.

lessons.title: Champagne: region and grapes
lessons.intro: This lesson covers where Champagne is, why its cool climate and chalk matter, the four main districts and the grapes grown in each. It also explains the village classification and the codes that tell you who made the wine.

p: Champagne lies east of Paris, around the towns of Reims and Épernay. Most vineyards are in the Marne department, with the Aube to the south and smaller areas in the Aisne and elsewhere. It is one of the most northerly quality wine regions of France.

The climate is cool, with both oceanic and continental influences. Grapes ripen slowly and keep high acidity, which suits sparkling wine. Spring frost, hail and rain at harvest are regular risks, so quality and quantity vary from year to year. Blending across villages, grapes and vintages evens out these differences.

Much of the Marne sits on chalk. Chalk drains well but is porous: it holds water and releases it to the vine roots in dry spells. The purest form, belemnite chalk, lies under many of the best slopes. The chalk also allowed the digging of the deep cellars, called crayères, where wine ages at a cool, steady temperature.

Not all of Champagne is chalk. The Vallée de la Marne has more clay, marl and sand. The Côte des Bar in the Aube sits on Kimmeridgian marl, the same soil as Chablis, which lies closer to it than Reims does.

The Montagne de Reims is a wooded plateau between Reims and Épernay. Its slopes face many directions, some even north, as at Verzenay. Pinot Noir dominates and gives structure and body. The Vallée de la Marne runs west from Épernay. Its cooler, frost-prone valley sites are planted mainly with Meunier, though Aÿ at its eastern end is famous for Pinot Noir.

The Côte des Blancs is an east-facing slope south of Épernay, planted almost entirely with Chardonnay. Villages such as Cramant, Avize, Oger and Le Mesnil-sur-Oger give fine, long-lived wines. The Côte des Bar, far to the south in the Aube, is mostly Pinot Noir and gives riper, fruitier wines.

Seven grapes are allowed, but three make almost all Champagne. Pinot Noir brings body, red fruit and structure. Meunier buds late and ripens early, so it avoids spring frost and suits cool, low-lying sites. It gives fruity, supple wines that are ready sooner. Chardonnay brings finesse, citrus, high acidity and long ageing.

The four minor grapes are Pinot Blanc, Pinot Gris, Arbane and Petit Meslier. They are rare but some producers use them in special cuvées. A disease-resistant variety, Voltis, is now also allowed in small amounts under a trial scheme. Grapes must be picked as whole bunches, which in practice means by hand, so black grapes can give clear juice.

Champagne ranks whole villages, not single vineyards. Under the échelle des crus, each village had a percentage that once set the price of its grapes. That price system has ended, but the terms remain: 17 villages are grand cru, such as Ambonnay, Bouzy, Aÿ, Avize and Cramant, and a larger group are premier cru.

Labels carry a code for the type of producer. NM (négociant manipulant) is a house that buys grapes, as most large houses do. RM (récoltant manipulant) is a grower who makes wine only from their own vineyards. CM (coopérative de manipulation) is a cooperative. Champagne received its AOC in 1936.

key: Champagne is cool and marginal: high acidity, variable vintages, and blending to even them out.
Chalk drains well yet stores water; the Côte des Bar has Kimmeridgian marl like Chablis.
Montagne de Reims: Pinot Noir. Vallée de la Marne: Meunier. Côte des Blancs: Chardonnay. Côte des Bar (Aube): Pinot Noir.
Seven traditional grapes are allowed; Pinot Noir, Meunier and Chardonnay dominate. Whole-bunch picking means hand harvesting.
17 villages are grand cru under the échelle des crus.
NM is a house that buys grapes, RM a grower using only its own fruit, CM a cooperative.

questions.q: Which grape is planted most widely in the Vallée de la Marne?
questions.explain: Meunier dominates the Vallée de la Marne because it buds late and ripens early, which suits the cooler, frost-prone valley sites.

questions.q: What soil is typical of the Côte des Bar?
questions.explain: The Côte des Bar in the Aube sits on Kimmeridgian marl, the same soil as nearby Chablis, rather than the chalk of the Marne.

questions.q: Which grape is planted almost exclusively on the Côte des Blancs?
questions.explain: The Côte des Blancs takes its name from its white grape, Chardonnay, which covers almost all of the slope.

questions.q: Why is chalk valued in Champagne's vineyards?
options: It drains well but stores water and releases it to the roots in dry spells
It is rich in organic matter and supports high yields
It is dark and absorbs heat, helping grapes ripen
It stops vines from rooting deeply, which lowers acidity
questions.explain: Chalk is free-draining yet porous, so it holds a reserve of water that the vine can draw on when the weather is dry.

questions.q: How many villages are classified grand cru under the échelle des crus?
questions.explain: Seventeen villages are grand cru, among them Ambonnay, Bouzy, Aÿ, Avize and Cramant.

questions.q: Why does Meunier suit the cooler, low-lying sites of Champagne?
options: It has the highest natural acidity of the three main grapes
It gives the most structured, long-lived base wines
It is the only grape that can be machine harvested
It buds late and ripens early, avoiding spring frost and fitting a short season
questions.explain: Late budding protects Meunier from spring frost, and early ripening lets it reach maturity in cool sites.

questions.q: What does the code RM on a Champagne label mean?
options: A house that buys grapes from growers
A cooperative that makes and sells wine
A grower who makes wine only from their own vineyards
A merchant who buys finished wine and adds a label
questions.explain: RM stands for récoltant manipulant: a grower who makes and sells Champagne from their own grapes.

questions.q: In which department does the Côte des Bar lie?
questions.explain: The Côte des Bar is in the Aube, far to the south of Reims and Épernay in the Marne.

lessons.title: Champagne: method and styles
lessons.intro: This lesson follows a bottle of Champagne from pressing to dosage. It covers the traditional method, the legal ageing minimums, the sweetness scale, the main styles and the two still-wine appellations of the region.

p: Grapes are pressed gently, as whole bunches. From 4,000 kg of grapes, the press may yield 2,550 litres of juice. The first 2,050 litres, the cuvée, are the finest. The last 500 litres, the taille, are fruitier and less fine. The juice ferments into a dry, high-acid still wine, the vin clair.

The base wines are then blended. This assemblage brings together grapes, villages and often years. Houses keep reserve wines from earlier harvests to give a non-vintage blend its consistent house style from year to year.

For the tirage, the blend is bottled with the liqueur de tirage: wine, sugar, yeast and a riddling aid. The bottles are sealed, usually with a crown cap. A second fermentation in the bottle, the prise de mousse, adds a little alcohol and traps the carbon dioxide, giving a pressure of around 5 to 6 atmospheres.

The wine then ages on its dead yeast cells, the lees. Yeast autolysis slowly gives flavours of bread, brioche and biscuit and a finer mousse. Non-vintage Champagne must age at least 15 months after tirage, 12 of them on the lees. Vintage Champagne must age at least three years after tirage.

Riddling, or remuage, moves the sediment into the neck. Bottles are turned and tilted step by step until they stand neck down, by hand on wooden pupitres or by machine in gyropalettes. For disgorgement, the neck is frozen and the cap removed, and the pressure pushes out the plug of frozen sediment.

The bottle is topped up with the liqueur d'expédition, a mix of wine and sugar. This dosage sets the sweetness. Brut Nature has 0 to 3 g/L and no added sugar, Extra Brut 0 to 6 g/L, and Brut under 12 g/L. Then come Extra Dry (12 to 17), Sec (17 to 32), Demi-Sec (32 to 50) and Doux (over 50).

Most Champagne is non-vintage (NV), a blend of several years. Vintage Champagne, or millésimé, comes from a single year's harvest and is usually made only in good years. Blanc de Blancs is made from white grapes only, in practice Chardonnay. Blanc de Noirs is a white wine made from black grapes, Pinot Noir, Meunier or both.

Rosé Champagne is made in two ways. Rosé d'assemblage blends a little still red wine from the region with white base wine before the second fermentation, a rare exception in European rules. The other way is saignée or maceration, where colour comes from brief skin contact with black grapes.

sections.h: Still wines: Coteaux Champenois and Rosé des Riceys
p: Coteaux Champenois is the appellation for still wines from the Champagne zone. It covers red, white and rosé. The best known are light red Pinot Noirs from villages such as Bouzy. Because the climate is cool, good still reds are made mainly in warm years.

Rosé des Riceys is a still rosé from Pinot Noir made in the commune of Les Riceys in the Aube. It is one of France's rarest appellations. Les Riceys is the only commune entitled to all three of the region's appellations: Champagne, Coteaux Champenois and Rosé des Riceys.

key: From 4,000 kg of grapes: 2,050 litres of cuvée and 500 litres of taille.
NV: at least 15 months after tirage, 12 on lees. Vintage: at least three years after tirage.
Autolysis gives bread, brioche and biscuit flavours.
Sweetness scale: Brut Nature, Extra Brut, Brut, Extra Dry, Sec, Demi-Sec, Doux.
Rosé can be made by blending in still red wine (assemblage) or by saignée.
Coteaux Champenois covers still wines; Rosé des Riceys is a still Pinot Noir rosé from Les Riceys in the Aube.

questions.q: What is the minimum ageing for non-vintage Champagne after tirage?
questions.explain: NV Champagne must age at least 15 months after tirage, of which at least 12 months on the lees.

questions.q: What is the minimum ageing for vintage Champagne after tirage?
questions.explain: Vintage Champagne must spend at least three years in the cellar after tirage.

questions.q: How much sugar may a Brut Champagne contain?
questions.explain: Brut means under 12 g/L of sugar. Extra Dry, confusingly, is sweeter at 12 to 17 g/L.

questions.q: Which sugar range applies to a Demi-Sec Champagne?
questions.explain: Demi-Sec has 32 to 50 g/L of sugar. Over 50 g/L is Doux.

questions.q: What is rosé d'assemblage?
options: Rosé made by leaving the juice briefly on black grape skins
Rosé made by blending a little still red wine with white base wine before the second fermentation
Rosé made by adding red wine in the dosage after disgorgement
Rosé made by blending finished rosés from several vintages
questions.explain: Champagne may blend still red wine into white base wine to make rosé, an exception in European rules. The colour is set before the second fermentation.

questions.q: Blanc de Noirs Champagne is made from which grapes?
options: Any of the seven permitted grapes
questions.explain: Blanc de Noirs is a white wine made from black grapes, Pinot Noir and Meunier.

questions.q: What is Rosé des Riceys?
options: A sparkling rosé made from Meunier
A still rosé made from Pinot Noir in the Aube
A still red wine from Bouzy
A sweet rosé made from Pinot Gris
questions.explain: Rosé des Riceys is a still Pinot Noir rosé from the commune of Les Riceys in the Aube.

questions.q: What is the purpose of disgorgement?
options: To add the sugar and yeast that start the second fermentation
To turn the bottles neck down so the sediment moves
To blend the base wines with reserve wines
To remove the yeast sediment that has collected in the neck
questions.explain: At disgorgement the frozen plug of sediment in the neck is pushed out by the pressure in the bottle. Riddling is the earlier step that moves it there.

lessons.title: Alsace
lessons.intro: This lesson explains why Alsace is so dry and sunny, which grapes it grows and how its wines are labelled. It covers the Alsace Grand Cru appellations, the late-harvest wines Vendanges Tardives and Sélection de Grains Nobles, and Crémant d'Alsace.

p: Alsace is a long, narrow strip in northeastern France, between the Vosges mountains to the west and the Rhine to the east. The vineyards lie on the lower slopes of the Vosges, mostly facing east and southeast. The region is split into the Bas-Rhin in the north and the Haut-Rhin in the south.

The Vosges block the rain carried by westerly winds. This rain shadow makes Alsace one of the driest parts of France, and Colmar is among the driest towns in the country. Summers are sunny and autumns long and dry, so grapes ripen fully despite the northern latitude. In some years noble rot develops late in the season.

Alsace wines are usually labelled by grape and sold in the tall, slim bottle called the flûte. Four grapes are called noble: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat. Riesling is dry and steely. Gewurztraminer is pink-skinned, with lychee and rose aromas, low acidity and high alcohol. Pinot Gris is rich and smoky. Muscat is usually dry and grapey.

Other grapes include Sylvaner, Pinot Blanc (often blended with Auxerrois under that name) and Pinot Noir, the only red grape. Edelzwicker is a blend of grapes. Klevener de Heiligenstein is a local speciality from Savagnin Rose. Some communes may add their name to Alsace for set grapes: Ottrott, Rodern and Saint-Hippolyte are known for Pinot Noir.

Alsace has a mosaic of soils, including granite, limestone, marl, sandstone, schist and volcanic rock. Different sites can give very different wines from the same grape. The Alsace AOC was created in 1962 and Alsace Grand Cru followed in 1975. There are now 51 grand cru sites, each with its own appellation.

Grand cru wines are generally limited to the four noble grapes. There are exceptions. Zotzenberg also allows Sylvaner, while Altenberg de Bergheim and Kaefferkopf allow blends. Since the 2022 vintage, Hengst and Kirchberg de Barr also allow Pinot Noir. Well-known sites include Schlossberg and Brand, both on granite, and Rangen at Thann, a steep site on volcanic rock in the far south.

sections.h: Vendanges Tardives and Sélection de Grains Nobles
p: Vendanges Tardives (VT) and Sélection de Grains Nobles (SGN) are legal terms, defined in 1984, for late-harvest wines. They may only be made from the four noble grapes. Each needs a minimum sugar level in the grapes, set higher for Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris than for Riesling and Muscat. Chaptalisation is not allowed.

VT is made from overripe grapes picked late, sometimes with some noble rot or shrivelling. Styles range from off-dry to sweet. SGN is made from grapes affected by noble rot, picked berry by berry or bunch by bunch in several passes. SGN wines are sweet, concentrated and rare, and only made in suitable years.

Crémant d'Alsace became an appellation in 1976. It is made by the traditional method, with the second fermentation in the bottle, and must age at least nine months on the lees. Pinot Blanc is the main grape, with Auxerrois, Pinot Gris, Pinot Noir, Riesling and Chardonnay also allowed.
Crémant d'Alsace rosé must be made from Pinot Noir only. The style is fresh and fruity, with less autolytic character than most Champagne because the lees ageing is usually shorter.

key: The Vosges rain shadow makes Alsace dry and sunny; Colmar is one of France's driest towns.
The four noble grapes are Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat. Pinot Noir is the only red.
Alsace AOC dates from 1962, Alsace Grand Cru from 1975; there are 51 grands crus.
Grands crus are mostly limited to the noble grapes; Zotzenberg allows Sylvaner.
VT and SGN (defined 1984) use only the noble grapes; SGN needs noble rot; no chaptalisation.
Crémant d'Alsace (1976) is traditional method, at least nine months on lees; rosé is Pinot Noir only.

questions.q: What is the main reason Alsace is so dry?
options: The Vosges mountains create a rain shadow
Warm winds blow north along the Rhine
Mediterranean air reaches it through the Rhône valley
Its vineyards lie at high altitude above the clouds
questions.explain: The Vosges block rain-bearing westerly winds, so the vineyards on their eastern slopes stay dry and sunny.

questions.q: Which of these is one of Alsace's four noble grapes?
questions.explain: The noble grapes are Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat. Sylvaner, Pinot Blanc and Auxerrois are not among them.

questions.q: How many Alsace Grand Cru appellations are there?
questions.explain: Alsace has 51 grand cru sites, each with its own appellation.

questions.q: What kind of soil is the Rangen grand cru known for?
questions.explain: Rangen, at Thann in the far south of Alsace, is a steep site on volcanic rock.

questions.q: What is required for Sélection de Grains Nobles?
options: Grapes affected by noble rot, picked in several passes
Grapes picked late but never affected by noble rot
Grapes frozen on the vine and pressed while frozen
A second fermentation in the bottle
questions.explain: SGN is made from botrytised grapes from the four noble varieties, picked selectively.

questions.q: Which grape must be used for Crémant d'Alsace rosé?
questions.explain: Crémant d'Alsace rosé is made from Pinot Noir only.

questions.q: Which grand cru also allows Sylvaner?
questions.explain: Zotzenberg is an exception to the noble-grape rule and allows Sylvaner.

questions.q: Which grape makes Klevener de Heiligenstein?
questions.explain: Klevener de Heiligenstein is a local speciality made from Savagnin Rose.

lessons.title: The western Loire: Muscadet and Anjou-Saumur
lessons.intro: This lesson covers the Atlantic end of the Loire. It explains Muscadet and the sur lie technique, then moves inland to Anjou and Saumur, where Chenin Blanc makes dry and sweet whites and Cabernet Franc makes the reds.

sections.h: The Loire and the Pays Nantais
p: The Loire is France's longest river. Its vineyards run inland from near the Atlantic at Nantes to the Centre of France. The climate changes along the way, from mild and maritime in the west to more continental in the east.

The Pays Nantais, around Nantes, has the most maritime climate: mild, humid and windy. Its main grape is Melon, often called Melon de Bourgogne, which gives light, dry, neutral whites with high acidity. Gros Plant du Pays Nantais is a tart white made from Folle Blanche.

sections.h: Muscadet sur lie and the crus communaux
p: There are four Muscadet appellations: Muscadet, Muscadet Sèvre et Maine, Muscadet Coteaux de la Loire and Muscadet Côtes de Grandlieu. Sèvre et Maine, southeast of Nantes, is the largest. Sur lie on the label means the wine stayed on its fine lees through the winter, until at least the March after harvest, and was bottled straight off them.

Lees contact adds texture, a little yeasty flavour and sometimes a slight prickle. Within Sèvre et Maine, the first three crus communaux were Clisson, Gorges and Le Pallet. These wines age much longer on the lees and can develop for years. Soils matter: Clisson is on granite, Gorges on gabbro.

Anjou lies inland around Angers. Its western part sits on dark schist of the Massif Armoricain, called Anjou noir. Further east, towards Saumur, the soils are pale tuffeau limestone, called Anjou blanc. The key white grape is Chenin Blanc. Reds come from Cabernet Franc and Cabernet Sauvignon, which ripens in the warmer schist sites.

Anjou is known for rosé. Rosé d'Anjou is off-dry, mainly from Grolleau. Cabernet d'Anjou is medium-sweet, from Cabernet Franc and Cabernet Sauvignon. Rosé de Loire is dry. For reds, Anjou Villages and Anjou Brissac (called Anjou Villages Brissac until 2020) give more structured wines than basic Anjou.

Savennières, on the north bank of the Loire, is best known for dry Chenin Blanc from steep slopes of schist and volcanic rock. The wines have high acidity and develop slowly. Two named crus stand out: Roche aux Moines and Coulée de Serrant, a monopole of the Joly family and an early biodynamic estate.

South of the Loire, along the Layon, autumn mists encourage noble rot. Coteaux du Layon makes sweet Chenin, picked by hand in several passes. Six villages may add their name, and Chaume is a premier cru. Bonnezeaux and Quarts de Chaume are the top sweet sites. Quarts de Chaume became the Loire's first grand cru in 2011.

Saumur sits on tuffeau, a soft, chalky limestone. It was quarried to build the châteaux of the Loire, and the caves left behind are used as cellars. Saumur makes Chenin Blanc whites, Cabernet Franc reds and a great deal of traditional-method sparkling wine, sold as Saumur mousseux and as Crémant de Loire.

Saumur-Champigny makes reds, mainly from Cabernet Franc, that are fresh, fruity and often drunk young. Coteaux de Saumur is a small appellation for sweet Chenin Blanc. Crémant de Loire can come from Anjou, Saumur and Touraine.

key: Muscadet is made from Melon; Gros Plant du Pays Nantais from Folle Blanche.
Sur lie: the wine stays on its fine lees until at least the March after harvest and is bottled off them.
The first crus communaux of Muscadet Sèvre et Maine were Clisson, Gorges and Le Pallet.
Anjou noir is schist, Anjou blanc is tuffeau. Chenin Blanc is the key white grape, Cabernet Franc the key red.
Savennières: dry Chenin. Coteaux du Layon, Bonnezeaux and Quarts de Chaume: sweet Chenin from noble rot.
Quarts de Chaume became the Loire's first grand cru in 2011. Saumur-Champigny is Cabernet Franc.

questions.q: Which grape makes Muscadet?
questions.explain: Muscadet is made from Melon, also called Melon de Bourgogne.

questions.q: What does sur lie mean on a Muscadet label?
options: The wine stayed on its fine lees over winter and was bottled straight off them
The wine was aged in new oak barrels
The wine underwent a second fermentation in the bottle
The wine was made from grapes affected by noble rot
questions.explain: Sur lie Muscadet rests on its fine lees until at least the March after harvest and is bottled without racking, which adds texture.

questions.q: Which of these is a cru communal of Muscadet Sèvre et Maine?
questions.explain: Clisson, with Gorges and Le Pallet, was one of the first three crus communaux of Muscadet Sèvre et Maine.

questions.q: Which grape makes Gros Plant du Pays Nantais?
questions.explain: Gros Plant du Pays Nantais is a tart white made from Folle Blanche.

questions.q: What style is Savennières best known for?
questions.explain: Savennières, on the north bank of the Loire, is famous for dry, high-acid Chenin Blanc that ages slowly.

questions.q: Which appellation became the Loire's first grand cru in 2011?
questions.explain: Quarts de Chaume, a sweet Chenin Blanc appellation in the Layon valley, became the Loire's first grand cru in 2011.

questions.q: Saumur-Champigny is made mainly from which grape?
questions.explain: Saumur-Champigny is a red appellation based on Cabernet Franc.

questions.q: What is tuffeau?
options: A soft, chalky limestone found around Saumur
A dark schist found in western Anjou
A volcanic rock found in Savennières
A gravel found along the Atlantic coast
questions.explain: Tuffeau is a soft, chalky limestone. It was used to build the Loire châteaux, and its caves serve as cellars.

lessons.title: Touraine and the Centre-Loire
lessons.intro: This lesson covers the middle and upper Loire. In Touraine it explains Vouvray and Montlouis for Chenin Blanc and Chinon and Bourgueil for Cabernet Franc. In the Centre-Loire it covers Sancerre, Pouilly-Fumé and their neighbours, the home of Loire Sauvignon Blanc.

p: Touraine lies around the city of Tours. The Atlantic influence is weaker here than in Anjou, and the climate is more continental. Many grapes are grown: Chenin Blanc and Sauvignon Blanc for whites, Cabernet Franc, Côt (Malbec) and Gamay for reds. The regional Touraine appellation is best known for crisp Sauvignon Blanc.

Some areas may add their name to Touraine, such as Amboise, Azay-le-Rideau, Chenonceaux and Oisly. Oisly is for Sauvignon Blanc only. To the east, Cheverny makes blended wines and Cour-Cheverny makes white wine from the rare local grape Romorantin.

Vouvray lies on the north bank of the Loire, just east of Tours. Its wines are made from Chenin Blanc, on tuffeau covered with clay and flint. The style depends on the year: sec, demi-sec or moelleux (sweet), with sweet wines made in the warmest vintages. Much Vouvray is also made sparkling.

Montlouis-sur-Loire faces Vouvray across the river, on the south bank, between the Loire and the Cher. It also makes Chenin Blanc in dry, off-dry, sweet and sparkling styles. Its soils are often sandier, and the wines can be a little lighter. North of Tours, Jasnières makes mostly dry Chenin Blanc on the Loir, a separate tributary.

Chinon lies west of Tours on the Vienne, close to where it joins the Loire. Its reds are made mainly from Cabernet Franc. Vines on sand and gravel near the river give lighter, fruity wines. Vines on tuffeau and clay-limestone slopes give firmer wines that can age. Some rosé and white Chenin Blanc are made too.

Bourgueil lies north of the Loire and makes red and rosé, mainly from Cabernet Franc. Its gravel terraces and tuffeau slopes give structured reds. Neighbouring Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil, to the west, has sandier soils and its wines are often lighter.

The Centre-Loire is far from the Atlantic, nearer to Chablis than to Nantes. The climate is continental, with cold winters and a risk of spring frost. Sancerre is on the left bank of the Loire. It is famous for white Sauvignon Blanc and also makes red and rosé from Pinot Noir.

Sancerre has three main soils. Terres blanches are Kimmeridgian marl and give fuller, structured wines. Caillottes are stony limestone and give aromatic wines for early drinking. Silex is flint, giving tight wines that need time. Many producers blend across soils, while others bottle them separately.

Pouilly-Fumé lies on the right bank, opposite Sancerre, around the town of Pouilly-sur-Loire. It makes white wine only, from Sauvignon Blanc, known locally as Blanc Fumé. The separate appellation Pouilly-sur-Loire is for whites from Chasselas.

West of Sancerre, Menetou-Salon makes Sauvignon Blanc whites and Pinot Noir reds and rosés. Further west, Quincy makes white wine only, from Sauvignon Blanc with some Sauvignon Gris. Reuilly makes Sauvignon Blanc whites, Pinot Noir reds and rosés that can include Pinot Gris. Coteaux du Giennois lies to the north.

key: Touraine grows Chenin Blanc, Sauvignon Blanc, Cabernet Franc, Côt and Gamay; Cour-Cheverny is Romorantin.
Vouvray (north bank) and Montlouis-sur-Loire (south bank) make Chenin Blanc from dry to sweet, plus sparkling.
Chinon (on the Vienne) and Bourgueil are mainly Cabernet Franc; Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil is often lighter.
Sancerre: Sauvignon Blanc whites, Pinot Noir reds and rosés; soils are terres blanches, caillottes and silex.
Pouilly-Fumé is white only from Sauvignon Blanc; Pouilly-sur-Loire is Chasselas.
Menetou-Salon and Reuilly make Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir; Quincy makes white only.

questions.q: Which grape makes Vouvray?
questions.explain: Vouvray is made from Chenin Blanc, in styles from dry to sweet and sparkling.

questions.q: Where does Montlouis-sur-Loire lie in relation to Vouvray?
options: North of Vouvray, on the Loir
West of Vouvray, on the Vienne
On the same bank, just upstream
On the south bank of the Loire, facing Vouvray
questions.explain: Montlouis-sur-Loire faces Vouvray across the Loire, on the south bank between the Loire and the Cher.

questions.q: On which river does Chinon lie?
questions.explain: Chinon lies on the Vienne, close to where it joins the Loire.

questions.q: Which grape makes red Sancerre?
questions.explain: Sancerre reds and rosés are made from Pinot Noir, while the whites are Sauvignon Blanc.

questions.q: In Sancerre, what is silex?
questions.explain: Silex is flint, which gives tight wines that need time. Caillottes are stony limestone and terres blanches are Kimmeridgian marl.

questions.q: Which grape makes the wines of the Pouilly-sur-Loire appellation?
questions.explain: Pouilly-sur-Loire is for Chasselas whites. The Sauvignon Blanc wines of the area are sold as Pouilly-Fumé.

questions.q: Which grape makes Cour-Cheverny?
questions.explain: Cour-Cheverny is a white made from the rare local grape Romorantin.

questions.q: Which of these Centre-Loire appellations makes white wine only?
questions.explain: Quincy makes only white wine from Sauvignon Blanc. Menetou-Salon, Reuilly and Sancerre also make Pinot Noir reds and rosés.

paths.title: Rhône and the French South
paths.summary: The Rhône valley from the granite slopes of the north to the Grenache blends of the south, then Provence, Languedoc and Roussillon with their rosés, red blends, sparkling wines and vins doux naturels.

lessons.title: The Northern Rhône
lessons.intro: This lesson covers the narrow, steep northern part of the Rhône valley, where Syrah is the only red grape and Viognier, Marsanne and Roussanne make the whites. You will learn each appellation, its bank of the river and its grape rules.

sections.h: A narrow valley of steep slopes
p: The Northern Rhône (Rhône septentrional) runs south from Vienne to just below Valence. The vineyards sit on steep slopes above the river, many of them terraced and worked by hand. The climate is moderately continental: warm summers, cold winters and rain spread more evenly through the year than in the south.

Soils are mostly granite and related rocks such as gneiss and schist, with patches of loess and river deposits. On the steepest sites vines are often tied to individual wooden stakes (échalas) to cope with the slope and the wind.
Syrah is the only red variety. Here it gives deep colour, black fruit, black pepper, violet and olive notes, firm tannins and fresh acidity. The best wines need years in bottle.

Three white grapes are used: Viognier, Marsanne and Roussanne. Several red appellations allow a small share of these white grapes in the blend. The amount differs by appellation, so learn each rule separately.

Côte-Rôtie lies on the west bank around Ampuis, the northernmost appellation. It makes red only, from Syrah with up to 20% Viognier. The Viognier is traditionally co-fermented with the Syrah, which can lift the perfume and help fix colour. Two famous slopes are the Côte Brune and the Côte Blonde.

Condrieu, just to the south, makes white wine only, from 100% Viognier. The wines are full-bodied and aromatic, with apricot, peach and blossom, and fairly low acidity. Most are drunk young. Château-Grillet is a small appellation inside the Condrieu area, also Viognier, and owned by a single estate.

Hermitage is a south-facing hill on the east bank above the town of Tain-l'Hermitage. The western end is granite. Famous plots include Les Bessards, Le Méal and L'Hermite. Red Hermitage is Syrah, with up to 15% Marsanne and Roussanne allowed. White Hermitage is made from Marsanne and Roussanne and can age for decades. A sweet vin de paille from dried grapes is also permitted.

Crozes-Hermitage surrounds the hill and is the largest Northern Rhône appellation. It includes flatter land in the south that is easier to work by machine. The wines follow the same grape rules as Hermitage but are usually lighter and ready sooner.

Saint-Joseph is a long, narrow appellation on the west bank between the Condrieu area and Cornas. Reds are Syrah with up to 10% Marsanne and Roussanne. Whites are Marsanne and Roussanne. Quality and style vary along its length.

Cornas, further south on the west bank, makes red only and must be 100% Syrah. Its granite slopes form a sheltered, warm amphitheatre, and the wines are dark and tannic in youth. Saint-Péray, the southernmost appellation, makes white only, from Marsanne and Roussanne, both still and traditional-method sparkling.

East of the main valley, along the Drôme river, the Diois makes sparkling wines. The best known is Clairette de Die Méthode Ancestrale (also called méthode dioise), at least 75% Muscat à Petits Grains, which finishes its only fermentation in bottle. Plain Clairette de Die is a traditional-method wine from Clairette alone, and Crémant de Die is made mainly from Clairette.

key: Syrah is the only red grape of the Northern Rhône; the whites are Viognier, Marsanne and Roussanne.
Côte-Rôtie allows up to 20% Viognier, Hermitage and Crozes-Hermitage up to 15% Marsanne and Roussanne, Saint-Joseph up to 10%.
Cornas is red only and 100% Syrah.
Condrieu and Château-Grillet are white only, from 100% Viognier; Château-Grillet belongs to a single estate.
Hermitage is on the east bank at Tain-l'Hermitage; Côte-Rôtie, Condrieu, Saint-Joseph, Cornas and Saint-Péray are on the west bank.
Saint-Péray makes white wine only, still and sparkling, from Marsanne and Roussanne.

questions.q: Which white grape may be co-fermented with Syrah in Côte-Rôtie, up to 20% of the blend?
questions.explain: Côte-Rôtie allows up to 20% Viognier, traditionally co-fermented with the Syrah.

questions.q: Which Northern Rhône appellation makes red wine only and must be 100% Syrah?
questions.explain: Cornas permits no white grapes in its reds. Saint-Joseph, Hermitage and Crozes-Hermitage all allow a share of Marsanne and Roussanne.

questions.q: What makes Château-Grillet unusual among French appellations?
options: It is the only Rhône appellation for sweet wine
It is planted only with Marsanne
It is on the east bank opposite Hermitage
It is a small Viognier appellation owned by a single estate
questions.explain: Château-Grillet lies inside the Condrieu area, grows Viognier and belongs to one estate.

questions.q: Above which town is the hill of Hermitage?
questions.explain: Hermitage is a south-facing hill on the east bank above Tain-l'Hermitage. Ampuis is the home of Côte-Rôtie.

questions.q: What style of wine does Saint-Péray produce?
options: White only, still and sparkling, from Marsanne and Roussanne
questions.explain: Saint-Péray, the southernmost Northern Rhône appellation, makes only white wine, both still and traditional-method sparkling.

questions.q: Which is the largest Northern Rhône appellation, including flatter land that can be worked by machine?
questions.explain: Crozes-Hermitage surrounds the Hermitage hill and includes flatter land in the south.

questions.q: How is the climate of the Northern Rhône best described?
questions.explain: The north has a moderately continental climate with cold winters; the south is Mediterranean.

questions.q: Clairette de Die Méthode Ancestrale, from the Diois east of the Rhône, is made mainly from which grape?
questions.explain: The méthode ancestrale version must be at least 75% Muscat à Petits Grains. Plain Clairette de Die and Crémant de Die are the traditional-method wines based on Clairette.

lessons.title: The Southern Rhône
lessons.intro: This lesson covers the wide, warm southern Rhône, where Grenache leads blended wines. You will learn the climate, the Côtes du Rhône pyramid, Châteauneuf-du-Pape and the other crus, including the sweet Muscat and Grenache wines.

p: South of Montélimar the valley opens into a wide plain. The Southern Rhône (Rhône méridional) has a Mediterranean climate: hot, dry summers, mild winters and a risk of drought. Much of the rain falls in autumn and can arrive as storms at harvest.

The mistral is a cold, dry wind that blows from the north down the valley. It dries the vines after rain and so limits rot and mildew, but it can also break shoots. Many vines are grown as low bush vines (gobelet), which stand up well to the wind.

Grenache is the main red grape. It ripens to high sugar levels, so the wines are often high in alcohol, with red fruit and spice, moderate colour and soft tannins. It is prone to oxidation, so it is usually blended.

Syrah adds colour, structure and black fruit. Mourvèdre adds tannin, dark fruit and gamey notes, but needs a lot of heat to ripen. Cinsault and Carignan are also common. White blends use Grenache Blanc, Clairette, Bourboulenc, Roussanne, Marsanne and Viognier.

Côtes du Rhône is the regional appellation for the whole valley, north and south, though most of it is made in the south. Above it, Côtes du Rhône Villages has stricter rules, such as lower yields and a higher minimum alcohol.

Some villages, and a few named areas, may add their name to the label, for example Côtes du Rhône Villages Séguret, Sablet, Valréas or Plan de Dieu, a plateau that spans several communes. At the top are the crus, which have their own appellations and do not use the Côtes du Rhône name. Over time several villages have been promoted to cru, among them Rasteau, Vinsobres and Cairanne.
Around the edges lie separate appellations that follow similar Grenache-based styles, such as Ventoux, Luberon, Grignan-les-Adhémar and Costières de Nîmes.

Châteauneuf-du-Pape lies on the east bank between Orange and Avignon. Its name recalls the popes who lived at Avignon in the 14th century. In 1923 Baron Le Roy of Château Fortia led local growers to draw up production rules, and these became a model for the French AOC system. The appellation was created in 1936.

Thirteen grape varieties are permitted, or eighteen if colour variants such as Grenache Blanc and Grenache Gris are counted separately. Reds are usually Grenache-led. White Châteauneuf is also made, but no rosé. Parts of the area are covered in galets roulés, large rounded stones that store heat by day and release it at night. Other sectors have sand or limestone.

sections.h: The other crus and the sweet wines
p: Gigondas sits below the limestone peaks of the Dentelles de Montmirail and makes powerful Grenache-led reds, some rosé and, since the 2023 vintage, white wine based on Clairette. Neighbouring Vacqueyras makes red, white and rosé. On the west bank, in the Gard, Tavel makes only rosé, Grenache-based and deeper in colour and fuller in body than most rosés. Lirac, next door, makes all three colours.

The south also makes vins doux naturels, sweet wines fortified during fermentation. Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise is made from Muscat à Petits Grains. Rasteau makes a Grenache-based sweet wine as well as dry red cru wine. The village of Beaumes de Venise also has a cru for dry red.

key: The Southern Rhône has a Mediterranean climate; the cold, dry mistral wind limits disease but can damage vines.
Grenache leads most red blends, supported by Syrah, Mourvèdre, Cinsault and Carignan.
The pyramid runs from Côtes du Rhône to Côtes du Rhône Villages, then Villages with a named village, then the crus.
Châteauneuf-du-Pape permits thirteen varieties, makes red and white but no rosé, and is known for its galets roulés.
Baron Le Roy's 1923 rules at Châteauneuf-du-Pape were a model for the French AOC system.
Tavel makes rosé only; Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise and Rasteau make vins doux naturels.

questions.q: What is the mistral?
options: A warm, humid wind from the sea
A cold, dry wind blowing from the north down the valley
A local name for bush-trained vines
questions.explain: The mistral is a cold, dry northerly wind. It limits rot and mildew but can break shoots.

questions.q: What are galets roulés?
options: Terraces built on steep granite slopes
Wooden stakes used to train vines
Large rounded stones that store heat by day and release it at night
Clay pots used for ageing wine
questions.explain: Galets roulés are large rounded stones found in parts of Châteauneuf-du-Pape that hold the day's heat.

questions.q: Which wine style is not permitted under the Châteauneuf-du-Pape appellation?
questions.explain: Châteauneuf-du-Pape makes red and white wine only, with no rosé.

questions.q: Who led the 1923 production rules at Châteauneuf-du-Pape that became a model for the AOC system?
options: Baron Le Roy of Château Fortia
The INAO in its first year
questions.explain: Baron Le Roy of Château Fortia led local growers in drawing up rules in 1923. The appellation itself followed in 1936.

questions.q: Which Southern Rhône appellation makes only rosé?
questions.explain: Tavel, on the west bank in the Gard, makes only rosé. Lirac next door makes all three colours.

questions.q: On a label, what sits directly above plain Côtes du Rhône Villages in the pyramid?
options: Côtes du Rhône Villages with a geographical name, such as Plan de Dieu
questions.explain: Some villages and named areas may add their name, such as Plan de Dieu, Séguret or Sablet. The crus sit above them.

questions.q: Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise is best described as:
options: A dry red cru from Grenache
A vin doux naturel from Muscat à Petits Grains
questions.explain: It is a sweet wine fortified during fermentation, made from Muscat à Petits Grains. The dry red of the village is sold as Beaumes de Venise.

questions.q: Which cru sits below the limestone peaks of the Dentelles de Montmirail and is known for powerful Grenache-led reds?
questions.explain: Gigondas lies below the Dentelles de Montmirail, next to Vacqueyras.

lessons.title: Provence
lessons.intro: This lesson covers Provence, France's great rosé region, and its small historic appellations. You will learn how Provence rosé is made, the main regional appellations, and the special cases of Bandol, Cassis, Palette and Bellet.

sections.h: An old vineyard by the sea
p: Provence has one of the oldest vineyards in France. Greek settlers founded Massalia, today's Marseille, around 600 BC and planted vines. The climate is Mediterranean, with long sunny summers, little summer rain and the mistral in the west.
Soils change from west to east. The west is mostly limestone. In the east, around the Maures hills, the rocks are crystalline, such as schist and granite.

Rosé makes up most of the region's production. The typical style is pale, dry and delicate, with red fruit, citrus and herbal notes. Common grapes are Grenache, Cinsault, Syrah and Mourvèdre, plus the local Tibouren.

To keep the colour pale, grapes are pressed directly or given only a short skin contact. Picking early in the day and cool fermentation help keep fresh aromas. The main white grape is Rolle, known in Italy as Vermentino.

Côtes de Provence is the largest appellation and stretches across much of the region. Some areas may add their name, such as Sainte-Victoire, near the mountain painted by Cézanne, and La Londe, close to the coast.

Coteaux d'Aix-en-Provence lies in the west around Aix and allows Cabernet Sauvignon alongside the Mediterranean grapes. Coteaux Varois en Provence sits in the centre, higher and cooler. Les Baux de Provence, in the Alpilles hills, is known for its many organic and biodynamic estates.

Bandol lies on the coast west of Toulon. Its vines grow on terraces, called restanques, on limestone and sandy soils facing the sea. Mourvèdre needs a lot of warmth to ripen, and this sheltered, sunny site suits it well.

Red Bandol must contain at least 50% Mourvèdre and spend at least 18 months in oak before release. The wines have dark fruit, firm tannins and notes of herbs and leather with age, and they can age for many years. Bandol also makes rosé and white.

Cassis, on the coast east of Marseille, makes mainly white wine, from Marsanne and Clairette above all. Its vines grow below steep limestone cliffs. It was among the first French appellations, created in 1936.

Palette is a tiny appellation just outside Aix on limestone soils, dominated by one estate, Château Simone. Its wines use many old local varieties. Bellet, in the hills above Nice, grows the local Braquet and Folle Noire for reds and Rolle for whites.

key: Greek settlers at Massalia (Marseille) planted vines in Provence around 600 BC.
Rosé is most of Provence's production: pale, dry, from Grenache, Cinsault, Syrah, Mourvèdre and Tibouren.
Côtes de Provence is the largest appellation, with named areas such as Sainte-Victoire and La Londe.
Red Bandol needs at least 50% Mourvèdre and at least 18 months in oak.
Cassis makes mainly white wine from Marsanne and Clairette; Palette is dominated by Château Simone.
Rolle (Vermentino) is the main white grape of Provence.

questions.q: Who first planted vines in Provence, around 600 BC?
questions.explain: Greek settlers founded Massalia, today's Marseille, around 600 BC and brought vines with them.

questions.q: Which grape must make up at least 50% of red Bandol?
questions.explain: Red Bandol must contain at least 50% Mourvèdre, a late-ripening grape that suits this warm coastal site.

questions.q: What is the minimum time red Bandol must spend in oak before release?
questions.explain: Red Bandol must spend at least 18 months in oak.

questions.q: Which estate dominates the tiny appellation of Palette?
questions.explain: Palette, just outside Aix, is dominated by Château Simone. Château Fortia is in Châteauneuf-du-Pape.

questions.q: What does the coastal appellation of Cassis mainly produce?
options: White wine from Marsanne and Clairette
questions.explain: Cassis makes mainly white wine, with Marsanne and Clairette as the leading grapes.

questions.q: Rolle, the main white grape of Provence, is known in Italy as:
questions.explain: Rolle and Vermentino are the same grape.

questions.q: Which Provence appellation lies in the west around Aix and allows Cabernet Sauvignon?
questions.explain: Coteaux d'Aix-en-Provence allows Cabernet Sauvignon alongside the Mediterranean grapes.

lessons.title: Languedoc
lessons.intro: This lesson covers Languedoc, the large arc of vineyards from Nîmes towards Spain. You will learn its hierarchy, the main red appellations and their soils, the sparkling wines of Limoux and the Muscats of the Hérault.

p: Languedoc stretches along the Mediterranean from near Nîmes to the borders of Roussillon. For much of the 20th century it made large volumes of cheap wine from high-yielding vines. Since the 1980s many of these vineyards have been pulled up, and growers have turned to quality, often working old bush vines on the hills.
The climate is Mediterranean, hot and dry, with wild herb scrub called garrigue on the hillsides. The main red grapes are Carignan, Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre and Cinsault.

Many varietal wines, including Chardonnay, Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon, are sold as IGP Pays d'Oc. The regional appellation is Languedoc, which replaced the old Coteaux du Languedoc name and covers Roussillon too.

Within Languedoc, some areas may add their name to the label, such as Montpeyroux, Saint-Saturnin and Cabrières. Above these are the sub-regional appellations and crus, such as Pic Saint-Loup, Faugères, Saint-Chinian, Minervois and Corbières.

Pic Saint-Loup lies north of Montpellier beneath a limestone peak of the same name. Its climate is cooler and wetter than most of Languedoc, and Syrah does well there, blended with Grenache and Mourvèdre. Terrasses du Larzac, further north-west towards the Larzac plateau, is also cooler, with large differences between day and night temperatures.
Near the coast, Picpoul de Pinet makes crisp white wine from Piquepoul, grown beside the Étang de Thau lagoon and often matched with its oysters.

Faugères and Saint-Chinian lie in the hills of the Hérault. Faugères is on schist. Saint-Chinian has schist in the north, where Berlou and Roquebrun may add their names, and clay and limestone in the south. Both make Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre and Carignan blends.

In the Aude, Minervois lies on the slopes of the Montagne Noire, with La Livinière as its cru. Corbières is large and rugged, with many soils and a strong Carignan tradition; Boutenac is its cru. These two crus were called Minervois-La Livinière and Corbières-Boutenac until they were renamed in 2024. Fitou, enclosed by Corbières, became in 1948 the first Languedoc-Roussillon appellation for red table wine. La Clape is a limestone massif by the sea near Narbonne.
Near Carcassonne in the west, Cabardès and Malepère feel some Atlantic influence and blend Bordeaux grapes such as Merlot and Cabernet with Mediterranean ones.

Limoux lies in the upper Aude valley, higher and cooler than the rest of Languedoc, with some Atlantic influence. Records from the abbey of Saint-Hilaire in 1531 mention sparkling wine there. Blanquette de Limoux is a traditional-method sparkling wine made mostly from the local Mauzac. Blanquette méthode ancestrale is pure Mauzac, bottled before the first fermentation ends so that it finishes in bottle.

Crémant de Limoux is a traditional-method wine based on Chardonnay and Chenin Blanc, with some Mauzac and Pinot Noir. Still white Limoux must be fermented in oak. The Hérault also makes sweet vins doux naturels from Muscat à Petits Grains: Muscat de Frontignan, Muscat de Lunel, Muscat de Mireval and Muscat de Saint-Jean-de-Minervois.

key: Languedoc is the regional appellation for Languedoc and Roussillon; varietal wines are often sold as IGP Pays d'Oc.
Faugères is on schist; Saint-Chinian has schist in the north (Berlou, Roquebrun) and clay-limestone in the south.
Pic Saint-Loup, north of Montpellier, is cooler than most of Languedoc and Syrah does well there.
La Livinière and Boutenac (until 2024 Minervois-La Livinière and Corbières-Boutenac) are the crus of Minervois and Corbières.
Blanquette de Limoux is based on Mauzac; Crémant de Limoux is based on Chardonnay and Chenin Blanc.
Frontignan, Lunel, Mireval and Saint-Jean-de-Minervois make Muscat vins doux naturels.

questions.q: Which grape is the base of Blanquette de Limoux?
questions.explain: Blanquette de Limoux is made mostly from Mauzac. Crémant de Limoux is based on Chardonnay and Chenin Blanc.

questions.q: What is the soil of Faugères?
questions.explain: Faugères is known for its schist soils.

questions.q: Which appellation lies north of Montpellier, under a limestone peak, with a cooler climate that suits Syrah?
questions.explain: Pic Saint-Loup is named after its limestone peak and is cooler and wetter than most of Languedoc.

questions.q: Picpoul de Pinet is:
options: A crisp white from Piquepoul grown near the Étang de Thau
questions.explain: Picpoul de Pinet is a white wine from Piquepoul, grown beside the Étang de Thau lagoon.

questions.q: Which cru sits within the Minervois appellation?
questions.explain: La Livinière, called Minervois-La Livinière until 2024, is the cru of Minervois. Boutenac belongs to Corbières.

questions.q: In 1948 which appellation became the first in Languedoc-Roussillon for red table wine?
questions.explain: Fitou, enclosed by Corbières, was the first Languedoc-Roussillon appellation for red table wine, in 1948.

questions.q: Which rule applies to still white Limoux?
options: It must be made from Muscat
It must be fermented in oak
questions.explain: Still white Limoux must be fermented in oak.

questions.q: How is Blanquette méthode ancestrale made?
options: By a second fermentation in tank
From pure Mauzac, bottled before the first fermentation ends
By adding grape spirit during fermentation
By blending still wine with Champagne
questions.explain: It is pure Mauzac, bottled while still fermenting so that the fermentation finishes in bottle.

lessons.title: Roussillon and the vins doux naturels
lessons.intro: This lesson covers Roussillon, France's southernmost mainland region, and the vins doux naturels made there and elsewhere in the south. You will learn the dry appellations, how mutage works, and the styles of Banyuls, Maury and Rivesaltes.

p: Roussillon covers the Pyrénées-Orientales, next to Spain. It has a Catalan culture and was part of Spain until the Treaty of the Pyrenees in 1659. The climate is hot, dry and very sunny, and the strong north-west wind, the tramontane, keeps the vines healthy.
Soils are varied, with schist, granite, gneiss and limestone. Grenache is grown in its three colours, Noir, Gris and Blanc, alongside Carignan, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Macabeu and Muscat.

Côtes du Roussillon makes red, white and rosé. Côtes du Roussillon Villages covers a smaller area, mostly in the north around the Agly valley, and makes red only. Some villages may add their name, such as Caramany, Lesquerde and Tautavel, and Les Aspres, south of Perpignan, is a named area too.
Collioure makes dry red, rosé and white wine from the same steep, terraced schist slopes on the coast as Banyuls. Many producers make both: dry Collioure and sweet Banyuls from the same vineyards.

sections.h: How a vin doux naturel is made
p: A vin doux naturel (VDN) is made by mutage: neutral grape spirit of high strength is added during fermentation. The yeasts stop working, so natural grape sugar stays in the wine. The finished wine is usually between 15% and 18% abv.

For red VDNs the spirit is often added while the juice is still on the skins, to extract more colour and tannin. After that the wine can be aged in two ways. Reductive ageing, with little contact with air, keeps fresh fruit. Oxidative ageing in barrels or in glass demijohns (bonbonnes) left in the sun gives dried fruit, nuts and the savoury taste called rancio.

Banyuls lies on the coast by the Spanish border, on steep terraced schist. It is made mainly from Grenache Noir. Banyuls Grand Cru must contain at least 75% Grenache Noir and be aged at least 30 months in wood. Rimage is a vintage style, bottled young to keep its fruit.
Maury lies inland in the Agly valley, on dark schist soils, and also makes Grenache-based VDNs in both fruity and oxidative styles. Red Banyuls and Maury are classic matches for chocolate desserts.

Rivesaltes is the largest VDN appellation. It uses Grenache in its three colours, Macabeu and other grapes. Its styles include Grenat, a red kept from air to stay fruity; Tuilé, a red aged oxidatively that turns tawny; and Ambré, from white grapes aged oxidatively. Hors d'âge wines are aged for at least five years.

Muscat de Rivesaltes is made from Muscat à Petits Grains and Muscat of Alexandria and is usually drunk young and fresh. Elsewhere in the south, VDNs include Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise and Rasteau in the Rhône and the Hérault Muscats such as Frontignan.

key: Roussillon (Pyrénées-Orientales) is hot, dry and sunny, with the tramontane wind and a Catalan heritage.
Côtes du Roussillon Villages makes red only; Collioure makes the dry wines of the Banyuls slopes.
VDNs are made by mutage: grape spirit added during fermentation keeps natural sugar; most reach 15–18% abv.
Banyuls Grand Cru needs at least 75% Grenache Noir and at least 30 months in wood.
Grenat is a reductive red style; Tuilé and Ambré are oxidative styles; rancio is the savoury taste of long oxidative ageing.
Muscat de Rivesaltes uses Muscat à Petits Grains and Muscat of Alexandria.

questions.q: What is mutage?
options: Adding grape spirit during fermentation to keep natural sugar
Adding sugar to the must before fermentation
questions.explain: Mutage stops fermentation with high-strength grape spirit, leaving natural grape sugar in the wine.

questions.q: What are the minimum rules for Banyuls Grand Cru?
options: 50% Grenache Noir and 12 months in wood
75% Grenache Noir and 30 months in wood
questions.explain: Banyuls Grand Cru must contain at least 75% Grenache Noir and spend at least 30 months in wood.

questions.q: Which appellation makes the dry wines from the same coastal schist slopes as Banyuls?
questions.explain: Collioure covers dry red, rosé and white wines from the Banyuls area.

questions.q: In Rivesaltes, which style is a red VDN kept away from air to stay fruity?
questions.explain: Grenat is the reductive red style. Tuilé is red aged oxidatively, and Ambré is from white grapes aged oxidatively.

questions.q: What is the typical alcohol level of a vin doux naturel?
questions.explain: Most vins doux naturels finish between 15% and 18% abv.

questions.q: Which grapes are used for Muscat de Rivesaltes?
options: Muscat à Petits Grains and Muscat of Alexandria
questions.explain: Muscat de Rivesaltes is made from Muscat à Petits Grains and Muscat of Alexandria.

questions.q: What is the tramontane?
options: A glass demijohn used for ageing
A strong north-west wind in Roussillon
questions.explain: The tramontane is the strong, dry north-west wind that keeps Roussillon's vines healthy.

questions.q: Where is Maury?
options: Inland in the Agly valley, on dark schist
On the coast at the Spanish border
questions.explain: Maury lies inland in the Agly valley. Banyuls is the one on the coast by the Spanish border.

paths.title: Italy
paths.summary: Italian wine law and climate, then the five regions students meet most: Piemonte, Toscana, Veneto, the north-east and the south with the islands. Grapes, styles, key appellations and legal ageing rules.

lessons.title: Italian wine law and climate
lessons.intro: This lesson sets out the quality categories on an Italian label and the terms Classico, Superiore and Riserva. It then shows how the Alps, the Apennines, altitude and the sea shape a climate that grows warmer from north to south.

p: Italy's modern wine law began with a 1963 law that created the DOC, Denominazione di Origine Controllata. The first DOCs were approved in 1966, and Vernaccia di San Gimignano was the very first. The same law also provided for a higher category, DOCG (Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita), but none was granted until 1980. The first DOCGs, approved in 1980, were Brunello di Montalcino, Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, Barolo and Barbaresco.

IGT (Indicazione Geografica Tipica) came with a 1992 law. It covers broad areas, such as IGT Toscana, with looser rules on grapes and yields. At the base is Vino, wine with no geographical indication. Under EU law, DOC and DOCG are both PDO (DOP in Italian) and IGT is PGI (IGP).

Each DOC and DOCG has its own production rules: the grapes allowed, maximum yields, minimum alcohol and often minimum ageing. DOCG rules are usually stricter than DOC rules, and every bottle of DOCG wine carries a numbered government strip on the neck or capsule.

IGT gave a legal home to wines that broke the DOC rules of their time. The best known are the Super Tuscans of the 1970s and 1980s, which used Cabernet Sauvignon or left out the white grapes that Chianti then required. Many top wines are still sold as IGT by choice, so IGT is not a ceiling on quality.
Classico marks the historic heart of an appellation, the original zone before its borders were widened. Chianti Classico, Valpolicella Classico and Soave Classico are examples.

Superiore usually means a higher minimum alcohol, and in some appellations lower yields or longer ageing. Riserva means a longer legal minimum ageing than the standard wine of the same appellation. Each appellation sets its own figures, so the terms do not mean the same number of months everywhere.

sections.h: Climate from the Alps to Sicily
p: The Alps shelter the far north, where Alto Adige and Trentino have warm days and cool nights. Below them the wide Po Valley is flat and fertile, with cold winters, hot summers and frequent fog. The Apennines run down the length of the peninsula and offer hill sites at many altitudes.

Central and southern Italy and the islands have a warm Mediterranean climate with dry summers. Here quality depends on what cools the vines: altitude, sea breezes and slope aspect. Etna in Sicily and Irpinia in Campania grow grapes high up, which keeps acidity in the wines despite the southern latitude.

key: A 1963 law created the DOC; the first DOCs came in 1966, starting with Vernaccia di San Gimignano.
DOCG is the top category, and every DOCG bottle carries a numbered government strip.
IGT dates from 1992; many famous Super Tuscans are sold as IGT Toscana.
Under EU law, DOC and DOCG are PDO (DOP) and IGT is PGI (IGP).
Classico is the historic original zone, Superiore usually means higher minimum alcohol, Riserva means longer minimum ageing.
Altitude, slopes and the sea moderate a climate that warms from north to south.

questions.q: In which year was the IGT category created?
questions.explain: IGT came with a 1992 law. The DOC dates from a 1963 law and the first DOCGs from 1980.

questions.q: Which wine was the first Italian DOC, approved in 1966?
questions.explain: Vernaccia di San Gimignano, a white from Toscana, was the first DOC in 1966.

questions.q: What does Classico mean on an Italian label?
options: The historic original zone of the appellation
A wine aged at least two years
A wine made from a single grape variety
A wine with a higher minimum alcohol
questions.explain: Classico marks the historic heart of an appellation, the zone before its borders were widened.

questions.q: Under EU law, which category corresponds to Italian IGT?
questions.explain: IGT is a PGI (IGP). DOC and DOCG are both PDO (DOP).

questions.q: What does Riserva indicate on an Italian label?
options: A sweet wine from dried grapes
A longer legal minimum ageing than the standard wine
questions.explain: Riserva means a longer minimum ageing period than the standard wine of the same appellation. Each appellation sets its own figure.

questions.q: What must every bottle of DOCG wine carry?
options: The name of a single vineyard
questions.explain: DOCG wines carry a numbered government strip on the neck or capsule.

questions.q: What keeps acidity in the wines of Etna and Irpinia despite their southern latitude?
questions.explain: Both areas grow grapes at altitude, where cooler temperatures preserve acidity.

questions.q: Why were the first Super Tuscans sold outside the DOC system?
options: Their grapes or blends did not fit the DOC rules of the time
They were made from dried grapes
questions.explain: They used Cabernet Sauvignon or left out the white grapes Chianti then required, so they did not fit the rules. IGT later gave them a legal home.

lessons.title: Piemonte
lessons.intro: Piemonte (Piedmont), in the north-west at the foot of the Alps, is the home of Nebbiolo. This lesson covers the Langhe and Roero, the two great Nebbiolo DOCGs Barolo and Barbaresco, and the region's Barbera, Dolcetto, Moscato and Cortese.

p: Piemonte means foot of the mountains. The Alps rise to the west and north and the Apennines to the south, giving a continental climate with cold winters, warm summers and autumn fog. Nebbiolo is said to take its name from nebbia, fog. It buds early and ripens late, so it needs the warmest slopes.
Nebbiolo wines are pale in colour but high in acidity and tannin. Young wines smell of roses and red cherry; with age come tar, dried herbs and leather.

The Langhe are the hills south of the Tanaro river around the town of Alba. Langhe DOC is a broad appellation for many grapes, and Langhe Nebbiolo often holds younger or declassified wine. North of the Tanaro lies Roero, with sandier soils. Roero DOCG covers Nebbiolo reds and whites from Arneis.

Barolo DOCG is 100% Nebbiolo from hills south-west of Alba. The main communes are Barolo, La Morra, Castiglione Falletto, Monforte d'Alba and Serralunga d'Alba. In the west, around La Morra and Barolo, younger Tortonian marls give more perfumed, open wines. In the east, around Serralunga and Monforte, older Helvetian soils with more sandstone give firmer, more structured wines.

Barolo must age at least 38 months, 18 of them in wood, counted from 1 November of the harvest year. Riserva needs 62 months, also with 18 in wood. Traditional producers use long maceration and large old casks (botti). Modernists use shorter maceration and small new French barriques for a fruitier, oak-marked style.

Barbaresco DOCG is also 100% Nebbiolo, from hills north-east of Alba around the communes of Barbaresco, Neive and Treiso. The zone is lower and closer to the Tanaro, so it is a little warmer and Nebbiolo ripens slightly earlier. The wines are often more approachable young than Barolo, though the best age for decades.

Barbaresco must age at least 26 months, 9 in wood; Riserva needs 50 months, also with 9 in wood. Both Barolo and Barbaresco now have official named vineyard areas, the MGA (Menzioni Geografiche Aggiuntive), which may appear on the label, such as Rabajà in Barbaresco or Cannubi in Barolo.

Barbera has high acidity, low tannin and deep colour, so many producers age it in barrique to add structure. Barbera d'Asti DOCG, from the Monferrato hills around Asti, and Barbera d'Alba DOC are its main appellations. Nizza DOCG, inside the Barbera d'Asti zone, is 100% Barbera.
