Dolcetto ripens early and gives soft, fruity reds with lower acidity, for drinking young. Dogliani DOCG is its leading appellation. In northern Piemonte, Nebbiolo, locally called Spanna, makes Gattinara and Ghemme DOCG, often with small amounts of other local grapes.

Moscato Bianco grows in the hills south of Asti, and Asti DOCG covers two main styles, both usually sweet. Asti, once called Asti Spumante, is fully sparkling. Moscato d'Asti is only lightly sparkling (frizzante), closed with a normal cork, and low in alcohol at around 5%. Most are made in pressurised tanks, with fermentation stopped while plenty of grape sugar remains. They smell of grapes, peach and orange blossom.

Gavi DOCG, in the south-east near Liguria, is a dry white from Cortese: light, crisp, with citrus and green apple. Wine from the commune of Gavi itself may be labelled Gavi del Comune di Gavi. Alta Langa DOCG is Piemonte's traditional method sparkling wine, from Pinot Nero and Chardonnay.

key: Nebbiolo buds early, ripens late, and gives pale wines with high acidity and tannin, rose and tar aromas.
Barolo: at least 38 months with 18 in wood; Riserva 62 months.
Barbaresco: at least 26 months with 9 in wood; Riserva 50 months.
La Morra and Barolo give more perfumed wines; Serralunga d'Alba and Monforte d'Alba more structured ones.
The Langhe lie south of the Tanaro, Roero north; Roero DOCG covers Nebbiolo and Arneis.
Moscato d'Asti is sweet, frizzante and about 5% alcohol; Gavi is a dry white from Cortese.

questions.q: What is the legal minimum ageing for Barolo (not Riserva)?
questions.explain: Barolo needs at least 38 months, 18 of them in wood. 26 months with 9 in wood is the rule for Barbaresco.

questions.q: Which of these communes lies in the Barbaresco zone?
questions.explain: Barbaresco's communes are Barbaresco, Neive and Treiso. The other three are Barolo communes.

questions.q: Which grape is Gavi made from?
questions.explain: Gavi DOCG is a dry white from Cortese, grown in south-east Piemonte near Liguria.

questions.q: Where does Roero lie in relation to the Langhe?
options: In the Monferrato hills east of Asti
questions.explain: The Langhe are south of the Tanaro around Alba; Roero is across the river to the north, with sandier soils.

questions.q: Which Barolo communes are known for firmer, more structured wines on older Helvetian soils?
questions.explain: The eastern communes of Serralunga d'Alba and Monforte d'Alba give structured wines. La Morra and Barolo, on Tortonian marls, are more perfumed.

questions.q: What is the MGA in Barolo and Barbaresco?
options: A system of official named vineyard areas
The minimum ageing rule for Riserva
questions.explain: The MGA (Menzioni Geografiche Aggiuntive) are official named vineyard areas, such as Cannubi or Rabajà, that may appear on the label.

questions.q: Which description fits Moscato d'Asti?
options: Dry, still and high in alcohol
Lightly sparkling, sweet and around 5% alcohol
Traditional method sparkling from Pinot Nero
questions.explain: Moscato d'Asti is frizzante, sweet and low in alcohol. Fully sparkling Asti is the other style of the same DOCG.

questions.q: What is the typical structure of Barbera?
questions.explain: Barbera has high acidity, low tannin and deep colour, which is why oak is often used to add structure.

lessons.title: Toscana
lessons.intro: Toscana (Tuscany) is the home of Sangiovese. This lesson covers Chianti and Chianti Classico, the two great Sangiovese DOCGs of the south, Brunello di Montalcino and Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, and the coast of Bolgheri where the Super Tuscans began.

p: Sangiovese is Italy's most widely planted red grape. It buds early and ripens late, and gives wines with high acidity and firm tannin, red cherry, plum and dried herb flavours, and earthy, leathery notes with age. It is sensitive to site: in hot places it loses freshness, in cool ones it may not ripen fully.
Sangiovese has local names. It is Brunello in Montalcino, Prugnolo Gentile in Montepulciano and Morellino in Scansano, in the southern Maremma.

Chianti DOCG covers a large area of central Toscana. Its rules ask for at least 70% Sangiovese; a change proposed in 2026 would lower this to 60%. It has subzones that may appear on the label, among them Rufina and Colli Senesi. Chianti Classico is the historic zone between Florence and Siena. It has been a separate DOCG since 1996, and its symbol is the black rooster (Gallo Nero).

Chianti Classico needs at least 80% Sangiovese, and white grapes are no longer allowed. Riserva must age at least 24 months, including 3 in bottle. Gran Selezione, introduced in 2014, is the top tier: estate-grown grapes, at least 90% Sangiovese since 2023, and at least 30 months of ageing, including 3 in bottle. Eleven village areas, the UGA (Unità Geografiche Aggiuntive), were later approved for Gran Selezione labels.

sections.h: Brunello di Montalcino and Vino Nobile di Montepulciano
p: Montalcino is a hill town south of Siena, warmer and drier than Chianti Classico. Brunello di Montalcino DOCG is 100% Sangiovese. It may not be released before 1 January of the fifth year after the harvest and must spend at least two years in wood. Riserva is released a year later. Rosso di Montalcino DOC, also 100% Sangiovese, is a fresher, earlier-released wine from the same zone.

Montepulciano is a hill town east of Montalcino. Vino Nobile di Montepulciano DOCG needs at least 70% Sangiovese, here called Prugnolo Gentile, and at least two years of ageing, three for Riserva. Rosso di Montepulciano DOC is the younger version. The town has nothing to do with the Montepulciano grape, which is grown mainly in Abruzzo.

Sassicaia, a Cabernet Sauvignon-based wine from Tenuta San Guido at Bolgheri on the coast, was first sold with the 1968 vintage, as a simple table wine. Inland, Antinori's Tignanello, first made in 1970, dropped the white grapes then required in Chianti from the 1975 vintage and added Cabernet Sauvignon to Sangiovese. Wines like these did not fit the rules and became known as Super Tuscans.

Bolgheri later became a DOC, and in 2013 Bolgheri Sassicaia became the first Italian DOC dedicated to a single estate. Bolgheri reds are mostly based on Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Cabernet Franc, grown on the warm coastal plain and low hills, with breezes from the sea.

key: Chianti DOCG needs at least 70% Sangiovese (a 2026 proposal would lower it to 60%); Chianti Classico DOCG at least 80%, and it has been a separate DOCG since 1996.
Chianti Classico Riserva needs 24 months; Gran Selezione (2014) needs 30 months and estate grapes.
Brunello di Montalcino is 100% Sangiovese, released no earlier than 1 January of the fifth year after harvest, with at least two years in wood.
Vino Nobile di Montepulciano needs at least 70% Sangiovese (Prugnolo Gentile); Montepulciano here is a town, not the grape.
Sassicaia (first vintage 1968) has had its own DOC, Bolgheri Sassicaia, since 2013.

questions.q: What is the minimum share of Sangiovese in Chianti Classico?
questions.explain: Chianti Classico requires at least 80% Sangiovese. Chianti DOCG asks for less.

questions.q: When may Brunello di Montalcino (not Riserva) first be released?
options: 1 January of the fifth year after the harvest
1 September of the year after the harvest
1 January of the third year after the harvest
questions.explain: Brunello may not be released before 1 January of the fifth year after the harvest. Riserva waits a further year.

questions.q: What is the minimum ageing for Chianti Classico Gran Selezione?
questions.explain: Gran Selezione needs at least 30 months, including 3 in bottle. 24 months is the rule for Chianti Classico Riserva.

questions.q: What is Prugnolo Gentile?
options: A white grape used for Vin Santo
The local name for Sangiovese in Montepulciano
A clone of Cabernet Sauvignon at Bolgheri
questions.explain: In Montepulciano, Sangiovese is called Prugnolo Gentile. The Montepulciano grape of Abruzzo is a different variety.

questions.q: What made Bolgheri Sassicaia DOC notable in 2013?
options: It was the first Italian DOC dedicated to a single estate
It was the first DOCG in Toscana
It was the first IGT in Italy
It was the first DOC for white wine in Toscana
questions.explain: Bolgheri Sassicaia was the first Italian DOC for a single estate, Tenuta San Guido.

questions.q: Which symbol identifies Chianti Classico?
questions.explain: The black rooster (Gallo Nero) is the symbol of Chianti Classico.

questions.q: Which grape is Sassicaia mainly made from?
questions.explain: Sassicaia is a Cabernet Sauvignon-based wine from Bolgheri, first sold with the 1968 vintage.

questions.q: Which appellation gives a fresher, earlier-released 100% Sangiovese from the Brunello zone?
questions.explain: Rosso di Montalcino DOC comes from the same zone as Brunello and is also 100% Sangiovese.

lessons.title: Veneto
lessons.intro: Veneto, in the north-east around Verona and Venice, makes Valpolicella and Amarone, Soave and Prosecco. This lesson covers the drying of grapes (appassimento), the Valpolicella family of styles, Soave, and the difference between Prosecco DOC and the hill DOCGs.

p: Valpolicella lies in the hills north of Verona, between Lake Garda and the Lessini mountains. The Classico zone covers the western valleys around Fumane, Marano and Negrar. The main grape is Corvina, with Corvinone and Rondinella. Basic Valpolicella is a light, fresh red with cherry fruit.
Nearby, on the eastern shore of Lake Garda, Bardolino uses the same grapes for an even lighter red and a rosé called Chiaretto.

Appassimento is the drying of grapes after harvest. Bunches are laid on racks or in crates in airy lofts called fruttai and left for some months. They lose water, so sugar, acid and flavour become concentrated.

Amarone della Valpolicella DOCG ferments the dried grapes to dryness or near dryness. The wine is full-bodied, with at least 14% alcohol, and flavours of dried cherry, plum, chocolate and spice. Recioto della Valpolicella DOCG is the older, sweet style: fermentation stops while much sugar remains.

Valpolicella Ripasso DOC sits between basic Valpolicella and Amarone. Young Valpolicella is passed over (ripassato) the pomace, the skins left after Amarone or Recioto has fermented, and goes through a short second fermentation. This adds alcohol, body, colour and tannin, and gives a richer wine at a lower price than Amarone.

Soave lies east of Verona. The main grape is Garganega, at least 70% of the blend, with Trebbiano di Soave or Chardonnay as partners. The Classico zone, in the hills around Soave and Monteforte d'Alpone, has volcanic basalt and limestone soils and gives more concentrated wines than the flatter land to the south. Good Soave shows almond, pear and citrus.
Soave Superiore DOCG is a separate, stricter appellation. Recioto di Soave DOCG is a sweet wine from dried Garganega.

Prosecco is made mainly from Glera, almost always by the tank method, which keeps fresh pear, apple and white flower aromas. Prosecco DOC, created in 2009, is a large area across nine provinces of Veneto and Friuli Venezia Giulia. The two DOCGs are smaller hill zones: Conegliano Valdobbiadene Prosecco Superiore and Asolo Prosecco (Colli Asolani).

Within Conegliano Valdobbiadene, Rive marks wine from a single commune or village area, and Superiore di Cartizze comes from a small, famous hill near Valdobbiadene. Sweetness terms can confuse: Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut, and Dry is sweeter still.

key: Corvina is the main grape of Valpolicella, with Corvinone and Rondinella.
Appassimento dries grapes for some months after harvest to concentrate sugar and flavour.
Amarone is dry with at least 14% alcohol; Recioto is sweet; both are DOCG.
Ripasso is Valpolicella refermented on Amarone or Recioto pomace.
Soave is at least 70% Garganega; the Classico hills have volcanic and limestone soils.
Prosecco is Glera, mostly tank method; the DOC dates from 2009, the DOCGs are Conegliano Valdobbiadene and Asolo.

questions.q: Which is the main grape of Valpolicella?
questions.explain: Corvina is the main grape, blended with Corvinone and Rondinella.

questions.q: What is appassimento?
options: Fermenting whole bunches under carbon dioxide
Ageing wine under a layer of yeast
Drying grapes after harvest to concentrate sugar and flavour
Adding grape spirit to stop fermentation
questions.explain: Appassimento dries the grapes in airy lofts for some months, concentrating sugar, acid and flavour.

questions.q: How does Amarone differ from Recioto della Valpolicella?
options: Amarone is dry, Recioto is sweet
Amarone is sweet, Recioto is dry
Amarone is white, Recioto is red
Amarone uses fresh grapes, Recioto uses dried grapes
questions.explain: Both use dried grapes. Amarone ferments to dryness or near dryness; Recioto stops fermentation with much sugar left.

questions.q: How is Valpolicella Ripasso made?
options: By blending Valpolicella with finished Amarone
By drying grapes on the vine
By ageing in new barrique for three years
By refermenting Valpolicella on the pomace left from Amarone or Recioto
questions.explain: Young Valpolicella is passed over Amarone or Recioto skins and goes through a short second fermentation.

questions.q: Which grape must make up at least 70% of Soave?
questions.explain: Soave is at least 70% Garganega, with Trebbiano di Soave or Chardonnay as partners.

questions.q: Which Prosecco sweetness term is sweeter than Brut?
questions.explain: Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut, and Dry is sweeter still. The other three terms are drier than Brut.

questions.q: Which of these is a Prosecco DOCG?
questions.explain: Conegliano Valdobbiadene Prosecco Superiore and Asolo Prosecco are the two hill DOCGs. The large Prosecco DOC sits below them.

questions.q: What is the minimum alcohol for Amarone della Valpolicella?
questions.explain: Amarone must reach at least 14% alcohol, reflecting the concentrated sugar of dried grapes.

lessons.title: The north-east: Alto Adige, Trentino and Friuli
lessons.intro: Italy's north-east, from the Alpine valleys of Alto Adige and Trentino to the hills of Friuli on the Slovenian border, makes many of Italy's best whites. This lesson covers the climate, grapes and key appellations of each area.

p: Alto Adige, Südtirol in German, is Italy's northernmost wine region, around Bolzano in the Adige valley. It was part of Austria until after the First World War, so most people speak German and labels are often bilingual. Vineyards climb steep slopes above the valley floor. Strong sunshine, warm days and cool nights give ripe fruit with fresh acidity. Cooperative wineries make a large share of the wine.

Whites include Pinot Grigio, Pinot Bianco, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Gewürztraminer, which is said to take its name from the village of Tramin (Termeno). Reds include Schiava (Vernatsch), which gives light, pale reds, the deeper Lagrein, and Pinot Nero. Lago di Caldaro (Kalterersee) DOC is a Schiava-based red.

Trentino lies south of Alto Adige in the same Adige valley, but is Italian-speaking and a little warmer. Trento DOC is a traditional method sparkling wine, mainly from Chardonnay, with Pinot Nero, Pinot Bianco and Pinot Meunier also allowed. It is marketed as Trentodoc.
Teroldego Rotaliano DOC is a deep-coloured red from the Teroldego grape, grown on the Campo Rotaliano, a flat gravel plain north of Trento.

Friuli Venezia Giulia lies in the far north-east, between the Alps and the Adriatic, on the border with Slovenia. The best hill sites are Friuli Colli Orientali, east of Udine, and Collio (Collio Goriziano) near Gorizia, which continues across the border as Brda in Slovenia. Their soil, called ponca, is layered marl and sandstone. The Alps shelter the hills from the north and the sea moderates temperatures.

Friulano is the signature white grape. It was called Tocai Friulano until an EU ruling protecting Hungary's Tokaji forced a new name from 2007. Ribolla Gialla is another native white. Collio producers such as Gravner and Radikon led the revival of skin-contact white, or orange, wines. On the flat plain, Friuli Grave makes larger volumes of lighter wine.

Picolit is a white grape that sets few berries per bunch, which makes it scarce. It gives sweet wines, often from dried grapes, with their own DOCG, Colli Orientali del Friuli Picolit. Ramandolo DOCG is a sweet white from Verduzzo, grown in the north of the Colli Orientali. Rosazzo DOCG is a dry white blend based on Friulano.
Native red grapes include Refosco dal Peduncolo Rosso, Schioppettino and Pignolo.

key: Alto Adige (Südtirol) is bilingual and Alpine, with sunny days and cool nights; cooperatives matter.
Schiava (Vernatsch) gives light reds, Lagrein deeper ones; Lago di Caldaro is Schiava-based.
Trento DOC is traditional method sparkling, mainly Chardonnay.
Teroldego Rotaliano is a deep red from the Campo Rotaliano gravel plain.
Friuli Colli Orientali and Collio are hill zones on ponca soils by the Slovenian border.
Friulano was Tocai Friulano until 2007; Picolit and Ramandolo (Verduzzo) are sweet DOCGs.

questions.q: What is Alto Adige called in German?
questions.explain: Alto Adige is Südtirol in German. The region was Austrian until after the First World War and is largely German-speaking.

questions.q: Which red grape gives the light, pale reds of Lago di Caldaro?
questions.explain: Schiava (Vernatsch) makes light, pale reds, including Lago di Caldaro. Lagrein and Teroldego give deeper wines.

questions.q: Which grape is the main base of Trento DOC sparkling wine?
questions.explain: Trento DOC is traditional method sparkling wine made mainly from Chardonnay.

questions.q: What is ponca?
options: A sweet wine from dried grapes
A cold wind from the Alps
The layered marl and sandstone soil of Collio and Colli Orientali
questions.explain: Ponca is the layered marl and sandstone soil of Friuli's best hill sites.

questions.q: What was Friulano called before 2007?
questions.explain: An EU ruling protecting Hungary's Tokaji ended the use of the name Tocai Friulano from 2007.

questions.q: Which grape makes Ramandolo DOCG?
questions.explain: Ramandolo is a sweet white from Verduzzo, grown in the north of the Colli Orientali.

questions.q: Where is Teroldego Rotaliano grown?
options: In the Collio hills near Gorizia
On the Campo Rotaliano, a gravel plain north of Trento
On the flat Grave plain of Friuli
questions.explain: Teroldego Rotaliano comes from the Campo Rotaliano, a flat gravel plain north of Trento.

questions.q: Why is Picolit wine scarce?
options: It is grown only in Trentino
It may only be sold as Riserva
It ripens too early in Friuli
The vine sets few berries per bunch
questions.explain: Picolit sets few berries per bunch, so yields are tiny. It makes sweet wines with their own DOCG.

lessons.title: The south and the islands
lessons.intro: Southern Italy and the islands are warm and sunny, and quality comes from altitude, volcanic soils and old native grapes. This lesson covers Campania's Taurasi, Fiano and Greco, Sicily's Etna and Nero d'Avola, Primitivo in Puglia and Cannonau in Sardegna.

p: Irpinia, the hilly inland area around Avellino in Campania, is cooler than its latitude suggests, with vineyards at altitude and volcanic soils. Its great red is Taurasi DOCG, made from at least 85% Aglianico. In 1993 it became the first DOCG of southern Italy.

Aglianico ripens late, often in late October or November, and gives deep-coloured wines with high acidity and high tannin, black fruit, and earthy, smoky notes with age. Taurasi must age at least three years, one of them in wood. Riserva needs four years, eighteen months of them in wood. Aglianico del Taburno DOCG, in the province of Benevento, is another Campanian Aglianico.

sections.h: Campania's white DOCGs: Fiano and Greco
p: Two white DOCGs come from the same Irpinia hills. Fiano di Avellino makes medium-bodied whites with pear, hazelnut and honeyed notes that can age well. Greco di Tufo takes its name from the Greco grape and the village of Tufo; its wines are firmer, with high acidity and a mineral character. The Mastroberardino family did much to save these grapes after the Second World War.

Etna DOC, created in 1968, was the first DOC in Sicilia (Sicily). Vineyards on the slopes of the volcano rise to around 1,000 metres, far higher than most Sicilian vineyards, on black volcanic soils. Old bush vines (alberello) are common. Single districts called contrade may appear on the label.

The red grape is Nerello Mascalese, often with Nerello Cappuccio. It gives pale, high-acid reds with firm tannin, often compared to Pinot Noir or Nebbiolo. The white grape is Carricante, and Etna Bianco Superiore comes from the commune of Milo on the eastern slope.

Nero d'Avola, named after the town of Avola in the south-east, is Sicily's most important red grape. It gives deep-coloured reds with ripe dark fruit and good acidity. Sicily's only DOCG, Cerasuolo di Vittoria, blends Nero d'Avola with the lighter, fragrant Frappato. Sicilia DOC covers the whole island.
Marsala, in the west, is a fortified wine. The island of Pantelleria makes sweet wines from Zibibbo (Muscat of Alexandria), often from dried grapes.

Puglia, the heel of Italy, is largely flat, hot and sunny. Primitivo gives ripe, high-alcohol reds with jammy black fruit, notably in Primitivo di Manduria and Gioia del Colle. DNA studies show it is the same variety as Zinfandel in California and Tribidrag (Crljenak Kaštelanski) in Croatia. Negroamaro is the other key red, mostly in the Salento peninsula.

In Sardegna (Sardinia), Cannonau is the main red grape. It is the same variety as Grenache (Garnacha in Spain) and makes warm, full-bodied reds under Cannonau di Sardegna DOC. The leading white is Vermentino, and Vermentino di Gallura in the north-east is the island's only DOCG.

key: Taurasi: at least 85% Aglianico, the first DOCG of southern Italy (1993); at least 3 years ageing, 4 for Riserva.
Fiano di Avellino and Greco di Tufo are the white DOCGs of Irpinia.
Etna DOC (1968): Nerello Mascalese reds and Carricante whites from high volcanic slopes.
Cerasuolo di Vittoria, Sicily's only DOCG, blends Nero d'Avola and Frappato.
Primitivo is the same variety as Zinfandel; Cannonau is the same as Grenache.

questions.q: Which grape is the main variety of Taurasi?
questions.explain: Taurasi DOCG is made from at least 85% Aglianico.

questions.q: What is the minimum ageing for Taurasi (not Riserva)?
options: Two years, none required in wood
Three years, one of them in wood
Five years, three of them in wood
questions.explain: Taurasi needs at least three years, one in wood. Riserva needs four years, eighteen months in wood.

questions.q: Greco di Tufo takes its name from the Greco grape and from what?
questions.explain: Tufo is a village in the Irpinia hills of Campania.

questions.q: Which is the main red grape of Etna?
questions.explain: Etna reds are based on Nerello Mascalese, often with Nerello Cappuccio.

questions.q: Which is the only DOCG in Sicilia?
questions.explain: Cerasuolo di Vittoria, a blend of Nero d'Avola and Frappato, is Sicily's only DOCG. Etna, Marsala and Sicilia are DOCs.

questions.q: Primitivo is the same variety as which grape?
questions.explain: DNA studies show Primitivo, Zinfandel and Tribidrag are the same variety.

questions.q: Cannonau, the main red grape of Sardegna, is the same variety as which grape?
questions.explain: Cannonau is Grenache, known as Garnacha in Spain.

questions.q: Which white grape is used for Etna Bianco?
questions.explain: Carricante is the white grape of Etna. Etna Bianco Superiore comes from Milo on the eastern slope.

paths.title: Spain and Portugal
paths.summary: Spanish wine law and ageing terms, then the key regions of Spain and Portugal: Rioja and Navarra, the Duero and the north-west, Catalunya and the Mediterranean, sherry, Port, Madeira and the main Portuguese table wine regions.

lessons.title: Spanish wine law and ageing terms
lessons.intro: This lesson explains how Spanish wines are classified, from Vino de la Tierra up to DOCa and Vino de Pago, and what the ageing terms Joven, Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva mean on a label.

p: Spain's wine law of 2003 sets out the categories. At the base is Vino, wine with no geographical indication. Above it is Vino de la Tierra, the Spanish term for a protected geographical indication (PGI). It covers wide areas and allows flexible rules on grapes and yields.

The protected designations of origin (PDO) sit higher: Vino de Calidad con Indicación Geográfica, Denominación de Origen (DO), Denominación de Origen Calificada (DOCa) and Vino de Pago. Textbooks usually show them in this order, with Vino de Pago at the top. Each DO is run by a Consejo Regulador, a regulatory council that sets and enforces its rules.
DOCa is the top regional tier. A region must have held DO status for at least ten years before it can apply, and all its wine must be bottled by registered wineries within the region.
Rioja became the first DOCa in 1991. Priorat followed. In Catalan it is called DOQ, for Denominació d'Origen Qualificada. These two remain the only DOCa regions.

A Vino de Pago is a single estate with its own soil, microclimate and proven reputation. It holds PDO status in its own right, so it does not need to sit inside a DO. The grapes must come from the estate, and the wine is made and bottled by the estate.

Many pagos are in Castilla-La Mancha. Dominio de Valdepusa, the estate of the Marqués de Griñón, was the first. Navarra recognizes its own pagos under regional law, such as Pago de Arínzano and Pago de Otazu.

Joven wines are released young, with little or no oak. Spanish law then sets three ageing terms. A red Crianza needs at least 24 months of ageing, with at least 6 in oak. A red Reserva needs 36 months, with at least 12 in oak. A red Gran Reserva needs 60 months, with at least 18 in oak.

For Reserva and Gran Reserva, the rest of the time is spent in bottle. White and rosé wines have shorter minimums: 18 months for Crianza, 24 for Reserva and 48 for Gran Reserva, each with at least 6 months in oak. The oak must be barrels of no more than 330 litres.

A Consejo Regulador can set stricter rules than the national minimums. Rioja and Ribera del Duero both require at least 12 months in oak for a red Crianza, double the national figure. A red Rioja Gran Reserva needs at least two years in oak and two years in bottle.
Rioja has also added place names to its labels. A 2017 reform created Viñedo Singular for single vineyards and set rules for wines named after a village (municipio) or one of its zones.

key: Vino de la Tierra is the Spanish term for a PGI. DO, DOCa and Vino de Pago are PDO categories.
Rioja became the first DOCa in 1991. Priorat is the second, called DOQ in Catalan.
A Vino de Pago is a single estate with PDO status of its own. Dominio de Valdepusa was the first.
National minimums for reds: Crianza 24 months (6 in oak), Reserva 36 (12 in oak), Gran Reserva 60 (18 in oak).
Ageing barrels may hold no more than 330 litres.
Rioja and Ribera del Duero require 12 months in oak for a red Crianza.

questions.q: What is the Spanish term for a protected geographical indication (PGI)?
questions.explain: Vino de la Tierra is Spain's PGI category. The other three are PDO categories.

questions.q: Which region became Spain's first DOCa, in 1991?
questions.explain: Rioja was the first DOCa, in 1991. Priorat followed as the second.

questions.q: What is a Vino de Pago?
options: A single estate with PDO status of its own
A village wine from within Rioja
A blend of wines from several DOs
A sweet wine made from dried grapes
questions.explain: A Vino de Pago is a single estate with its own soil, microclimate and reputation, holding PDO status in its own right.

questions.q: Under national Spanish law, what is the minimum total ageing for a red Gran Reserva?
questions.explain: A red Gran Reserva needs at least 60 months of ageing, with at least 18 in oak. 48 months is the figure for white and rosé Gran Reserva.

questions.q: Under national Spanish law, how long must a red Reserva spend in oak at minimum?
questions.explain: A red Reserva needs 36 months of ageing in total, with at least 12 in oak.

questions.q: What is the largest barrel size allowed for oak ageing under the Spanish ageing terms?
questions.explain: The oak ageing must take place in barrels of no more than 330 litres.

questions.q: How long must a red Rioja Crianza spend in oak at minimum?
questions.explain: Rioja requires at least 12 months in oak for a red Crianza, double the national minimum of 6 months.

lessons.title: Rioja and Navarra
lessons.intro: This lesson covers Rioja's setting on the Ebro, its three zones, its grapes and its oak tradition, then looks at its neighbour Navarra.

p: Rioja lies along the upper Ebro river in northern Spain. The Sierra de Cantabria to the north shelters the vineyards from cold, wet Atlantic winds. Most of the DOCa lies in La Rioja, the Basque province of Álava and Navarra, with a tiny enclave in Burgos.

The climate grows warmer and drier from west to east, as Atlantic influence gives way to Mediterranean influence. The main soils are clay-limestone, ferrous clay and alluvial deposits near the rivers.

Rioja Alta is the western part, in La Rioja. It is relatively high and cool, and its town of Haro is home to many historic bodegas. Rioja Alavesa lies north of the Ebro in Álava, on clay-limestone soils at the foot of the Sierra de Cantabria.

Rioja Oriental is the eastern zone, warmer and drier than the other two. Until 2018 it was called Rioja Baja. Garnacha does well here. Many wines blend grapes from more than one zone, so a zone is not always shown on the label.

Tempranillo is the main grape. Its name comes from temprano, early, because it ripens early. It gives red fruit and medium acidity. Garnacha adds body, alcohol and ripe fruit. Graciano, used in small amounts, adds acidity, colour and aroma. Mazuelo, the local name for Carignan, adds acidity and tannin.
Viura, known elsewhere in Spain as Macabeo, is the main white grape. Malvasía and Garnacha Blanca are also used. Rioja makes white and rosado wines as well as red.

In the mid 19th century, the Marqués de Murrieta and the Marqués de Riscal brought Bordeaux methods to Rioja, including the 225-litre barrica. Later in the century, when phylloxera destroyed French vineyards, French merchants came to Rioja to buy wine. This shaped the region's style and trade.

The traditional style is long ageing in American oak. It gives pale, mellow reds with notes of vanilla, coconut, dill and dried fruit. Since the late 20th century many producers have also used French oak, shorter ageing and riper fruit, for darker and more concentrated wines.

Navarra lies north-east of Rioja and has its own DO. It was long known for fresh Garnacha rosado. Today it makes mostly red wine from Tempranillo and Garnacha, alongside international varieties such as Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Chardonnay. It also makes sweet whites from Moscatel de Grano Menudo.

The north of Navarra is cooler and wetter, the south along the Ebro hotter and drier. Navarra has also recognized single estates as pagos, among them Pago de Arínzano, Pago de Otazu and Prado de Irache.

key: Rioja follows the upper Ebro and is sheltered by the Sierra de Cantabria. It gets warmer and drier from west to east.
The three zones are Rioja Alta, Rioja Alavesa (in Álava, north of the Ebro) and Rioja Oriental (called Rioja Baja until 2018).
Tempranillo leads, with Garnacha, Graciano and Mazuelo (Carignan). Viura (Macabeo) is the main white.
The 225-litre barrica came from Bordeaux in the 19th century. Traditional Rioja ages long in American oak.
Navarra was long known for Garnacha rosado and now makes mostly red wine.

questions.q: Which Rioja zone lies north of the Ebro in the Basque province of Álava?
questions.explain: Rioja Alavesa is the zone in Álava, on clay-limestone soils at the foot of the Sierra de Cantabria.

questions.q: What was Rioja Oriental called until 2018?
questions.explain: The eastern zone was renamed from Rioja Baja to Rioja Oriental in 2018.

questions.q: Which mountain range shelters Rioja from cold, wet Atlantic winds?
questions.explain: The Sierra de Cantabria, to the north, protects the vineyards from Atlantic weather.

questions.q: Which grape is used in small amounts in Rioja to add acidity, colour and aroma?
questions.explain: Graciano adds acidity, colour and aroma. Garnacha adds body and alcohol, and Viura and Malvasía are white grapes.

questions.q: What size is the traditional Rioja barrica?
questions.explain: The 225-litre barrica came to Rioja from Bordeaux in the 19th century. 330 litres is the legal maximum for ageing barrels, not the traditional size.

questions.q: Notes of vanilla, coconut and dill in a traditional Rioja come mainly from which type of oak?
questions.explain: Long ageing in American oak gives the classic vanilla, coconut and dill notes of traditional Rioja.

questions.q: What is the main white grape of Rioja?
questions.explain: Viura, called Macabeo elsewhere in Spain, is Rioja's main white grape.

questions.q: What style was Navarra long known for?
questions.explain: Navarra built its name on fresh Garnacha rosado, though today it makes mostly red wine.

lessons.title: The Duero valley and the north-west
lessons.intro: This lesson follows the Duero across Castilla y León, through Ribera del Duero, Toro and Rueda, then turns to the Atlantic north-west: Rías Baixas, Bierzo and the Mencía regions of Galicia.

p: Ribera del Duero follows the Duero river across the high plateau of Castilla y León. Many vineyards are at 750 metres or more, among the highest in Spain. Summers are hot, winters cold and nights cool, which helps keep acidity and colour. Spring frost is a real risk.

The main grape is Tempranillo, known here as Tinto Fino or Tinta del País, and it must make up most of the blend. Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Malbec are allowed in smaller amounts. The reds are deep in colour and structured, with dark fruit and firm tannins.

Vega Sicilia, founded in 1864, made the region's name with its Único. The DO was created in 1982, and producers such as Alejandro Fernández of Pesquera brought it wide fame in the years that followed.

Toro lies downstream to the west, in the province of Zamora. It is lower and hotter than Ribera del Duero. Its local Tempranillo, Tinta de Toro, gives powerful, full-bodied reds with high alcohol and ripe dark fruit.

Rueda, also on the Duero, is known for white wine. Verdejo is the key grape, often with Sauvignon Blanc or Viura. Typical Rueda Verdejo is crisp, with citrus and herbal notes and a slightly bitter finish. Many producers harvest at night to keep the grapes cool and protect the juice from oxidation.

Galicia, in the far north-west, has an Atlantic climate: mild, wet and green. Rías Baixas lies along the coast, where the rías (drowned river valleys) cut inland. Soils are mostly granite. Vines are often trained on high pergolas, which lets air move around the grapes and reduces the risk of rot.

Albariño dominates. It gives fresh, aromatic whites with high acidity, citrus and stone fruit, and often a saline note. The five subzones are Val do Salnés, Condado do Tea, O Rosal, Soutomaior and Ribeira do Ulla. Val do Salnés, on the coast, is the coolest and wettest. Condado do Tea, inland along the Miño, is warmer.

Bierzo lies in the province of León, between Galicia and the plateau, and mixes Atlantic and continental influences. Its red grape is Mencía, grown on slate and granite slopes. It gives fresh, fragrant reds with red fruit and floral notes. Godello is the leading white grape.

Bierzo gained new attention after 1999, when Álvaro Palacios and his nephew Ricardo Pérez founded Descendientes de J. Palacios there. In Galicia, Mencía is also the key red of Ribeira Sacra, with steep terraces above the Sil and Miño rivers. Valdeorras is best known for Godello.

key: Ribera del Duero is a high, continental region. Tempranillo is called Tinto Fino or Tinta del País here.
Toro is hotter and lower, and its Tinta de Toro gives powerful, high-alcohol reds.
Rueda is a white wine region led by Verdejo, often harvested at night.
Rías Baixas has an Atlantic climate, granite soils and pergola-trained Albariño. Val do Salnés is the coolest subzone.
Mencía is the red grape of Bierzo and Ribeira Sacra. Godello is the leading white of Bierzo and Valdeorras.

questions.q: What is Tempranillo called in Ribera del Duero?
questions.explain: In Ribera del Duero Tempranillo is called Tinto Fino or Tinta del País. Tinta de Toro is the name used in Toro.

questions.q: Which region, lower and hotter than Ribera del Duero, is known for powerful, high-alcohol Tempranillo?
questions.explain: Toro, in the province of Zamora, makes full-bodied, high-alcohol reds from Tinta de Toro.

questions.q: What is the key grape of Rueda?
questions.explain: Rueda is a white wine region led by Verdejo, often blended with Sauvignon Blanc or Viura.

questions.q: Why do many Rueda producers harvest at night?
options: To keep the grapes cool and protect the juice from oxidation
To raise sugar levels in the grapes
To extract more colour from the skins
questions.explain: Night harvesting keeps the grapes cool, which protects the fresh aromas of Verdejo from oxidation.

questions.q: Why are vines in Rías Baixas often trained on high pergolas?
options: To shade the grapes from strong sun
To let air move around the grapes and reduce rot
To protect the vines from winter frost
questions.explain: In this wet Atlantic climate, high pergolas improve airflow around the bunches and reduce the risk of rot.

questions.q: Which Rías Baixas subzone, on the coast, is the coolest and wettest?
questions.explain: Val do Salnés, on the coast, is the coolest and wettest subzone. Condado do Tea, inland along the Miño, is warmer.

questions.q: Mencía is the key red grape of which region?
questions.explain: Mencía is the red grape of Bierzo, and also of Ribeira Sacra in Galicia.

questions.q: What is the main soil type of Rías Baixas?
questions.explain: Rías Baixas soils are mostly granite. Albariza is the soil of Jerez and llicorella that of Priorat.

lessons.title: Catalunya and the Mediterranean
lessons.intro: This lesson covers Priorat and its llicorella soils, its neighbour Montsant, Penedès and Cava, and the Monastrell country of Jumilla in the hot south-east.

p: Priorat lies in the hills inland from Tarragona, in Catalunya (Cataluña in Spanish). Its vineyards climb steep slopes and terraces. The key soil is llicorella, a dark, brittle slate that splits into thin layers. It holds little water, so roots go deep and yields are very low.

Garnacha and Cariñena (Carignan) are the traditional grapes, often from old bush vines. Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah and Merlot are also grown. The wines are concentrated, high in alcohol and structured, with dark fruit and an earthy, mineral note.

Carthusian monks founded the monastery of Scala Dei here in the 12th century and planted vines. After phylloxera the region declined. In the late 1980s a small group including René Barbier and Álvaro Palacios settled around the village of Gratallops. Their first wines, from the 1989 vintage, showed what the old vines and llicorella could do.
Priorat later became Spain's second DOCa, or DOQ in Catalan. It has since added a village tier, Vi de Vila.

Montsant almost surrounds Priorat. It was once a subzone of the Tarragona DO and became a DO in its own right in 2001. It uses the same main grapes, Garnacha and Cariñena, but has more varied soils with less llicorella. The wines are usually softer and better value.

Penedès lies south-west of Barcelona, between the coast and the inland hills. It rises from the warm Baix Penedès near the sea to the higher, cooler Alt Penedès. It makes still wines from local and international grapes, and it is the heart of Cava production.

Cava is a traditional method sparkling wine, with the second fermentation in the bottle. Unusually, the DO is not one continuous area. It is a list of municipalities in several parts of Spain, including Aragón, Navarra, La Rioja, the Basque Country, Valencia and Extremadura. Most Cava is made in Penedès, around Sant Sadurní d'Anoia.
The traditional grapes are Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada. Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are also allowed. Josep Raventós of Codorníu made the first Cava in 1872.
Cava must spend at least 9 months on its lees. Cava Reserva needs at least 18 months, Gran Reserva at least 30 months, and Cava de Paraje Calificado, from a single site, at least 36 months.

Further south the climate turns hot and dry. Jumilla, inland in Murcia and Albacete, is the home of Monastrell, the grape called Mourvèdre in France. It needs plenty of heat to ripen. Vines are often bush trained and grown on poor, limestone soils.

Monastrell gives deep-coloured reds with ripe black fruit, high alcohol and firm tannins. Neighbouring Yecla and Alicante also rely on it. Alicante makes a rare, long-aged style from very ripe Monastrell called Fondillón.

key: Llicorella is Priorat's dark, brittle slate. It gives deep roots and very low yields.
Priorat is based on Garnacha and Cariñena. Its modern revival began with the 1989 vintage around Gratallops.
Montsant surrounds Priorat and became a DO in 2001, after being a subzone of Tarragona.
Cava is made by the traditional method from Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada. Most is made around Sant Sadurní d'Anoia in Penedès.
Cava lees ageing minimums: 9 months, Reserva 18, Gran Reserva 30, Paraje Calificado 36.
Monastrell (Mourvèdre) is the grape of Jumilla, Yecla and Alicante.

questions.explain: Llicorella is the dark slate of Priorat. It splits into thin layers and holds little water.

questions.q: Which two grapes are the traditional base of Priorat?
questions.explain: Garnacha and Cariñena, often from old bush vines, are the traditional grapes of Priorat.

questions.q: Which monastery's monks first planted vines in Priorat?
questions.explain: Carthusian monks founded the monastery of Scala Dei in the 12th century and planted vines there.

questions.q: Before becoming a DO in 2001, Montsant was a subzone of which DO?
questions.explain: Montsant was part of the Tarragona DO before gaining its own DO in 2001.

questions.q: What is the minimum time on lees for a basic Cava?
questions.explain: All Cava must spend at least 9 months on its lees. 18 months is the minimum for Cava Reserva.

questions.q: What is the minimum lees ageing for Cava Gran Reserva?
questions.explain: Cava Gran Reserva needs at least 30 months. 36 months applies to Cava de Paraje Calificado.

questions.q: Which grapes are the traditional trio for Cava?
options: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier
questions.explain: Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada are the traditional Cava grapes. Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are also allowed.

questions.q: Monastrell, the grape of Jumilla, is known in France as which variety?
questions.explain: Monastrell is the Spanish name for Mourvèdre.

lessons.title: Jerez and sherry
lessons.intro: This lesson explains where sherry comes from, why albariza and Palomino matter, how flor and the solera work, and how the main styles from fino to Pedro Ximénez differ.

p: Sherry comes mainly from the province of Cádiz in Andalucía, in the far south-west of Spain. The DO is Jerez-Xérès-Sherry, its name in Spanish, French and English. Traditionally the wine is aged in three towns that form the sherry triangle: Jerez de la Frontera, El Puerto de Santa María and Sanlúcar de Barrameda.
The climate is hot and sunny. Two winds matter. The poniente blows in from the Atlantic and brings humidity. The levante blows from the east and is hot and dry.

The best vineyards are on albariza, a bright white soil rich in calcium carbonate. It soaks up winter rain and holds it like a sponge. In summer its surface hardens into a crust that slows evaporation, so the vines get through the long dry season.

Palomino is the main grape. It gives a neutral, low-acid base wine that suits the sherry process. Pedro Ximénez (PX) and Moscatel are used for sweet wines. For PX the grapes are often laid out in the sun to dry and concentrate their sugar, a practice called asoleo.

The base wine is fermented dry and then classified. Wines chosen for fino and manzanilla are fortified to about 15 to 15.5% abv. In butts that are not filled to the top, a film of yeast called flor grows on the surface. Flor shields the wine from oxygen and feeds on alcohol and glycerol. This is called biological ageing.

Flor gives a pale wine with sharp, pungent aromas of bread dough and almond. Wines chosen for oloroso are fortified to about 17% or more. At this strength flor cannot survive, so the wine ages in contact with oxygen. This oxidative ageing darkens the colour and gives nutty, toasty, dried fruit flavours.

Sherry is aged in a solera system. Butts are grouped in tiers by age. The oldest tier is itself called the solera, and the younger tiers are the criaderas. Wine for bottling is drawn from the solera, which is then topped up from the next oldest criadera, and so on up the line.

Because younger wine is constantly blended into older wine, the style stays consistent and most sherry carries no vintage. In biological soleras, the fresh wine also feeds the flor. VOS (Very Old Sherry) and VORS (Very Old Rare Sherry) are certified as at least 20 and 30 years old on average.

Fino is pale, dry and tangy, aged entirely under flor. Manzanilla is the same style aged in Sanlúcar de Barrameda, with its own DO, Manzanilla-Sanlúcar de Barrameda. The cool, humid sea air keeps the flor thick, and the wine is light and salty. Both are best drunk fresh and chilled.

Amontillado starts under flor. When the flor fades, it is usually fortified further and ages on in contact with oxygen, becoming amber, dry and nutty. Oloroso is aged only oxidatively: dark, rich and naturally dry. Pedro Ximénez is intensely sweet, dark and raisined. Cream sherry is a sweetened blend, often of oloroso and PX.
Nearby Montilla-Moriles, in the province of Córdoba, makes similar styles mainly from Pedro Ximénez. Its finos often reach their strength naturally, without fortification.

key: Sherry is traditionally aged in Jerez de la Frontera, El Puerto de Santa María and Sanlúcar de Barrameda.
Albariza is a white soil rich in calcium carbonate that stores winter rain.
Palomino makes the dry styles. PX and Moscatel make the sweet ones, PX often from sun-dried grapes.
Fino and manzanilla are fortified to about 15 to 15.5% and age under flor. Oloroso is fortified to about 17% or more and ages oxidatively.
In a solera, wine is drawn from the oldest tier and topped up from the criaderas, so most sherry has no vintage.
Manzanilla must be aged in Sanlúcar de Barrameda. Amontillado starts under flor and finishes oxidatively.

questions.q: In which town must manzanilla be aged?
questions.explain: Manzanilla is fino-style sherry aged in Sanlúcar de Barrameda, with its own DO, Manzanilla-Sanlúcar de Barrameda.

questions.q: What is albariza?
options: A white soil rich in calcium carbonate
questions.explain: Albariza is the bright white soil of Jerez. It stores winter rain and forms a crust in summer.

questions.q: Which grape is the main variety for dry sherry?
questions.explain: Palomino gives the neutral, low-acid base wine used for the dry styles. PX and Moscatel are used for sweet wines.

questions.q: What does flor do to a fino as it ages?
options: It adds sugar to the wine
It shields the wine from oxygen
questions.explain: Flor forms a film on the wine that protects it from oxygen, while it feeds on alcohol and glycerol.

questions.q: To roughly what strength is a wine fortified when it is chosen for oloroso?
questions.explain: Oloroso is fortified to about 17% or more, which prevents flor from growing, so the wine ages oxidatively.

questions.q: In a solera system, what is the oldest tier of butts called?
questions.explain: The oldest tier is the solera. Wine is drawn from it and topped up from the younger criaderas.

questions.q: How is amontillado made?
options: It is aged oxidatively from the start
It is a sweetened blend of oloroso and PX
It is aged entirely under flor
It starts under flor, then ages in contact with oxygen
questions.explain: Amontillado begins as a fino under flor. When the flor fades it continues ageing oxidatively, becoming amber and nutty.

questions.q: What is asoleo?
options: Drying grapes in the sun to concentrate sugar
Adding grape spirit to the base wine
Drawing wine from the oldest tier
questions.explain: Asoleo is the practice of laying grapes, usually Pedro Ximénez, in the sun to dry before pressing.

lessons.title: Portugal
lessons.intro: This lesson covers the Douro and the main styles of Port, the table wine regions of Vinho Verde, Dão and Alentejo, and a brief look at Madeira.

p: The Douro river runs west across northern Portugal from Spain to the sea at Porto. In 1756, under the Marquês de Pombal, the Douro became one of the first demarcated wine regions in the world. Vines grow on steep slopes of schist, often on terraces. Mountains to the west block much of the Atlantic rain, so summers are hot and dry.

There are three subregions. Baixo Corgo, in the west, is the coolest and wettest. Cima Corgo, around Pinhão, is the heart of fine Port. Douro Superior, towards the Spanish border, is the hottest and driest. The region makes both Port, under the DO Porto, and unfortified wines, under the DO Douro.
Many grapes are allowed. The best known are Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz (Tempranillo), Tinta Barroca and Tinto Cão. They give deep colour, tannin and intense fruit.

Port is fortified during fermentation. Grape spirit (aguardente) at about 77% abv is added while the wine still holds much of its sugar. This stops fermentation and leaves a sweet wine of about 19 to 22% abv. Because fermentation is short, colour and tannin must be extracted fast, traditionally by treading in shallow stone troughs called lagares.
Port has traditionally been aged in the lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia, across the river from the city of Porto.

Ruby styles age in large vessels to keep their fruit and colour. Reserve Ruby is a higher quality ruby. Late Bottled Vintage (LBV) comes from a single year and is bottled four to six years after harvest. Vintage Port is made only in declared years, bottled in its second or third year, and needs long ageing in bottle. It throws a sediment and needs decanting.

Tawny styles age in small casks, where slow oxidation turns them amber and gives nutty, dried fruit flavours. Tawnies with an indication of age, such as 10, 20, 30 or 40 years, show the average character of a blend. Colheita is a tawny from a single harvest, aged at least seven years in wood. White and rosé Port are also made.

Vinho Verde, in the rainy, green north-west, makes light, fresh whites, often low in alcohol and sometimes slightly sparkling. Verde means young, not green in colour. Key grapes are Alvarinho, Loureiro, Arinto and Avesso. In the subregion of Monção e Melgaço, on the Minho river facing Galicia, Alvarinho gives fuller wines. Red Vinho Verde is made mainly from Vinhão.

Dão lies on a granite plateau in central Portugal, ringed by mountains such as the Serra da Estrela, which shelter it from Atlantic rain and continental extremes. Reds from Touriga Nacional, Jaen (Mencía) and Alfrocheiro are fresh and elegant. Encruzado is the leading white grape.

Alentejo, in the south, is hot, dry and mostly flat, with forests of cork oak. Reds come from Aragonez (Tempranillo), Trincadeira and Alicante Bouschet. Antão Vaz and Arinto are key whites. The old practice of fermenting in large clay jars survives in the DO's Vinho de Talha wines.

Madeira is an island in the Atlantic, west of Morocco. Its fortified wine is heated during ageing, a practice that grew from the discovery that the wine improved on long tropical sea voyages. In estufagem the wine is heated in tanks for at least three months. The finest wines use the canteiro method, ageing slowly in casks in warm lofts.

Four classic grapes also name the sweetness. Sercial is the driest, then Verdelho, Boal (Bual) and Malvasia (Malmsey), the sweetest. Tinta Negra is the most planted grape. All styles keep high acidity, and because they are already heated and oxidised they last for decades, even once opened. Unfortified wines from the island use the DO Madeirense.

key: The Douro was demarcated in 1756 under the Marquês de Pombal. Its vineyards are on steep schist slopes.
Douro subregions from west to east: Baixo Corgo, Cima Corgo, Douro Superior, getting hotter and drier.
Port is fortified with grape spirit during fermentation, which leaves natural sweetness.
LBV is bottled four to six years after harvest. Vintage Port is bottled in its second or third year. Colheita is a single-harvest tawny with at least seven years in wood.
Vinho Verde is fresh and light. Alvarinho is the grape of Monção e Melgaço. Dão is a granite plateau with Touriga Nacional and Encruzado.
Madeira is heated during ageing. Sercial is the driest style and Malvasia (Malmsey) the sweetest.

questions.q: In which year was the Douro demarcated under the Marquês de Pombal?
questions.explain: The Douro was demarcated in 1756, making it one of the first demarcated wine regions in the world.

questions.q: What is the main soil of the Douro vineyards?
questions.explain: Douro vines grow on steep slopes of schist, often on terraces.

questions.q: Which Douro subregion, towards the Spanish border, is the hottest and driest?
questions.explain: Douro Superior in the east is the hottest and driest. Baixo Corgo in the west is the coolest and wettest.

questions.q: Why is Port sweet?
options: Grape spirit is added during fermentation, stopping it before all the sugar is used
The grapes are dried in the sun before pressing
A sweetened wine is blended in before bottling
questions.explain: Adding aguardente at about 77% abv stops fermentation and leaves some of the grape sugar in the wine.

questions.q: When is a Late Bottled Vintage (LBV) Port bottled?
options: In its second or third year
Four to six years after harvest
After at least seven years in wood
After at least ten years in wood
questions.explain: LBV is bottled four to six years after harvest. Vintage Port is bottled in its second or third year.

questions.q: What is a Colheita Port?
options: A ruby blend from several years
A white Port aged in large vats
A tawny from a single harvest aged at least seven years in wood
A Vintage Port from a single estate
questions.explain: Colheita is a single-harvest tawny that must spend at least seven years in wood.

questions.q: In which Vinho Verde subregion does Alvarinho give its fullest wines?
questions.explain: Monção e Melgaço, on the Minho river facing Galicia, is the home of fuller Alvarinho.

questions.q: Which is the driest of the classic Madeira styles?
questions.explain: Sercial is the driest, followed by Verdelho, Boal and Malvasia (Malmsey), the sweetest.

paths.title: Germany and Austria
paths.summary: How German and Austrian wine law works and how to read the labels, then the key regions: the Mosel, the Rhine regions, Germany's red wine and outer regions, and Austria from the Wachau to the Neusiedlersee.

lessons.title: German wine law and labels
lessons.intro: German labels carry a lot of information once you know the code. This lesson covers the quality categories, the six Prädikat levels, the sweetness terms, the place hierarchy of the 1971 wine law and the VDP's private classification, which sits outside the law.

p: German wine law sorts wine into four tiers. Deutscher Wein (once called Tafelwein) and Landwein are the basic levels, Landwein being Germany's protected geographical indication. Above them come the two protected designations of origin: Qualitätswein and Prädikatswein.

Qualitätswein must come from one of the 13 Anbaugebiete, the official wine-growing regions, and the label must name that region. The must may be enriched with sugar before fermentation (chaptalisation). Every Qualitätswein and Prädikatswein passes an official analysis and tasting and carries an AP number, the Amtliche Prüfungsnummer.
Prädikatswein was called Qualitätswein mit Prädikat (QmP) until 2007. It must reach a set ripeness at harvest and may not be enriched. Its sugar and alcohol come from the grapes alone.

The six Prädikate are set by must weight, the sugar content of the grape juice at harvest. In rising order: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese, with Eiswein sharing the Beerenauslese minimum. The level tells you how ripe the grapes were, not how sweet the finished wine is.

Kabinett is the lightest. Spätlese means late harvest. Auslese is made from selected bunches. Beerenauslese (BA) uses individually selected overripe berries, usually affected by noble rot. Trockenbeerenauslese (TBA) uses shrivelled, botrytised berries and gives very sweet, concentrated wine. Eiswein is pressed from grapes frozen on the vine and must reach the same minimum must weight as a Beerenauslese.

Because a Prädikat measures ripeness, a Spätlese or Auslese can be fermented dry. The label then adds a sweetness term. Trocken means dry and halbtrocken means off-dry; both are defined in law. Lieblich and süß describe clearly sweet wines.

Feinherb is widely used for off-dry wines but has no legal definition, so its meaning varies by producer. A Kabinett or Spätlese with no sweetness term on the label is often made in a fruity style with residual sugar, especially in the Mosel, but you cannot assume it.

The 1971 wine law divides each Anbaugebiet into Bereiche (districts), Großlagen (collective sites) and Einzellagen (single vineyards). Place names are usually written as the village plus the suffix -er, then the site: Wehlener Sonnenuhr means the Sonnenuhr vineyard of Wehlen.

A Großlage groups many single vineyards, sometimes across several villages, and is named in exactly the same village plus site style. Piesporter Michelsberg is a large Großlage, while Piesporter Goldtröpfchen is a famous Einzellage. Niersteiner Gutes Domtal in Rheinhessen is another Großlage known for simple bulk wine. Under the 1971 rules nothing on the label told the drinker which kind of site was meant. From the 2026 vintage, a Großlage or Bereich name on the label must be preceded by the word Region.

The VDP (Verband Deutscher Prädikatsweingüter) is an association of leading estates whose roots go back to 1910. Members put an eagle with a grape cluster on the capsule. Its classification is private: it binds only members and is not part of German wine law.

The VDP pyramid has four levels: VDP.Gutswein, VDP.Ortswein, VDP.Erste Lage and VDP.Große Lage. A dry wine from a Große Lage is called Großes Gewächs (GG). VDP members generally keep Prädikat names for wines with natural residual sugar. Do not confuse the VDP's Große Lage, its top sites, with the legal Großlage, a collective site.
In 2021 the wine law itself was amended to give origin more weight, a change that is being phased in.

key: Germany has 13 Anbaugebiete for Qualitätswein and Prädikatswein.
Prädikatswein may not be chaptalised; Qualitätswein may.
The Prädikate, in rising order of must weight: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese, Trockenbeerenauslese; Eiswein has the same minimum as Beerenauslese.
Trocken and halbtrocken are legally defined; feinherb is not.
A Großlage is a collective site under the 1971 law; until the 2026 vintage it was labelled like a single vineyard.
The VDP classification (Gutswein, Ortswein, Erste Lage, Große Lage) is private; Großes Gewächs is a dry wine from a Große Lage.

questions.q: How many Anbaugebiete can produce German Qualitätswein?
questions.explain: German Qualitätswein and Prädikatswein must come from one of the 13 Anbaugebiete, the official quality wine regions.

questions.q: Which German category may not be enriched with sugar before fermentation?
questions.explain: Prädikatswein must reach its ripeness naturally and may not be chaptalised. Qualitätswein may be enriched.

questions.q: What do the German Prädikat levels measure?
options: Residual sugar in the finished wine
Must weight of the grapes at harvest
questions.explain: Prädikate are based on the sugar content of the must at harvest, so a Spätlese can still be fermented fully dry.

questions.q: Which Prädikat is pressed from grapes frozen on the vine?
questions.explain: Eiswein is made from grapes frozen on the vine and must reach the same minimum must weight as a Beerenauslese.

questions.q: What does feinherb on a German label mean?
options: A legally defined term for bone-dry wine
An unregulated term usually used for off-dry wine
A Prädikat level between Kabinett and Spätlese
The VDP name for its top vineyards
questions.explain: Feinherb is widely used for off-dry wines but has no legal definition, unlike trocken and halbtrocken.

questions.q: Under the 1971 wine law, what is Piesporter Michelsberg?
questions.explain: Michelsberg is a Großlage, a collective site that groups many vineyards. Piesporter Goldtröpfchen is the famous single vineyard.

questions.q: What is a Großes Gewächs (GG)?
options: A dry wine from a VDP Große Lage
A sweet wine from a legal Großlage
questions.explain: In the VDP's private classification, GG is the name for a dry wine from one of its top sites, a Große Lage.

questions.q: Which statement about the VDP classification is correct?
options: It was set out in the 1971 wine law
It was introduced by the EU in 2009
It applies to every producer in a region
It is a private classification that binds only member estates
questions.explain: The VDP is an association of estates. Its four-level classification is private and separate from German wine law.

lessons.title: The Mosel
lessons.intro: The Mosel is the home of light, racy Riesling grown on slate. This lesson covers the river's landscape and soils, the Mosel style, the great villages of the Middle Mosel, the cooler Saar and Ruwer, and the Großlage names to watch for.

p: The Mosel rises in the Vosges in France, forms part of the border with Luxembourg and joins the Rhine at Koblenz. The region was called Mosel-Saar-Ruwer until 2007, when it was renamed Mosel. It is cool and northerly, so site is everything.

The best vineyards sit on steep slopes above the river's tight meanders, facing south or south-west. Devonian slate dominates. The dark stone absorbs heat by day and the river reflects light onto the vines. Many slopes can only be worked by hand. The Calmont at Bremm is often called one of the steepest vineyards in Europe.

Riesling dominates the quality vineyards. Classic Mosel Riesling is light in body and alcohol, with high acidity and aromas of green apple, citrus and peach, often with a stony or smoky note. Many Kabinett and Spätlese wines keep residual sugar that balances the acidity, though dry wines are now common too.
The Upper Mosel (Obermosel), near Luxembourg, lies on limestone rather than slate. Here the old Elbling grape is still grown, often for sparkling wine.

The Middle Mosel (Mittelmosel) is the heart of the region. Bernkastel is known for the Doctor vineyard, among the most famous in Germany. Wehlen's Sonnenuhr takes its name from a sundial in the vineyard. Graach, Zeltingen, Ürzig, with its red soils in the Würzgarten, and Brauneberg are other great names.

Upriver, Piesport's Goldtröpfchen is a south-facing slope shaped like an amphitheatre. These villages also give their names to Großlagen: Bernkasteler Badstube and Kurfürstlay, Graacher Münzlay for Wehlen, Graach and Zeltingen, and Piesporter Michelsberg.

The Saar and the Ruwer are tributaries that join the Mosel near Trier. Both valleys are cooler than the Middle Mosel. In cool years the grapes struggle to ripen; in warm years the wines are some of the most finely etched Rieslings in the world, with steely acidity.

The Scharzhofberg at Wiltingen is the Saar's most famous vineyard; the whole Saar falls in the Großlage Scharzberg. On the Ruwer, Maximin Grünhaus and the Karthäuserhofberg at Eitelsbach are the best-known estates and sites. Trier and the Ruwer share the Großlage Römerlay.
Downstream towards Koblenz, the Lower Mosel is also called the Terrassenmosel for its terraced slopes. The Calmont lies here.

Some Mosel Großlagen are better known than any vineyard in them because they were used for large volumes of simple wine. Zeller Schwarze Katz, with its black cat label, and Kröver Nacktarsch are the classic examples. They show why reading the site name alone can mislead.

key: The region was named Mosel-Saar-Ruwer until 2007.
Steep south-facing slopes of Devonian slate above the river give the best sites.
Classic Mosel Riesling: low alcohol, high acidity, often balanced by residual sugar.
Great Middle Mosel sites: Bernkasteler Doctor, Wehlener Sonnenuhr, Piesporter Goldtröpfchen.
The Saar and Ruwer are cooler side valleys; Scharzhofberg is the Saar's top vineyard.
The Upper Mosel lies on limestone and grows Elbling.

questions.q: What was the Mosel region called until 2007?
questions.explain: The Anbaugebiet was renamed from Mosel-Saar-Ruwer to Mosel in 2007.

questions.q: Which soil dominates the best Middle Mosel vineyards?
questions.explain: Devonian slate is the classic Mosel soil. It warms quickly and drains well on the steep slopes.

questions.q: Which famous vineyard lies in the village of Wehlen?
questions.explain: The Wehlener Sonnenuhr is named after the sundial set in the vineyard.

questions.q: How is the Piesporter Goldtröpfchen vineyard best described?
options: A flat site on the river bank
A south-facing slope shaped like an amphitheatre
questions.explain: Goldtröpfchen is a curved, south-facing amphitheatre of slate above Piesport.

questions.q: How do the Saar and Ruwer differ from the Middle Mosel?
options: They are warmer and give fuller wines
They are cooler, with harder ripening in cool years and steely acidity
They are planted mainly to red grapes
They lie on limestone rather than slate
questions.explain: Both side valleys are cooler. In good years they give very fine Riesling with steely acidity.

questions.q: Where in the Mosel is Elbling still grown on limestone?
questions.explain: The Upper Mosel near Luxembourg lies on limestone, and the old Elbling grape survives there.

questions.q: Zeller Schwarze Katz and Kröver Nacktarsch are examples of what?
options: Großlagen widely used for simple wine
questions.explain: Both are Großlagen whose names became famous through large volumes of simple wine.

questions.q: Which description fits a classic Mosel Riesling Kabinett?
options: Full body, high alcohol, low acidity
Light body, low alcohol, high acidity, often with some residual sugar
questions.explain: Mosel Kabinett is light and racy, and residual sugar often balances its high acidity.

lessons.title: The Rhine regions
lessons.intro: This lesson covers five Anbaugebiete on the Rhine and its tributary the Nahe. It covers the Rheingau, Rheinhessen and its Roter Hang, the Pfalz, the Nahe and the Mittelrhein gorge.

p: Between Wiesbaden and Rüdesheim the Rhine flows from east to west, so the vineyards on its north bank face south. The Taunus hills shelter them from cold north winds. Riesling is the main grape, with Spätburgunder (Pinot Noir) second, famously at Assmannshausen on the bend of the river.

The Rheingau has a long history. Tradition says the value of late-harvested grapes was discovered at Schloss Johannisberg in 1775, when the courier bringing permission to pick arrived late. The Cistercians of Kloster Eberbach shaped its vineyards. Hochheim, on the Main, gave the English word hock for Rhine wine.

Rheinhessen is Germany's largest Anbaugebiet by vineyard area, a gentle landscape of rolling hills inside the bend of the Rhine. It was long known for bulk wine such as Liebfraumilch and for Müller-Thurgau and Silvaner. Since the 1990s, a new generation of growers has transformed its reputation.

The Rheinterrasse is a band of slopes along the river at Nackenheim, Nierstein and Oppenheim. Its heart is the Roter Hang, the red slope, where red Permian clay-slate and sandstone give rich, spicy Riesling. Pettenthal and Hipping, two Roter Hang sites, lie in the Großlage Rehbach. In the south, the Wonnegau around Westhofen has become a source of top dry Riesling from limestone.

The Pfalz lies west of the Rhine and north of Alsace. The Haardt mountains, the northern continuation of the Vosges, put it in a rain shadow, so it is one of Germany's warmest and driest regions. Almonds and figs grow along the Deutsche Weinstraße, the wine road.

The Mittelhaardt, with Forst, Deidesheim, Wachenheim and Bad Dürkheim, is the Riesling heartland. Forst has patches of basalt, notably in the Pechstein vineyard. The Südliche Weinstraße to the south grows much Weißburgunder, Grauburgunder and Spätburgunder. The red crossing Dornfelder is also widely planted.

The Nahe flows from the west and joins the Rhine at Bingen. Its soils are unusually varied for a small region: volcanic rock, porphyry, slate, sandstone and quartzite all occur, sometimes within one village. The Rotenfels cliff near Bad Münster is a landmark.

Riesling is the leading grape. Nahe Riesling is often said to sit between the mineral delicacy of the Mosel and the weight of the Rheingau. Some of its finest sites lie in the middle Nahe: the Kupfergrube and Felsenberg at Schlossböckelheim and the Hermannshöhle at Niederhausen.

Below Bingen the Rhine cuts a narrow gorge through slate hills. This landscape of castles and terraces, including the Lorelei rock, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2002 as the Upper Middle Rhine Valley.

The Mittelrhein is small. Its steep slate slopes grow mostly Riesling, with Bacharach and Boppard among the best-known villages. Steep slopes and hand work mean many vineyards have been abandoned over time.

key: In the Rheingau the Rhine flows east to west, so the main slopes face south; the Taunus shelters them.
Assmannshausen in the Rheingau is known for Spätburgunder.
Rheinhessen is Germany's largest Anbaugebiet; the Roter Hang at Nierstein has red Permian soils.
The Pfalz lies in the rain shadow of the Haardt, the continuation of the Vosges; the Mittelhaardt is its Riesling heart.
The Nahe is known for very varied soils, including volcanic rock and slate.
The Mittelrhein gorge is a UNESCO World Heritage Site with steep slate vineyards.

questions.q: Why do most Rheingau vineyards face south?
options: The Rhine flows from east to west along this stretch
The vineyards lie on the west bank of a north-flowing river
They are planted on terraces cut into a gorge
The Haardt mountains block the morning sun
questions.explain: Between Wiesbaden and Rüdesheim the Rhine runs east to west, so the north bank faces south.

questions.q: Which Rheingau village is best known for Spätburgunder?
questions.explain: Assmannshausen, on the bend of the Rhine, is the Rheingau's classic source of red Spätburgunder.

questions.q: What is the Roter Hang?
options: A red-slate site in the Ahr
A slope of red Permian soils at Nierstein in Rheinhessen
questions.explain: The Roter Hang, the red slope, is the heart of Rheinhessen's Rheinterrasse, with red clay-slate and sandstone.

questions.q: Which is Germany's largest Anbaugebiet by vineyard area?
questions.explain: Rheinhessen has the largest vineyard area of the 13 regions, with the Pfalz second.

questions.q: What makes the Pfalz one of Germany's warmest and driest regions?
options: The rain shadow of the Haardt mountains
questions.explain: The Haardt, the northern continuation of the Vosges, shelters the Pfalz from rain coming from the west.

questions.q: Which group of villages belongs to the Mittelhaardt in the Pfalz?
questions.explain: Forst, Deidesheim, Wachenheim and Bad Dürkheim make up the Riesling heartland of the Mittelhaardt.

questions.q: What is the Nahe best known for in terms of terroir?
options: A wide variety of soils, including volcanic rock, porphyry and slate
questions.explain: The Nahe packs volcanic rock, porphyry, slate, sandstone and quartzite into a small area.

questions.q: Which region is a gorge with steep slate vineyards inside a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
questions.explain: The Upper Middle Rhine Valley has been a World Heritage Site since 2002. Its slate slopes grow mostly Riesling.

lessons.title: Spätburgunder and Germany beyond the Rhine
lessons.intro: Germany is not only Riesling. This lesson covers the red wines of the Ahr and Baden, Silvaner in Franken, the red grapes of Württemberg, and the small northern regions of Saale-Unstrut and Sachsen.

sections.h: Ahr: red wine in the north
p: The Ahr is a narrow, steep valley that joins the Rhine south of Bonn. Although it is one of Germany's most northerly regions, it is planted mainly to red grapes. Slate and greywacke on steep slopes store heat and help ripening.

Spätburgunder (Pinot Noir) is the main grape, joined by Frühburgunder, an early-ripening form of Pinot. The region has a single Großlage, Klosterberg. In July 2021 a severe flood caused great damage to the valley and its wineries.

Baden is Germany's most southerly region, stretching from the Tauberfranken in the north to Lake Constance (Bodensee). It is the only German region in EU wine-growing zone B, the same zone as Alsace, while the rest of Germany is in zone A.

The Burgunder family leads: Spätburgunder, Grauburgunder and Weißburgunder. The Kaiserstuhl, an extinct volcano covered in loess, is one of Germany's warmest spots. The Markgräflerland grows Gutedel (Chasselas), and the Ortenau, on granite, is known for Riesling, locally called Klingelberger.

Franken follows the river Main around Würzburg. The climate is continental, with cold winters and a risk of spring frost. Shell limestone (Muschelkalk) around Würzburg and Keuper further east are the main soils. The Würzburger Stein is the best-known vineyard.
Silvaner is the signature grape, giving dry, earthy, savoury wines; Müller-Thurgau is also widely planted. Franken wine is traditionally bottled in the Bocksbeutel, a flat, round flask.

Württemberg follows the Neckar and its tributaries around Stuttgart. It is unusual in Germany because red grapes dominate. Trollinger (the Schiava of Alto Adige) gives light, pale reds drunk locally. Lemberger (Blaufränkisch) gives deeper, firmer wines, and Schwarzriesling is Pinot Meunier.
Riesling is the main white grape. Cooperatives make a large share of the wine.

Saale-Unstrut and Sachsen lie in the former East Germany and are Germany's most north-easterly regions. Sachsen follows the Elbe around Dresden and Meissen. Both have a continental climate with frost risk, and both mostly make dry whites from grapes such as Müller-Thurgau, Weißburgunder and Riesling.
Hessische Bergstraße is a small region on the east side of the Rhine plain, south of Darmstadt, known mainly for Riesling.

key: The Ahr is a northerly region planted mainly to Spätburgunder on slate and greywacke.
Baden is Germany's only region in EU wine zone B; the Kaiserstuhl is an extinct volcano covered in loess.
Gutedel is Chasselas; Klingelberger is the Ortenau name for Riesling.
Franken: Silvaner on shell limestone, bottled in the Bocksbeutel.
Württemberg is red-dominated: Trollinger (Schiava), Lemberger (Blaufränkisch), Schwarzriesling (Pinot Meunier).
Sachsen lies on the Elbe around Dresden and Meissen.

questions.q: Which grape dominates the Ahr?
questions.explain: Despite its northern position, the Ahr is planted mainly to Spätburgunder, helped by heat-storing slate slopes.

questions.q: Which German region lies in EU wine-growing zone B?
questions.explain: Baden is the only German region in zone B, the same zone as Alsace. The rest of Germany is zone A.

questions.q: What is the Kaiserstuhl?
options: A slate gorge in the Mittelrhein
An extinct volcano covered in loess in Baden
A shell limestone vineyard in Würzburg
questions.explain: The Kaiserstuhl is an extinct volcano in Baden, one of Germany's warmest spots, known for Burgunder varieties.

questions.q: Which grape and bottle are traditional in Franken?
questions.explain: Franken's signature grape is Silvaner, traditionally bottled in the flat, round Bocksbeutel.

questions.q: Lemberger, widely grown in Württemberg, is the same grape as which variety?
questions.explain: Lemberger is the German name for Blaufränkisch. Trollinger is Schiava and Schwarzriesling is Pinot Meunier.

questions.q: Gutedel, grown in Baden's Markgräflerland, is known elsewhere as what?
questions.explain: Gutedel is Chasselas, the grape best known in Switzerland.

questions.q: Which region follows the Elbe around Dresden and Meissen?
questions.explain: Sachsen lies along the Elbe around Dresden and Meissen in the former East Germany.

questions.q: What is the soil most associated with Würzburg in Franken?
questions.explain: Shell limestone around Würzburg, including the famous Würzburger Stein, gives Franken Silvaner its savoury character.

lessons.title: Austria
lessons.intro: Austria makes dry whites of great precision from Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, serious reds from Blaufränkisch and Zweigelt, and some of the world's great sweet wines. This lesson covers the DAC system, the Wachau and its three categories, Kamptal and Kremstal, and Burgenland.

p: Austria's vineyards lie in the east of the country, in four broad wine areas: Niederösterreich (Lower Austria), Burgenland, Steiermark (Styria) and Wien (Vienna). The climate is continental, with warm Pannonian influence from the east. Grüner Veltliner is the most planted grape and Zweigelt the most planted red.

A scandal in 1985, when some producers added diethylene glycol to wine, led to one of Europe's strictest wine laws. Austria uses Prädikat names like Germany, with differences: Kabinett counts as Qualitätswein, and Austria adds Ausbruch and Strohwein. Wien is known for Gemischter Satz, a field blend, and Südsteiermark for Sauvignon Blanc on steep hills near Slovenia.

DAC stands for Districtus Austriae Controllatus. A DAC links a region to its typical grapes and style, much like an appellation. Weinviertel DAC, for Grüner Veltliner only, was the first, introduced in 2002.

Other DACs followed. Kamptal, Kremstal and Traisental are for Grüner Veltliner and Riesling. Mittelburgenland and Eisenberg are for Blaufränkisch, Neusiedlersee for Zweigelt, and Leithaberg for both whites and Blaufränkisch. Most DACs use a three-level origin pyramid: Gebietswein (regional wine), Ortswein (village wine) and Riedenwein (single-vineyard wine). Ried means single vineyard.

The Wachau is a short stretch of the Danube west of Krems. Terraces with dry-stone walls climb steep slopes of gneiss and other primary rock, often favoured for Riesling, while loess lower down suits Grüner Veltliner. Cool air from the Waldviertel to the north-west meets warm Pannonian air from the east, giving cool nights and slow ripening.

Vinea Wachau, a growers' association founded in 1983, uses three categories of dry wine. Steinfeder, named after a feather grass, is the lightest, at no more than 11.5% alcohol. Federspiel, named after falconry, sits between 11.5% and 12.5%. Smaragd, named after an emerald-green lizard, is the ripest and fullest, at 12.5% or more. Wachau DAC was added in 2020.

East of the Wachau the valleys open out. Kremstal surrounds the town of Krems, with primary rock near Stein and deep loess terraces to the east.
