Kamptal follows the Kamp river around Langenlois; its Zöbinger Heiligenstein is a famous steep hill for Riesling. Traisental, south of the Danube, is the smallest of the three.

All three are DACs for Grüner Veltliner and Riesling. The Österreichische Traditionsweingüter (ÖTW), an association of estates, began classifying top Rieden as Erste Lage privately, much like the VDP in Germany. Since 2023 Austrian law allows official Erste Lage and Große Lage classification, which is being phased in.

Burgenland, on the Hungarian border, is warm and the home of Austrian red wine. Blaufränkisch is the star of Mittelburgenland, of Eisenberg in the south, with its iron-rich soils, and of the Leithaberg hills north-west of the lake. Zweigelt, a crossing of St. Laurent and Blaufränkisch made in 1922 by Fritz Zweigelt, is the grape of Neusiedlersee DAC.

The Neusiedlersee is a large, shallow lake. In autumn its humidity and morning mists encourage noble rot, especially in the Seewinkel on the eastern shore around Illmitz. This makes the area a centre for Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese. Rust, on the western shore, is famous for Ruster Ausbruch, a botrytis sweet wine with a long history.

key: Grüner Veltliner is Austria's most planted grape; Zweigelt is the most planted red.
DAC means Districtus Austriae Controllatus; Weinviertel DAC (Grüner Veltliner) was the first, in 2002.
Most DACs use the pyramid Gebietswein, Ortswein, Riedenwein.
Vinea Wachau's dry categories, lightest to fullest: Steinfeder, Federspiel, Smaragd.
Blaufränkisch leads in Mittelburgenland, Eisenberg and Leithaberg; Zweigelt in Neusiedlersee DAC.
Mists from the shallow Neusiedlersee favour noble rot; Rust is known for Ausbruch.

questions.q: What was Austria's first DAC?
questions.explain: Weinviertel DAC, for Grüner Veltliner only, was introduced in 2002.

questions.q: In the Wachau, which category names the ripest and fullest dry wines?
questions.explain: Smaragd, named after an emerald-green lizard, is the fullest of Vinea Wachau's three dry categories.

questions.q: What does Riedenwein mean on an Austrian DAC label?
options: A sweet wine from botrytised grapes
A wine from a single vineyard
questions.explain: Ried means single vineyard. Riedenwein is the top level of the Gebietswein, Ortswein, Riedenwein pyramid.

questions.q: Which grapes are permitted for Kamptal DAC?
questions.explain: Kamptal, Kremstal and Traisental are DACs for Grüner Veltliner and Riesling. Weinviertel DAC is Grüner Veltliner only.

questions.q: Which climatic effect shapes the Wachau?
options: Cool air from the Waldviertel meeting warm Pannonian air from the east
questions.explain: Cool air from the north-west and warm air from the east give the Wachau cool nights and slow ripening.

questions.q: Which red grape is the focus of Mittelburgenland DAC?
questions.explain: Mittelburgenland, like Eisenberg, is a DAC for Blaufränkisch.

questions.q: Why is the area around the Neusiedlersee a centre for sweet wine?
options: Its humid autumns and morning mists encourage noble rot
Grapes are dried on straw in high mountain huts
Winter frosts allow Eiswein every year
Its limestone soils raise sugar levels
questions.explain: The large, shallow lake creates humidity and mist in autumn, ideal for botrytis, especially in the Seewinkel.

questions.q: How does Austrian law treat Kabinett, compared with Germany?
options: It counts as Qualitätswein, not Prädikatswein
It is not allowed in Austria
questions.explain: In Austria Kabinett is a Qualitätswein category, while Austria adds Ausbruch and Strohwein to its Prädikat levels.

paths.title: United States
paths.summary: How American wine law works, then the main regions: Napa Valley, Sonoma County, the Central Coast and Lodi in California, and the Willamette Valley, the Columbia Valley and the Finger Lakes further north.

lessons.title: How American wine law works
lessons.intro: This lesson explains what an American Viticultural Area is, why it controls only geography, and the percentages that govern origin, variety and vintage on a US wine label.

p: An American Viticultural Area (AVA) is a grape-growing region with a legal boundary. The federal Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau (TTB), part of the US Treasury, approves AVAs and controls wine labels. The system dates from regulations of 1978. The first AVA was Augusta, Missouri, in 1980. Napa Valley followed in 1981 as the first in California.

An AVA defines geography only. It sets no rules on grape varieties, yields, vine training, alcohol, ageing or wine style. This is the main difference from a French AOC or an Italian DOC. A producer in Napa Valley may plant any variety, make any style, and still use the name.

Anyone can petition the TTB for a new AVA. The petition must show that the name is known locally for that area and that the area has features that set it apart, such as climate, soils, elevation or landforms. The boundary is drawn on official maps. Nothing in the process judges quality, so an AVA is not a quality ranking.

AVAs can be nested. Oakville lies inside Napa Valley, which lies inside the multi-county North Coast AVA. AVAs can also cross state lines: Columbia Valley and Walla Walla Valley both reach from Washington into Oregon.

An AVA on the label means at least 85% of the grapes come from that AVA. A state name needs at least 75% from that state under federal law, but several states ask for more. California requires 100% California grapes. A county name needs at least 75% from that county.

A varietal name, such as Cabernet Sauvignon, needs at least 75% of that variety. Some native labrusca varieties such as Concord have a lower limit. Oregon is stricter: it asks for 90%, for example for Pinot Noir. A listed group, such as Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah, keeps 75%. A vintage date needs 95% of the wine from that year when an AVA is named, and 85% with a state or county name.

A named vineyard requires 95% of the grapes from that vineyard. Estate Bottled is stricter: the winery must be in the AVA named, must grow all the grapes on vineyards it owns or controls in that AVA, and must make and bottle the whole wine on its own premises. Terms such as Reserve and Old Vine have no federal definition.

Many top wines are blends with no single variety at 75%. They are sold under a brand name or as Red Wine. Meritage is a registered term for blends of Bordeaux varieties made by members of the Meritage Alliance. A California state law also requires a wine labelled with a Napa sub-AVA, such as Rutherford, to show Napa Valley on the label.

key: An AVA is a geographic boundary approved by the TTB. It has no rules on grapes, yields, ageing or style.
AVA on the label: at least 85% of the grapes from that AVA.
State name: 75% federal minimum, but California requires 100%. County name: 75%.
Varietal name: at least 75% of the variety. Oregon asks for 90%, except for a listed group such as Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah.
Vintage: 95% from that year with an AVA, 85% with a state or county name.
The first AVA was Augusta, Missouri (1980). Napa Valley (1981) was the first in California.

questions.q: Which body approves new AVAs?
options: The Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau (TTB)
questions.explain: AVAs are federal. The TTB, part of the US Treasury, approves them and controls wine labels.

questions.q: What does an AVA regulate?
options: The grape varieties that may be planted
Only the geographic origin of the grapes
questions.explain: An AVA is purely geographic. Unlike an AOC or DOC, it sets no rules on varieties, yields, ageing or style.

questions.q: A wine labelled with an AVA must contain at least what share of grapes from that AVA?
questions.explain: The AVA rule is 85%. The 75% figure applies to state and county names and to varietal labelling.

questions.q: A wine labelled California must contain what share of California grapes?
questions.explain: Federal law asks for 75% for a state name, but California requires 100% of its own grapes.

questions.q: Under federal law, a wine labelled Cabernet Sauvignon must contain at least how much Cabernet Sauvignon?
questions.explain: The federal varietal minimum is 75%. The lower limit applies only to some labrusca varieties, and 90% is Oregon's stricter rule for varieties such as Pinot Noir.

questions.q: A vintage-dated wine labelled with an AVA must contain what share of wine from that vintage?
questions.explain: With an AVA the vintage rule is 95%. With a state or county name it is 85%.

questions.q: Which was the first AVA to be approved?
questions.explain: Augusta in Missouri became the first AVA in 1980. Napa Valley followed in 1981 as California's first.

questions.q: Which of these AVAs crosses a state line?
questions.explain: Walla Walla Valley, like Columbia Valley, reaches from Washington into Oregon. AVAs are not bound by state borders.

lessons.title: Napa Valley
lessons.intro: This lesson covers the geography and climate of Napa Valley, its Cabernet Sauvignon, the 1976 Judgment of Paris, and the main sub-AVAs on the valley floor and in the mountains.

p: Napa Valley runs about 30 miles (50 km) from the town of Calistoga in the north to the city of Napa in the south. The Mayacamas Mountains form its western side and separate it from Sonoma. The Vaca Range forms the eastern side. The Napa Valley AVA covers most of Napa County, including the hills, not only the valley floor.

sections.h: Fog and the north to south gradient
p: San Pablo Bay, the northern arm of San Francisco Bay, lies at the southern end. Cool air and fog move up the valley from the bay in the evening and often stay until late morning. The south is therefore the coolest part and the north, around Calistoga, the warmest. Wide swings between day and night help the grapes keep acidity as they ripen.

Fog rarely reaches the higher slopes. Mountain vineyards sit above the fog line: they get more morning sun but stay cooler at the hottest time of day. Thin soils and wind give small berries and firm tannins. Valley floor sites have deeper alluvial soils, washed down from the hills in fans and benches.

sections.h: Cabernet Sauvignon and the Judgment of Paris
p: Cabernet Sauvignon is Napa's leading grape. Typical wines are full bodied, with ripe black fruit, ripe but firm tannins and often new French oak. Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot go into Bordeaux-style blends. Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc are the main whites, and Chardonnay does best in the cooler south.

At the 1976 Judgment of Paris, a blind tasting organised by Steven Spurrier, French judges placed two Napa wines first: Stag's Leap Wine Cellars 1973 Cabernet Sauvignon among the reds and Chateau Montelena 1973 Chardonnay among the whites. The result brought California world attention.

Oakville and Rutherford, in the middle of the valley, are famous for Cabernet Sauvignon. Oakville holds the To Kalon vineyard and Opus One, the joint venture of Robert Mondavi and Baron Philippe de Rothschild whose first vintage was 1979. Rutherford's gravelly western bench gave rise to the phrase Rutherford dust, a dusty tannin texture linked to winemaker André Tchelistcheff.

Stags Leap District lies on the east side, below rocky cliffs of the Vaca Range. Afternoon breezes from the bay cool its vineyards, and its Cabernet is known for soft, silky tannins. St. Helena, Yountville, Oak Knoll District and Calistoga are also valley AVAs. Coombsville, east of the city of Napa, is one of the coolest.

On the Mayacamas side are Mt. Veeder, Spring Mountain District and Diamond Mountain District. On the Vaca side are Howell Mountain and Atlas Peak. Howell Mountain starts at 1,400 feet (about 425 m), above the fog, and its volcanic and red clay soils give powerful, tannic Cabernet Sauvignon.

Los Carneros lies at the southern end, on the shore of San Pablo Bay, and crosses into Sonoma County. It is cool and windy, with shallow clay soils. It is known for Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and sparkling wine, and has drawn investment from Champagne and Cava houses.

key: Mayacamas Mountains to the west, Vaca Range to the east, San Pablo Bay to the south.
Fog and cool air come up from the bay: the south is coolest, Calistoga in the north is warmest.
Cabernet Sauvignon is the leading grape, alone or in Bordeaux-style blends.
1976 Judgment of Paris: Stag's Leap Wine Cellars 1973 Cabernet and Chateau Montelena 1973 Chardonnay came first.
Mountain AVAs such as Howell Mountain lie above the fog and give firmer tannins.
Los Carneros straddles Napa and Sonoma and is known for Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and sparkling wine.

questions.q: Which mountains form the western side of Napa Valley?
questions.explain: The Mayacamas Mountains form the western side and separate Napa from Sonoma. The Vaca Range is on the east.

questions.q: Where do the cooling fog and air in Napa Valley come from?
questions.explain: Fog and cool air move up the valley from San Pablo Bay at the southern end, the northern arm of San Francisco Bay.

questions.q: Which part of Napa Valley is generally the warmest?
questions.explain: Calistoga is at the northern end, furthest from the bay. Los Carneros and Coombsville in the south are the coolest.

questions.q: Which wine was placed first among the reds at the 1976 Judgment of Paris?
options: Stag's Leap Wine Cellars 1973 Cabernet Sauvignon
questions.explain: Stag's Leap Wine Cellars 1973 won the reds. Chateau Montelena won the whites, with its 1973 Chardonnay.

questions.q: In which AVA is the To Kalon vineyard?
questions.explain: To Kalon is in Oakville, home also to Opus One. Rutherford is known for its western bench and Rutherford dust.

questions.q: Which statement about Howell Mountain is correct?
options: It lies on the Mayacamas side next to Sonoma
Its lower boundary is 1,400 feet, above the fog
It is a cool AVA on the shore of San Pablo Bay
It is best known for sparkling wine
questions.explain: Howell Mountain is on the Vaca side and starts at 1,400 feet, above the fog. It gives powerful, tannic Cabernet Sauvignon.

questions.q: Which AVA straddles Napa and Sonoma counties and is known for Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and sparkling wine?
questions.explain: Los Carneros lies on San Pablo Bay across both counties. Its cool, windy climate suits Burgundy varieties and sparkling wine.

questions.q: Cabernet Sauvignon from Stags Leap District is best known for which feature?
options: Very light body and high acidity
questions.explain: Cooled by afternoon breezes from the bay, Stags Leap District is known for Cabernet with soft, silky tannins.

lessons.title: Sonoma County and the North Coast
lessons.intro: This lesson covers Sonoma County, from the foggy Russian River Valley and the true Sonoma Coast to the warmer Dry Creek, Alexander and Sonoma valleys, with Zinfandel and a look north to Mendocino.

p: Sonoma County lies west of Napa, across the Mayacamas Mountains, and reaches the Pacific Ocean. It is cooler and more varied than Napa. The cold ocean creates fog that flows inland through gaps in the coastal hills. The Petaluma Gap, an AVA defined by its wind, funnels marine air from the coast towards San Pablo Bay.
The broad North Coast AVA takes in Sonoma, Napa, Mendocino and Lake counties, with parts of others. Within Sonoma, the Northern Sonoma AVA groups the valleys around the town of Healdsburg.

The Russian River flows to the Pacific, and fog follows it inland most evenings. Russian River Valley is one of California's leading areas for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Many vineyards are on Goldridge, a fine sandy loam that drains well. Cool nights keep acidity in the grapes.
Green Valley of Russian River Valley, in the south-west, is among the coolest and foggiest parts. Chalk Hill, in the east, is warmer. Despite its name, its soils are volcanic, not chalk.

sections.h: Sonoma Coast and the true coast
p: Sonoma Coast is a very large AVA that runs from the Mendocino border to San Pablo Bay. It was criticised for including warmer inland sites, so smaller AVAs now define the true coast. Fort Ross-Seaview takes in ridges close to the ocean, many above the fog. The more recent West Sonoma Coast AVA covers the coastal strip.
These cool, windy sites give Pinot Noir and Chardonnay with high acidity and moderate alcohol, and cool-climate Syrah with peppery notes.

Dry Creek Valley, north-west of Healdsburg, is warm and known for Zinfandel, often from old vines on the benches, and for Sauvignon Blanc. Alexander Valley, along the upper Russian River north-east of Healdsburg, is also warm and best known for ripe, round Cabernet Sauvignon. Knights Valley, next to Napa's Calistoga, also grows Cabernet.

Sonoma Valley, called the Valley of the Moon, lies between the Mayacamas and the Sonoma Mountains. In 1857 Agoston Haraszthy founded Buena Vista Winery here, one of California's oldest commercial wineries. Moon Mountain District and Sonoma Mountain are hillside AVAs within it.

sections.h: Zinfandel, and Mendocino to the north
p: Zinfandel is DNA-identical to Italy's Primitivo and to the Croatian variety Crljenak Kaštelanski, also called Tribidrag. Its berries ripen unevenly in the bunch, so wines can show fresh and raisined fruit together, often with high alcohol. Old vineyards are often field blends with Petite Sirah and Carignan.

North of Sonoma, much of Mendocino County is warm and inland. The exception is Anderson Valley, close to the ocean and cool, which makes Pinot Noir, Gewürztraminer, Riesling and traditional-method sparkling wine.

key: Sonoma is cooler and more varied than Napa because of Pacific fog and wind gaps such as the Petaluma Gap.
Russian River Valley: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, fog along the river, Goldridge sandy loam.
Sonoma Coast is very large. Fort Ross-Seaview and West Sonoma Coast mark the true coast.
Dry Creek Valley: Zinfandel and Sauvignon Blanc. Alexander Valley: Cabernet Sauvignon.
Zinfandel is DNA-identical to Primitivo and Crljenak Kaštelanski (Tribidrag).
Anderson Valley in Mendocino is cool: Pinot Noir, aromatic whites and sparkling wine.

questions.q: Which Sonoma AVA is defined by the wind that carries marine air from the coast towards San Pablo Bay?
questions.explain: The Petaluma Gap is a break in the coastal hills that funnels cool marine air inland.

questions.q: Which grapes is Russian River Valley best known for?
questions.explain: Fog along the Russian River gives cool nights that suit Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

questions.q: What are the soils of Chalk Hill?
questions.explain: Despite its name, Chalk Hill has volcanic soils, not chalk.

questions.q: Why were smaller AVAs such as Fort Ross-Seaview created within Sonoma Coast?
options: Sonoma Coast was too small to be known abroad
Sonoma Coast included warmer inland sites as well as the true coast
Sonoma Coast did not allow Pinot Noir
questions.explain: Sonoma Coast is very large and includes warmer inland areas. Fort Ross-Seaview and West Sonoma Coast define the cool coastal sites.

questions.q: Dry Creek Valley is best known for which grapes?
questions.explain: Dry Creek Valley is warm, with old-vine Zinfandel on the benches and Sauvignon Blanc.

questions.q: Zinfandel is DNA-identical to which Italian variety?
questions.explain: Zinfandel, Primitivo and the Croatian Crljenak Kaštelanski (Tribidrag) are the same variety.

questions.q: In which AVA did Agoston Haraszthy found Buena Vista Winery in 1857?
questions.explain: Buena Vista is in Sonoma Valley, the Valley of the Moon, between the Mayacamas and the Sonoma Mountains.

questions.q: Which Mendocino AVA is cool and known for Pinot Noir, Gewürztraminer and sparkling wine?
questions.explain: Anderson Valley lies close to the ocean and is the cool exception in a mostly warm county.

lessons.title: The Central Coast and inland California
lessons.intro: This lesson covers the long Central Coast, from Monterey and the Santa Lucia Highlands to Paso Robles and Santa Barbara County, then the warm interior with Lodi.

sections.h: A long coast cooled by the Pacific
p: The Central Coast AVA runs from San Francisco Bay south to Santa Barbara County. The ocean here is cold, and marine air reaches inland wherever valleys open to the sea. The result is a long growing season with cool nights, so grapes can hang late into autumn and keep their acidity.

The Santa Cruz Mountains AVA, south of San Francisco, is defined by mountain terrain. Ridge Vineyards' Monte Bello Cabernet Sauvignon comes from here, and cooler sites make fine Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

sections.h: Monterey and the Santa Lucia Highlands
p: Monterey's Salinas Valley opens north onto Monterey Bay. Each afternoon cold, strong winds blow up the valley from the bay. Budbreak is early and harvest is late, so the growing season is one of the longest in California. Arroyo Seco, known for its stony soils, lies further south in the valley.

The Santa Lucia Highlands sit on terraces on the eastern flank of the Santa Lucia Range, above the valley floor. Wind and cool air make it a leading area for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, with some Syrah. Across the valley, in the Gabilan Mountains, Chalone and Mt. Harlan have rare limestone soils.

Paso Robles, in San Luis Obispo County, is warm by day and has some of the widest day to night temperature swings in California. Marine air enters through the Templeton Gap. The west side is hillier and wetter, with calcareous soils. The east side is flatter, warmer and drier. In 2014 the AVA was divided into 11 sub-AVAs.

Paso Robles is known for Zinfandel, Cabernet Sauvignon and Rhône varieties. Tablas Creek, a partnership between the Perrin family of Château de Beaucastel and importer Robert Haas, imported Rhône vine cuttings and helped spread Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre and Roussanne in the region.

sections.h: Santa Barbara County and the Sta. Rita Hills
p: In Santa Barbara County the mountain ranges run east to west, not north to south as on most of the coast. The valleys open straight onto the Pacific, so fog and wind travel far inland, and sites get warmer the further east they are. Santa Maria Valley, in the north of the county, is cool and known for Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

Sta. Rita Hills lies at the cool western end of the Santa Ynez Valley, between Lompoc and Buellton. It makes Pinot Noir and Chardonnay with high acidity. The short form Sta. was agreed after an objection from the Chilean producer Viña Santa Rita. Further east, Ballard Canyon focuses on Syrah, and warm Happy Canyon of Santa Barbara on Bordeaux varieties.

sections.h: Inland: Lodi and the Central Valley
p: The Central Valley is California's hot, flat interior. Irrigated vineyards here produce most of the state's wine by volume, much of it for inexpensive brands. Lodi, at the northern end, is cooled in the afternoon by breezes from the delta where the Sacramento and San Joaquin rivers meet.

Lodi is famous for old-vine Zinfandel. In the Mokelumne River sub-AVA, many old vines grow on their own roots in deep sandy soils, which resist phylloxera. Lodi has seven sub-AVAs, approved in 2006. To the east, the Sierra Foothills also have old Zinfandel vines, a legacy of the Gold Rush.

key: The Central Coast AVA runs from San Francisco Bay to Santa Barbara County, with a long, cool growing season.
Monterey: strong afternoon winds from Monterey Bay. Santa Lucia Highlands: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay on terraces.
Paso Robles: warm days, wide diurnal range, Zinfandel, Cabernet and Rhône varieties. 11 sub-AVAs since 2014.
Santa Barbara's east to west ranges let ocean air far inland. Sta. Rita Hills: cool, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
Lodi: delta breezes, old-vine Zinfandel, own-rooted vines on sandy soils in Mokelumne River.

questions.q: What cools the vineyards of Monterey's Salinas Valley?
options: Strong afternoon winds from Monterey Bay
Breezes from the Sacramento and San Joaquin delta
questions.explain: The Salinas Valley opens north onto Monterey Bay, and cold winds blow up the valley each afternoon.

questions.q: Which grapes are the Santa Lucia Highlands best known for?
questions.explain: Its windy, cool terraces above the Salinas Valley make it a leading area for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

questions.q: In which year was Paso Robles divided into 11 sub-AVAs?
questions.explain: The 11 Paso Robles sub-AVAs, such as Adelaida District, were approved in 2014. 2006 is the year of Lodi's seven sub-AVAs.

questions.q: Tablas Creek in Paso Robles is a partnership with the family behind which estate?
questions.explain: The Perrin family of Château de Beaucastel founded Tablas Creek with Robert Haas and brought in Rhône vine cuttings.

questions.q: Why can ocean air travel far inland in Santa Barbara County?
options: The vineyards are at very high altitude
The mountain ranges run east to west and the valleys open onto the Pacific
The county lies further north than Napa
questions.explain: Unlike most of the coast, Santa Barbara's ranges run east to west, so fog and wind flow straight up the valleys.

questions.q: Where is the Sta. Rita Hills AVA?
options: At the warm eastern end of the Santa Ynez Valley
At the cool western end of the Santa Ynez Valley, between Lompoc and Buellton
On the terraces of the Santa Lucia Range
questions.explain: Sta. Rita Hills is at the cool western end of the Santa Ynez Valley. Happy Canyon is at the warm eastern end.

questions.q: What cools Lodi in the afternoon?
options: Its high altitude in the Sierra Nevada
Breezes from the delta of the Sacramento and San Joaquin rivers
questions.explain: Lodi, at the northern end of the Central Valley, gets cooling afternoon breezes from the delta.

questions.q: Which Santa Barbara County AVA is the warmest and focuses on Bordeaux varieties?
questions.explain: Happy Canyon lies at the warm eastern end of the Santa Ynez Valley. Ballard Canyon focuses on Syrah.

lessons.title: Oregon, Washington and New York
lessons.intro: This lesson covers the Willamette Valley and its soil-based sub-AVAs in Oregon, the Columbia Valley and Walla Walla in Washington, and the Finger Lakes and Long Island in New York.

p: The Willamette Valley runs south from Portland towards Eugene, between the Coast Range to the west and the Cascade Mountains to the east. The Coast Range shields it from the worst Pacific weather. Summers are warm and dry, winters mild and wet, and autumn rain can threaten the harvest. Vintages vary more than in California.

Pinot Noir is the leading grape, followed by Pinot Gris and Chardonnay. In 1965 David Lett planted Pinot Noir in the valley, and he later founded The Eyrie Vineyards in the Dundee Hills. Burgundy took note: the Drouhin family founded Domaine Drouhin Oregon in the Dundee Hills in 1987.

Soil type defines many sub-AVAs. Dundee Hills is known for red volcanic Jory soil, formed from basalt. Yamhill-Carlton has marine sedimentary soils such as Willakenzie. Ribbon Ridge, a small ridge within the Chehalem Mountains, is also sedimentary. Chehalem Mountains mixes volcanic, sedimentary and windblown loess soils, and its Laurelwood District takes its name from the loess-based Laurelwood soil.

The Van Duzer Corridor is a gap in the Coast Range. Cold ocean air flows through it in the afternoon and over the Eola-Amity Hills, cooling the vines and helping keep acidity. Other sub-AVAs include McMinnville and Tualatin Hills.
Southern Oregon, with the Umpqua and Rogue valleys, is warmer and drier. It grows a wider range of grapes, including Syrah, Tempranillo and Bordeaux varieties.

Most of Washington's vineyards lie east of the Cascade Mountains, in their rain shadow. The Columbia Valley AVA is semi-desert, so vines need irrigation from the Columbia River and its tributaries. Summer days are long and sunny at this northern latitude, nights are cool and acidity stays fresh. Winters are cold, and hard freezes can kill vines.

Soils are mostly sand and silt over basalt, left by the Missoula Floods at the end of the last ice age. Sandy soils and cold winters keep phylloxera rare, so many vines grow on their own roots. Columbia Valley is a huge AVA that crosses into Oregon. Within it, Yakima Valley became Washington's first AVA in 1983.

Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Chardonnay and Riesling are the main grapes. Red Mountain, a small, warm AVA within Yakima Valley, is known for powerful, tannic Cabernet Sauvignon. West of the Cascades, the Puget Sound AVA is cool and wet.

sections.h: Walla Walla Valley and The Rocks
p: Walla Walla Valley, in the south-east of the Columbia Valley, crosses the state line into Oregon. It makes Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah. Within it, The Rocks District of Milton-Freewater lies entirely in Oregon. Its soils are a bed of basalt cobblestones, and it is best known for savoury, earthy Syrah.

sections.h: New York: the Finger Lakes and Long Island
p: The Finger Lakes are long, narrow, deep lakes in upstate New York, carved by glaciers. The largest, Seneca and Cayuga, have their own AVAs. The deep water stores heat: it softens winter cold, holds back budbreak in spring until frost risk has passed, and extends the autumn. Vineyards sit on slopes above the lakes, where cold air drains away.

Riesling is the signature grape, made from dry to sweet, alongside Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. In the 1950s and 1960s Dr. Konstantin Frank showed that European vinifera vines could survive the winters when grafted onto suitable rootstocks. Native varieties such as Concord and French-American hybrids are still widely grown.
On Long Island, the North Fork has a maritime climate moderated by the Atlantic and the surrounding bays. It is known for Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Chardonnay.

key: Willamette Valley lies between the Coast Range and the Cascades. Pinot Noir leads, with Pinot Gris and Chardonnay.
Dundee Hills: red volcanic Jory soil. Yamhill-Carlton: marine sedimentary soils. Laurelwood District: loess.
Columbia Valley is semi-desert in the Cascades rain shadow: irrigation, long summer days, cold winters, many own-rooted vines.
Yakima Valley (1983) was Washington's first AVA. Red Mountain is known for powerful Cabernet Sauvignon.
The Rocks District of Milton-Freewater, within Walla Walla Valley, lies in Oregon and is known for Syrah on basalt cobbles.
Finger Lakes: deep glacial lakes moderate the climate. Riesling is the signature grape.

questions.q: Between which mountain ranges does the Willamette Valley lie?
options: The Coast Range and the Cascade Mountains
The Mayacamas Mountains and the Vaca Range
The Cascade Mountains and the Rocky Mountains
The Santa Lucia Range and the Gabilan Mountains
questions.explain: The Coast Range lies to the west and shields the valley from Pacific weather. The Cascades lie to the east.

questions.q: What is the Jory soil of the Dundee Hills?
options: Red volcanic soil formed from basalt
questions.explain: Jory is a red volcanic soil from basalt. Willakenzie in Yamhill-Carlton is sedimentary, and Laurelwood is loess.

questions.q: Who planted Pinot Noir in the Willamette Valley in 1965 and founded The Eyrie Vineyards?
questions.explain: David Lett was the Willamette pioneer. The Drouhin family arrived later, founding Domaine Drouhin Oregon in 1987.

questions.q: What is the Van Duzer Corridor?
options: A river valley that brings warm southern winds
A volcanic ridge with Jory soil
A gap in the Coast Range that lets cold ocean air in
A lake that moderates winter temperatures
questions.explain: Cold Pacific air flows through this gap in the afternoon and over the Eola-Amity Hills, helping keep acidity.

questions.q: Why do vines in the Columbia Valley need irrigation?
options: Autumn rain washes the soils away
The sandy soils hold too much water
Fog from the Pacific blocks the sun
The region lies in the rain shadow of the Cascades
questions.explain: The Cascade Mountains block Pacific rain, leaving the Columbia Valley semi-desert. Water comes from the Columbia River and its tributaries.

questions.q: Why do many Washington vines grow on their own roots?
options: Sandy soils and cold winters keep phylloxera rare
All the vines are French-American hybrids
questions.explain: Phylloxera struggles in sandy soils and cold winters, so grafting is less needed in eastern Washington.

questions.q: The Rocks District of Milton-Freewater lies in which state, and which grape is it best known for?
questions.explain: It sits within Walla Walla Valley but entirely in Oregon, and its basalt cobblestones give savoury, earthy Syrah.

questions.q: Which grape is the signature of the Finger Lakes?
questions.explain: Riesling, made from dry to sweet, is the flagship of the Finger Lakes. Merlot is more typical of Long Island's North Fork.

paths.title: The Southern Hemisphere
paths.summary: Five lessons on the classic wine countries of the southern hemisphere: Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Chile and Argentina. Each lesson covers the origin system, the climate drivers, the key regions and the signature grapes and styles.

lessons.title: Australia: zones, regions and styles
lessons.intro: This lesson explains how Australia names the origin of its wines and then visits the regions that matter most in exams: the Barossa, McLaren Vale, Clare Valley and Coonawarra in South Australia, the Hunter Valley in New South Wales, and the cool regions of the Yarra Valley, Margaret River and Tasmania.

p: Australian wine origins are defined as Geographical Indications, or GIs, registered by Wine Australia. The system is a map of boundaries, not a set of production rules: a GI does not limit grape varieties, yields or winemaking. The hierarchy runs from state to zone, then region, then subregion.

An example: the state of South Australia contains the Barossa zone, which contains the Eden Valley region, which contains the High Eden subregion. There is also a multi-state GI, South Eastern Australia, used for large-volume blends sourced across several states.

Under Australian wine law, a wine that states a GI, a grape variety or a vintage must contain at least 85% of that GI, variety or vintage. The Label Integrity Program, with its record-keeping and audits, checks that such label claims are true.

The Barossa Valley lies north-east of Adelaide. It was settled in the 1840s by German-speaking Lutherans from Silesia. The valley floor is warm and dry, and it is best known for full-bodied Shiraz with ripe black fruit, as well as Grenache and Mourvèdre.
South Australia has never had phylloxera, thanks to strict quarantine rules. Many Barossa vines are therefore very old and grow on their own roots.

Eden Valley sits in the hills to the east, inside the same Barossa zone. It is higher and cooler, with poorer soils. It is famous for dry Riesling with lime and citrus flavours, and for elegant Shiraz such as Henschke's Hill of Grace.

sections.h: McLaren Vale, Clare Valley and Coonawarra
p: McLaren Vale, in the Fleurieu zone south of Adelaide, has a warm Mediterranean climate cooled by breezes from Gulf St Vincent. Shiraz, Grenache and Cabernet Sauvignon are the main grapes.

Clare Valley, in the Mount Lofty Ranges zone north of Adelaide, has warm days and cool nights. It makes bone-dry Riesling with high acidity and lime flavours that turn toasty with age. In 2000 a group of Clare Riesling producers switched together to screwcaps, a step that helped the closure spread across Australia.

Coonawarra, in the Limestone Coast zone, is a narrow strip of terra rossa: red clay loam over a bed of limestone. The climate is cool. Its Cabernet Sauvignon shows blackcurrant with a typical mint or eucalyptus note.

The Hunter Valley, north of Sydney in New South Wales, is hot and humid, with much of its rain falling in summer and often at harvest. Afternoon sea breezes and cloud cover temper the heat. The Hunter region has three subregions: Pokolbin, Broke Fordwich and Upper Hunter Valley.

Hunter Semillon is picked early, at low sugar, to avoid the rain. It is fermented in stainless steel without oak, and often has around 11% alcohol or less. Young, it is lean and citrusy. After some years in bottle it develops toast, honey and nut aromas, even though it has never seen oak. Hunter Shiraz is medium-bodied and earthy.

sections.h: Cool climates: Yarra Valley, Margaret River, Tasmania
p: The Yarra Valley, near Melbourne in Victoria, is cool. It is known for Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and traditional method sparkling wine, as well as Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz.

Margaret River, in the South West Australia zone, has a maritime climate shaped by the Indian Ocean to the west and the Southern Ocean to the south. Planting began in the late 1960s after scientific studies compared its climate to Bordeaux. It makes Cabernet Sauvignon, Bordeaux-style blends, Chardonnay, and Semillon and Sauvignon Blanc blends.
Tasmania, the island south of the mainland, is the coolest part of Australia. It is a leading source of traditional method sparkling wine, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Riesling.

key: The GI hierarchy runs state, zone, region, subregion; GIs set boundaries but not production rules.
The 85% rule applies to a stated GI, grape variety or vintage.
South Australia has never had phylloxera, so the Barossa has many old own-rooted vines.
Eden Valley and Clare Valley are the classic sources of dry, lime-scented Riesling.
Coonawarra means terra rossa over limestone and Cabernet Sauvignon.
Hunter Semillon is picked early, unoaked and low in alcohol, and becomes toasty with bottle age.

questions.q: What is the order of the Australian GI hierarchy, from largest to smallest?
questions.explain: Australian GIs run from state to zone, then region, then subregion, for example South Australia, Barossa, Eden Valley, High Eden.

questions.q: An Australian label names a single grape variety. What share of the wine must come from that variety?
questions.explain: Under Australian wine law, a stated GI, variety or vintage must make up at least 85% of the wine. The Label Integrity Program checks these claims.

questions.q: Why does the Barossa Valley have so many very old vines on their own roots?
options: The vines were grafted onto American rootstock in the 1840s
Its sandy soils are too dry for vines to need grafting
Old vines were protected by a law banning replanting
South Australia has never had phylloxera
questions.explain: Strict quarantine has kept phylloxera out of South Australia, so old own-rooted vines survive.

questions.q: How does Eden Valley differ from the Barossa Valley?
options: It is lower and warmer, and focuses on fortified wine
It is higher and cooler, and is known for dry Riesling
It is a separate zone with sandy coastal soils
It is a subregion of McLaren Vale
questions.explain: Eden Valley lies in the hills east of the Barossa Valley, in the same zone. It is higher and cooler and famous for dry Riesling.

questions.q: Which soil and grape define Coonawarra?
options: Terra rossa over limestone and Cabernet Sauvignon
questions.explain: Coonawarra is a narrow strip of red terra rossa over limestone, best known for Cabernet Sauvignon.

questions.q: Which description fits classic Hunter Valley Semillon?
options: Late-picked, barrel-fermented and high in alcohol
Blended with Sauvignon Blanc and aged in new oak
Picked early, unoaked and low in alcohol, gaining toasty notes with age
questions.explain: Hunter Semillon is picked early to avoid harvest rain, made without oak, and develops toast and honey in bottle.

questions.q: Clare Valley Riesling producers acted together in 2000 to adopt which change?
questions.explain: In 2000 a group of Clare Valley Riesling makers moved to screwcaps together, which helped the closure spread across Australia.

questions.q: What shapes the climate of Margaret River?
options: The Indian Ocean to the west and the Southern Ocean to the south
High altitude in the Great Dividing Range
questions.explain: Margaret River is maritime, bordered by the Indian Ocean to the west and the Southern Ocean to the south.

lessons.title: New Zealand: cool and maritime
lessons.intro: This lesson covers New Zealand's maritime climate and its four classic names for exams: Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc, Central Otago Pinot Noir, the Bordeaux blends and Syrah of Hawke's Bay and the Gimblett Gravels, and the Pinot Noir of Martinborough.

p: New Zealand is two long, narrow islands with a cool maritime climate. No vineyard is far from the sea. Prevailing westerly winds bring rain to the west coast, while mountain ranges shelter the east. Most wine regions lie on the eastern side, in the rain shadow, where it is sunnier and drier.

Regional names are protected as geographical indications under the Geographical Indications (Wine and Spirits) Registration Act 2006. As in Australia, a stated region, variety or vintage must account for at least 85% of the wine.

Marlborough, at the north-east tip of the South Island, is sunny and fairly dry, with cool nights. The long, cool ripening season keeps acidity high while flavours develop. The main areas are the Wairau Valley, the Southern Valleys and the cooler, drier Awatere Valley.

Commercial planting began in 1973, and Cloudy Bay, first made in 1985, brought the style world fame. Classic Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc is pungent, with high acidity and flavours of passion fruit, gooseberry, green bell pepper and cut grass. Most is fermented in stainless steel and drunk young. The region also makes Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and sparkling wine.

Central Otago lies inland in the south of the South Island, among mountains. It is the only New Zealand region with a continental climate: hot, dry summers, cold winters, a high risk of frost and low rainfall, so irrigation is common. Soils are mainly schist-derived, with loess.

Pinot Noir dominates. It is typically ripe and fruit-forward, with red and dark cherry flavours and fresh acidity. Subregions differ in warmth: Bannockburn is one of the warmest and earliest-ripening, while Gibbston is higher and cooler. Riesling, Pinot Gris and Chardonnay are also grown.

sections.h: Hawke's Bay and the Gimblett Gravels
p: Hawke's Bay, on the east coast of the North Island, is one of New Zealand's warmest and sunniest regions, sheltered from westerly rain by inland ranges. It is the country's main source of Bordeaux-style reds, mostly based on Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon, as well as Syrah and Chardonnay.

The Gimblett Gravels is a district of deep, stony, infertile soils on the former bed of the Ngaruroro River. The stones drain freely and store heat, helping late-ripening varieties ripen fully. The name is a trademark managed by a local winegrowers' association, not an official GI.

Martinborough is a subregion of Wairarapa, at the south-east of the North Island near Wellington. It is cool, dry and very windy, and spring winds often reduce yields. Free-draining gravel terraces and small producers, many planted from around 1980, have made its Pinot Noir known for concentration and structure.
Other regions to know: Gisborne for Chardonnay, Nelson, Waipara Valley in North Canterbury for Riesling and Pinot Noir, and Waiheke Island near Auckland for Bordeaux blends and Syrah.

key: Most New Zealand regions lie on the east side of the islands, in the rain shadow of the mountains.
Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc: pungent, high acid, passion fruit, gooseberry and green pepper; fame came with Cloudy Bay in 1985.
Central Otago is New Zealand's only continental region; schist and loess soils; Pinot Noir.
Hawke's Bay is warm and makes Bordeaux blends and Syrah; the Gimblett Gravels is a former riverbed, trademarked rather than a GI.
Martinborough is a subregion of Wairarapa, known for structured Pinot Noir and strong winds.

questions.q: Which is the only New Zealand wine region with a continental climate?
questions.explain: Central Otago lies inland among mountains, with hot dry summers, cold winters and frost risk.

questions.q: Which set of flavours is typical of classic Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc?
options: Passion fruit, gooseberry and green bell pepper
questions.explain: Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc is pungent and high in acid, with passion fruit, gooseberry and green pepper notes.

questions.q: What are the Gimblett Gravels?
options: Stony soils on the former bed of the Ngaruroro River
questions.explain: The Gimblett Gravels is an area of deep, free-draining stones left by the Ngaruroro River in Hawke's Bay.

questions.q: Which wines are the Gimblett Gravels best known for?
questions.explain: The warm, heat-storing gravels help late-ripening Bordeaux varieties and Syrah ripen fully.

questions.q: Martinborough is a subregion of which New Zealand region?
questions.explain: Martinborough lies within Wairarapa at the south-east of the North Island.

questions.q: Which wine, first made in 1985, brought Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc to world attention?
questions.explain: Cloudy Bay's first Sauvignon Blanc in 1985 made the Marlborough style famous.

questions.q: Which soils are typical of Central Otago?
questions.explain: Central Otago soils are mainly schist-derived, with windblown loess.

questions.q: Why do most New Zealand wine regions lie on the eastern side of the islands?
options: The east is warmed by a tropical current
Mountains shelter the east from westerly rain
The east has a continental climate
questions.explain: Westerly winds drop their rain on the west coast; the east lies in the rain shadow and is sunnier and drier.

lessons.title: South Africa: Wine of Origin and the Cape
lessons.intro: This lesson explains South Africa's Wine of Origin scheme, the cold current and strong wind that shape the Cape, the key areas of Stellenbosch, Swartland and Constantia, and the two grapes most linked to the country: Chenin Blanc and Pinotage.

p: South Africa's Wine of Origin (WO) scheme was introduced in 1973. It defines nested areas. From largest to smallest they are the geographical unit, the region, the district and the ward. Estates and single vineyards can also be registered.

An example: the Western Cape geographical unit contains the Coastal Region, which contains the Stellenbosch district, which contains the Simonsberg-Stellenbosch ward. If a WO area is stated, all the grapes must come from it. A stated variety or vintage must make up at least 85% of the wine.

sections.h: The Benguela Current and the Cape Doctor
p: The Cape has a Mediterranean climate with warm, dry summers. Without cooling it would be too hot for fine wine in many places. The cold Benguela Current flows north from the Antarctic along the west coast and cools the land near the sea.

The Cape Doctor is a strong, dry south-easterly wind that blows in summer. It cools vineyards near False Bay and keeps the canopy dry, which reduces fungal disease. It can also damage leaves and reduce yields.

Cooler areas closer to the south coast, such as Elgin and the Hemel-en-Aarde wards of Walker Bay, suit Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Hot inland areas such as Robertson and Worcester in the Breede River Valley rely on irrigation.

Stellenbosch, east of Cape Town, is a district of mountain slopes, valleys and breezes from False Bay. Soils on the slopes are mostly granite-derived, with sandstone elsewhere. It is best known for Cabernet Sauvignon and Bordeaux-style blends, as well as Pinotage, Shiraz and Chenin Blanc. Its wards include Simonsberg-Stellenbosch, Jonkershoek Valley and Banghoek.

Constantia, south of Cape Town, is the Cape's most historic fine wine area. Governor Simon van der Stel founded the Constantia estate in 1685. Its sweet, unfortified Muscat wine, Vin de Constance, was famous across Europe in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Today Constantia is a cool ward, now in the Cape Town district, known for Sauvignon Blanc.
Swartland, north of Cape Town, is warm and dry. Its name, black land, comes from a dark native shrub. Much of it is farmed without irrigation, with old bush vines on granite and shale soils.

For a long time the area made bulk wine for cooperatives. From around 2000 a new wave of independent producers began making old-vine Chenin Blanc, white blends and Rhône-style reds from Syrah, Grenache, Cinsaut and Mourvèdre, often with minimal intervention. Swartland is now one of the Cape's most dynamic areas.

Chenin Blanc is South Africa's most planted grape, once known locally as Steen. It is made in every style: fresh and dry, rich and oaked from old vines, sweet, and traditional method sparkling, called Méthode Cap Classique.

Pinotage was created in 1925 by Professor Abraham Perold at Stellenbosch University by crossing Pinot Noir with Cinsaut, which was then called Hermitage in South Africa. It gives deeply coloured reds with dark fruit, sometimes with smoky notes. A Cape Blend is a red blend that includes Pinotage, though the term has no legal definition.

key: Wine of Origin dates from 1973; units are geographical unit, region, district, ward.
A stated WO area means 100% of the grapes; a variety or vintage needs at least 85%.
The cold Benguela Current and the summer south-easterly Cape Doctor cool the Cape and reduce disease.
Constantia: van der Stel, 1685, and the sweet Muscat Vin de Constance.
Swartland: warm, dry-farmed old bush vines, Chenin Blanc and Rhône varieties.
Pinotage is Pinot Noir crossed with Cinsaut, made by Abraham Perold in 1925.

questions.q: In which year was South Africa's Wine of Origin scheme introduced?
questions.explain: The Wine of Origin scheme began in 1973. 1925 is the year Pinotage was created and 1685 the founding of Constantia.

questions.q: What is the order of Wine of Origin units, from largest to smallest?
questions.explain: For example: Western Cape (geographical unit), Coastal Region, Stellenbosch (district), Simonsberg-Stellenbosch (ward).

questions.q: What is the Benguela Current?
options: A warm current flowing south along the east coast
A hot wind from the interior
A cold current flowing north along the west coast
A river that irrigates the Breede River Valley
questions.explain: The Benguela Current carries cold water north from the Antarctic along the west coast, cooling the vineyards near the sea.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of the Cape Doctor for vineyards?
options: It cools vines and keeps the canopy dry, reducing fungal disease
It brings summer rain to dry areas
It protects vines from spring frost
It speeds up ripening in cool areas
questions.explain: The strong, dry south-easterly wind cools the vines and dries the canopy, although it can also damage leaves.

questions.q: Which two grapes are the parents of Pinotage?
questions.explain: Abraham Perold crossed Pinot Noir with Cinsaut, then known in South Africa as Hermitage, in 1925.

questions.q: What was Vin de Constance?
options: A traditional method sparkling wine from Stellenbosch
A fortified red from the Klein Karoo
A dry Sauvignon Blanc from Elgin
A sweet, unfortified Muscat wine from Constantia
questions.explain: Vin de Constance was the sweet Muscat wine of Constantia, famous in Europe in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

questions.q: Which description fits Swartland viticulture?
options: Old bush vines, often without irrigation, on granite and shale
Cool, wet vineyards near the south coast
questions.explain: Swartland is warm and dry, with many old, dry-farmed bush vines on granite and shale soils.

questions.q: What was the old South African name for Chenin Blanc?
questions.explain: Chenin Blanc, the most planted grape in South Africa, was known locally as Steen. Hermitage was the old name for Cinsaut.

lessons.title: Chile: between the Andes and the Pacific
lessons.intro: This lesson shows how Chile's shape, the Andes and the cold Humboldt Current create its climates, how the valleys run from north to south and from the coast to the mountains, and why Carmenère and the coastal valleys of Casablanca and San Antonio matter.

p: Chile is a thin strip of land between the Andes to the east and the Pacific to the west, with the Atacama Desert to the north and the ice fields of Patagonia to the south. These natural barriers have kept phylloxera out, so most Chilean vines grow on their own roots.
The central wine lands have a Mediterranean climate with dry summers. Rain falls mostly in winter, and many vineyards are irrigated with snowmelt from the Andes. Disease pressure is low.

sections.h: The Humboldt Current: coast, middle and mountains
p: The cold Humboldt Current flows north along the coast. It cools the land near the sea and brings morning fog and cloud. A Coastal Range runs parallel to the shore and blocks this influence in many places, except where valleys open towards the sea.

Between the Coastal Range and the Andes lies the Central Valley, the warmest and flattest part, long used for high-yield production. Near the Andes, cold air flows down at night, giving a wide difference between day and night temperatures.
Since 2011 labels can add three terms that describe this east to west contrast: Costa (coast), Entre Cordilleras (between the ranges) and Andes.

sections.h: The valleys from north to south
p: Chile's denominación de origen system divides the country into regions, which are split into subregions, mostly named after river valleys, then zones and areas. The regions from north to south are Atacama, Coquimbo, Aconcagua, Valle Central, Sur and Austral.

In Coquimbo, Elqui and Limarí are dry and bright; Limarí has limestone soils and is known for Chardonnay. Aconcagua includes the Aconcagua Valley itself and the coastal valleys of Casablanca and San Antonio.

Valle Central holds Maipo, home of Chile's classic Cabernet Sauvignon, especially in Alto Maipo at Puente Alto and Pirque; Rapel, divided into Cachapoal and Colchagua; Curicó; and Maule. Further south, Itata and Biobío are cooler and wetter. Maule and Itata are known for old, dry-farmed bush vines of País, Carignan and Cinsault.

Carmenère is an old Bordeaux variety that reached Chile in the nineteenth century. For a long time it was mixed up with Merlot in Chilean vineyards. In 1994 the French ampelographer Jean-Michel Boursiquot identified it, and it became Chile's signature grape.

Carmenère ripens late and needs a warm site and a long season. Picked underripe, it tastes of green pepper. Ripe, it gives deep colour, black fruit, spice and a herbal note. Peumo in Cachapoal and Apalta in Colchagua are well-known sources.

Casablanca, between Santiago and the port of Valparaíso, was developed from the 1980s and was Chile's first major cool coastal valley. Morning fog and sea breezes keep it cool. Frost and scarce water are its main problems. It is known for Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

San Antonio lies just to the south and closer to the sea. It was planted from the late 1990s and is cooler still. Its best-known zone is Leyda. Sauvignon Blanc here is crisp, citrusy and herbal, and Pinot Noir and cool-climate Syrah also do well.

key: Natural barriers have kept phylloxera out of Chile, so most vines are ungrafted.
The cold Humboldt Current flows north along the coast, bringing fog and cooling.
Since 2011 labels may add Costa, Entre Cordilleras or Andes.
Carmenère was confused with Merlot until it was identified in 1994.
Casablanca (from the 1980s) and San Antonio with Leyda (from the late 1990s) are the key cool coastal valleys.
Maule and Itata hold old dry-farmed País, Carignan and Cinsault.

questions.q: Why are most Chilean vines planted on their own roots?
options: Phylloxera has never reached Chile because of its natural barriers
Chilean soils are too rich for phylloxera
Vines were replanted on own roots after phylloxera in the 1990s
questions.explain: The Andes, the Pacific, the Atacama and the southern ice fields have kept phylloxera out.

questions.q: What does the Humboldt Current do?
options: It brings warm tropical water south
It carries snowmelt from the Andes to the vineyards
It flows north along the coast and cools it, bringing fog
It brings hot winds over the Coastal Range
questions.explain: The cold Humboldt Current flows north and cools the coast, with morning fog and cloud.

questions.q: Which three terms can Chilean labels use since 2011 to describe an east to west position?
questions.explain: Costa, Entre Cordilleras and Andes describe the coast, the area between the ranges and the mountain side.

questions.q: Which grape was Carmenère long confused with in Chile?
questions.explain: Carmenère grew mixed with Merlot until Jean-Michel Boursiquot identified it in 1994.

questions.q: When was the Casablanca Valley first developed for wine?
questions.explain: Casablanca was developed from the 1980s as Chile's first major cool coastal valley.

questions.q: Leyda is part of which Chilean valley?
questions.explain: Leyda is the best-known zone of the San Antonio Valley, south of Casablanca and close to the sea.

questions.q: Which northern valley has limestone soils and is known for Chardonnay?
questions.explain: Limarí, in the Coquimbo region, has limestone soils and a reputation for Chardonnay.

questions.q: Maule and Itata are known for which kind of vineyards?
options: Young irrigated Sauvignon Blanc on the coast
Old, dry-farmed bush vines of País, Carignan and Cinsault
questions.explain: These southern areas hold old, unirrigated bush vines of País, Carignan and Cinsault.

lessons.title: Argentina: altitude, Malbec and Torrontés
lessons.intro: This lesson explains how altitude and a desert climate shape Argentine wine, then visits Mendoza and the Valle de Uco, the high Calchaquí Valleys of Salta, and Patagonia, with the two grapes most linked to the country: Malbec and Torrontés.

p: Most Argentine vineyards lie east of the Andes, in their rain shadow. The climate is continental and very dry, so vines depend on irrigation with Andean snowmelt. Dry air keeps disease pressure low.

Altitude is the key factor. Higher vineyards are cooler, have a wide difference between day and night temperatures, and receive intense sunlight. This gives thick-skinned grapes with deep colour while keeping acidity. Hazards include hail, so many vineyards use nets, and the Zonda, a hot, dry wind from the Andes that can damage flowering in spring.
A 1999 law set three tiers of origin: Indicación de Procedencia (IP), Indicación Geográfica (IG) and Denominación de Origen Controlada (DOC). Luján de Cuyo and San Rafael are the DOCs.

Mendoza is by far the largest wine province. Its traditional heart for fine wine, known as the Primera Zona, lies just south of the city in Luján de Cuyo and Maipú, with areas such as Agrelo, Vistalba, Las Compuertas and Lunlunta. East Mendoza is lower and warmer and makes large volumes. San Rafael lies to the south.

Malbec came from south-west France. In the mid-nineteenth century the French agronomist Michel Aimé Pouget brought French varieties, Malbec among them, to Mendoza. Argentine Malbec is deeply coloured, with plum, blackberry and violet aromas and soft, ripe tannins. Bonarda is the second red grape.

The Valle de Uco lies south-west of Mendoza city, at the foot of the Andes. It covers three departments: Tupungato, Tunuyán and San Carlos. Its vineyards are higher and cooler than the Primera Zona, on stony alluvial soils, some with calcareous deposits.

Malbec from Uco tends to have fresher acidity, more floral notes and finer tannins. Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Cabernet Franc also do well. Several smaller geographical indications are now used on labels, including Paraje Altamira and La Consulta in San Carlos, and Los Chacayes, Vista Flores and San Pablo in Tunuyán.

sections.h: Salta, the Calchaquí Valleys and Torrontés
p: Salta lies in the far north, close to the tropics, where only altitude makes quality wine possible. Its vineyards sit in the Calchaquí Valleys, with Cafayate as the main centre. Some vineyards in Salta are above 3,000 m, among the highest in the world. Soils are sandy and poor, and sunlight is intense.

Torrontés is Argentina's signature white. There are three types; Torrontés Riojano is the most planted and the finest. It is a crossing of Muscat of Alexandria and Criolla Chica. It gives aromatic, usually dry wines with floral and peach notes. Cafayate is its best-known source. Salta also makes powerful Malbec.

Patagonia, in the south, takes a different route to freshness. Its vineyards are at much lower altitude than Mendoza or Salta, and it is latitude that keeps them cool. The climate is dry and windy, with a wide difference between day and night temperatures.

Río Negro has a long history, with old vineyards in the Alto Valle. Neuquén was developed more recently. Pinot Noir, Malbec and Merlot are the main reds. Chubut, further south, has some of the most southerly vineyards in the country.

key: Argentine vineyards lie in the Andean rain shadow, are irrigated with snowmelt and owe their freshness to altitude.
Hail and the hot, dry Zonda wind are the main climatic hazards.
The Primera Zona is Luján de Cuyo and Maipú; Luján de Cuyo and San Rafael are DOCs.
The Valle de Uco covers Tupungato, Tunuyán and San Carlos, with higher, cooler vineyards.
Torrontés Riojano is a crossing of Muscat of Alexandria and Criolla Chica; Cafayate in Salta is its home.
Patagonia is cool because of latitude, not altitude.

questions.q: What is the Zonda?
options: A cold current off the Pacific coast
A hot, dry wind from the Andes
questions.explain: The Zonda is a hot, dry wind that comes down from the Andes and can damage flowering in spring.

questions.q: Which effect does high altitude have on Argentine vineyards?
options: Cooler temperatures and a wide day to night range
questions.explain: Higher vineyards are cooler, with big day to night differences and intense sunlight, which keeps acidity and builds colour.

questions.q: Which three departments make up the Valle de Uco?
options: Luján de Cuyo, Maipú and San Rafael
questions.explain: The Valle de Uco covers Tupungato, Tunuyán and San Carlos, south-west of Mendoza city.

questions.q: Paraje Altamira lies in which department of the Valle de Uco?
questions.explain: Paraje Altamira, like La Consulta, is in San Carlos.

questions.q: Which type of Torrontés is the most planted and gives the finest wines?
questions.explain: Torrontés Riojano is the most planted and the finest of the three Argentine types.

questions.q: Torrontés Riojano is a crossing of which two grapes?
options: Muscat of Alexandria and Criolla Chica
questions.explain: DNA work shows Torrontés Riojano is a cross of Muscat of Alexandria and Criolla Chica, which explains its floral, Muscat-like aroma.

questions.q: What keeps Patagonian vineyards cool?
questions.explain: Patagonian vineyards are at lower altitude than Mendoza; their freshness comes from latitude.

questions.q: Cafayate is the main wine centre of which area?
options: The Valle de Uco in Mendoza
The Alto Valle de Río Negro
The Tulum Valley in San Juan
questions.explain: Cafayate is the hub of the high Calchaquí Valleys in Salta, home of Argentina's best Torrontés.
